It slows your heart and helps your body calm down.

days.guide: Make a glitter calm-down jar; watch it settle while breathing.

questions.q: How is the jar like your feelings?
questions.a: Shaken glitter is like upset feelings; as you breathe, it settles and you calm down.
Until most glitter settles.

days.guide: Do a GoNoodle Flow video; tell how your body feels after.

questions.a: Calmer, slower, relaxed.
When feeling upset, worried, or wiggly.

days.guide: Set up a calm corner with 3 tools.

questions.a: Calm-down jar, pillow, feelings chart.
When you feel big feelings and need to calm down.

days.guide: Role-play a frustrating moment (tower falls) and use a strategy.

questions.q: Your tower fell. What can you do?
questions.a: Take 3 belly breaths, use the calm jar, then try again or ask for help.

questions.q: Is it okay to feel frustrated?
questions.a: Yes — it's what we do next that matters.

weeks.assessment_key: Rubric: 4 = names the feeling, chooses a calm-down strategy (belly breathing, calm jar, calm corner), uses it correctly, then names a next step; 3 = uses strategy with prompting; 2 = names strategy but doesn't use it; 1 = does not use a strategy.

weeks.prep: A sentence-frame card ('I feel ___ when ___. I need ___.'), paper for a hand outline, and phone numbers of trusted adults.
misconceptions: Blaming in I-messages ('I feel mad when YOU are mean'): describe the action, not the person.
Thinking asking for help is babyish: everyone asks for help.
Thinking any adult is a trusted adult: trusted adults are people your family knows and trusts.

days.guide: Learn the I-message frame; practice with 3 problems.

questions.q: Your sister takes your crayon. Make an I-message.
questions.a: I feel upset when you take my crayon. I need you to ask first.
They tell your feelings calmly without blaming.

days.guide: Practice good listening while a family member shares.

questions.q: What are the three parts of good listening?
questions.a: Eyes on the speaker, ears listening, quiet body.

questions.q: How do you show you listened?
questions.a: Repeat back or ask a question about it.

days.guide: Trace your hand; write a trusted adult on each finger.

questions.a: A grown-up your family trusts who keeps you safe — parent, grandparent, teacher, doctor.
Answers vary.

days.guide: Role-play asking a trusted adult for help when lost, hurt, or sad.

questions.q: You're lost in a store. Who can you ask?
questions.a: A store worker at the counter or a parent with kids.
I'm lost. Can you help me find my mom/dad?

days.guide: Your child uses an I-message to solve a pretend problem.

questions.q: Problem: friend won't share the swing.
questions.a: I feel sad when I don't get a turn. I need us to take turns.

questions.q: What's the last part of an I-message?
questions.a: I need ___.

weeks.assessment_key: Rubric: 4 = complete I-message with feeling, specific action, and need, said calmly; trusted adults hand has 5 appropriate names; 3 = I-message missing one part; 2 = blames instead; 1 = cannot form an I-message.

weeks.prep: 'Last Stop on Market Street' by Matt de la Peña (library) and recipe-card paper.
misconceptions: Thinking kindness means only big gestures: small acts count.
Thinking people who are different can't be friends: differences make friendships interesting.
Waiting for others to include you: you can be the one to invite.

days.guide: Read 'Last Stop on Market Street'; discuss how CJ learns to see beauty.

questions.q: Where are CJ and Nana going?
questions.a: On the bus to the last stop on Market Street to help at a soup kitchen.

questions.q: What does Nana help CJ notice?
questions.a: Beauty in everyday things — music from the man with the guitar, the people on the bus, the city.

questions.q: How does CJ feel at the end?
questions.a: Glad they came.

days.guide: List 3 ways you are the same as and 3 ways different from a friend.

questions.q: Name a way you're the same.
questions.a: Example: we both like soccer.
Example: we speak different languages at home.

days.guide: Do one kind act each day; record it.

questions.a: Helping a sibling, saying something nice, sharing.

questions.q: How do kind acts make others feel?
questions.a: Happy, cared for.

days.guide: Role-play inviting someone new to play.

questions.a: Hi, I'm ___. Do you want to play with us?
So no one feels left out.

days.guide: Make a 'kindness recipe' card with 4 ingredients.

questions.a: 1 cup sharing, 2 spoons of smiles, a pinch of patience, a bowl of helping.
A kind friend.

weeks.assessment_key: Rubric: 4 = card names 4 specific kind actions (sharing, including, helping, kind words) with a creative recipe format; 3 = 3 ingredients; 2 = 1–2; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: A conflict-resolution poster (Stop, Talk, Listen, Solve), stuffed animals, and teasing vs. bullying scenario cards. Note: bullying talk may bring up your child's own experiences — listen calmly.
misconceptions: Thinking every mean moment is bullying: bullying is mean on purpose and repeated, often with a power difference.
Thinking you should fight back: say 'Stop!' firmly, walk away, and tell a trusted adult.
Thinking telling an adult is tattling: telling to get someone out of trouble or keep them safe is reporting.

days.guide: Learn Stop, Talk, Listen, Solve; act it out with stuffed animals.

questions.q: What do you do first in a conflict?
questions.a: Stop and calm down.
Listen, then solve together.

days.guide: Practice taking turns or sharing to solve a toy conflict.

questions.q: Two kids want the same truck. Name a solution.
questions.a: Take turns with a timer, or play together.
Each person gives a little so both are okay.

days.guide: Learn that bullying is mean on purpose and repeated; sort cards.

questions.q: A kid bumps you by accident once. Bullying?
questions.a: No — it was an accident.

questions.q: A kid calls you names every day on purpose. Bullying?
questions.a: Yes — mean on purpose and repeated.

days.guide: Role-play saying 'Stop!' and getting a trusted adult.

questions.a: Someone who helps when they see bullying.
Say 'Stop, that's not kind,' help the person get away, and tell an adult.

days.guide: Give the Unit 1 assessment.

questions.a: Happy, sad, angry (any).
Belly breathing, calm jar.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 1 assessment: 1) Names 4 feelings from face cards 2) Demonstrates a calm-down tool correctly 3) Solves a scenario ('Your brother knocked over your blocks') with Stop–Talk–Listen–Solve and an I-message 4) Says what to do about bullying (say stop, walk away, tell a trusted adult). Proficient = all 4.

weeks.prep: Lotion, glitter, a spray bottle with water, paper towels, disinfectant wipes (adult use), and a KidsHealth article on germs (kidshealth.org/kids).
misconceptions: Thinking germs are only on dirty-looking things: germs are too small to see.
Sneezing into hands: hands then spread germs; sneeze into your elbow or a tissue.
Thinking all germs are harmful: some germs make us sick; many tiny living things are harmless or helpful.

days.guide: Put lotion and glitter on hands; shake hands with family and see 'germs' spread.

questions.a: How germs spread from hand to hand.

questions.q: Why can't we see real germs?
questions.a: They're too tiny — you need a microscope.

days.guide: Use a spray bottle to show how far a sneeze travels; practice the elbow sneeze.

questions.q: How far can a sneeze spray?
questions.a: Several feet (across a room).
Into your elbow or a tissue.

days.guide: Find germ hideouts and wipe them with an adult.

questions.a: Doorknobs, phones, remotes, faucet handles.
An adult (or with an adult helping).

days.guide: Read a KidsHealth article on germs.

questions.q: How do germs get into our bodies?
questions.a: Through mouth, nose, eyes, and cuts.
Colds, flu, stomach bugs.

days.guide: Your child explains 3 ways to stop germs and shows the elbow sneeze.

questions.a: Wash hands, sneeze/cough into elbow, keep hands away from face.
Cover nose and mouth with inside of elbow.

weeks.assessment_key: Rubric: 4 = names 3 correct ways (wash hands, sneeze/cough into elbow or tissue, keep hands away from face/eyes/mouth) and demonstrates elbow sneeze; 3 = 2 ways; 2 = 1 way; 1 = none.

weeks.prep: Soap, a bowl of water with black pepper, a timer, poster paper, lotion with glitter.
misconceptions: Washing too fast: scrub for 20 seconds (sing 'Happy Birthday' twice).
Skipping backs of hands, between fingers, and under nails.
Thinking water alone cleans hands: soap is needed to lift germs off.

days.guide: Sprinkle pepper on water; touch with a soapy finger.

questions.a: It moved away from the soapy finger.
Soap helps push away and lift off germs.

days.guide: Learn six handwashing steps; sing 'Happy Birthday' twice.

questions.a: 1) Wet hands 2) Add soap 3) Scrub 20 seconds — palms, backs, between fingers, under nails 4) Rinse 5) Dry with a clean towel 6) Turn off faucet with the towel.
20 seconds.

days.guide: Make a poster of times to wash.

questions.a: Before eating, after using the bathroom, after coughing/sneezing, after playing outside, after touching pets.
Yes.

days.guide: Rub on lotion with glitter, wash, and check what's left.

questions.a: Often under nails, between fingers, thumbs.

questions.q: What does leftover glitter tell you?
questions.a: Those spots need more scrubbing.

days.guide: Your child demonstrates all steps.

questions.a: Wet, soap, scrub 20 seconds, rinse, dry, turn off faucet with towel.
Wet hands spread germs more easily.

weeks.assessment_key: Demonstration checklist (1 point each): wets hands; uses soap; scrubs palms; backs; between fingers; under nails/thumbs; scrubs at least 20 seconds; rinses; dries with clean towel; turns off faucet with towel. Proficient 9–10.

weeks.prep: A toothbrush and toothpaste, floss, a hard-boiled egg (white shell), a cup of cola, a 2-minute timer, play-dough, and food cards (apple, cheese, carrots, candy, raisins, soda, crackers, milk).
misconceptions: Brushing for only a few seconds: brush 2 minutes, twice a day.
Thinking only sugar from candy hurts teeth: sticky snacks and sugary drinks count too.
Skipping the back teeth: brush outer, inner, and chewing surfaces of every tooth.

days.guide: Place an egg in cola overnight. Next day, brush the stain.

questions.a: It turned brown from the cola.
Removes stains and plaque from teeth.

days.guide: Practice brushing in circles 2 minutes on all surfaces.

questions.a: 2 minutes.
Twice a day — morning and bedtime.

days.guide: Practice flossing with help; use a play-dough teeth model.

questions.a: To clean between teeth where the brush can't reach.
Once a day.

days.guide: Sort foods into tooth-friendly and sticky/sugary.

questions.a: Yes.
No — sticky/sugary.

days.guide: Fill in a 1-week brushing chart; explain dentist visits.

questions.a: To clean teeth and check for cavities.
About every 6 months.

weeks.assessment_key: Brushing chart: proficient = 14 checks (morning and night for 7 days) or close; explanation: 'The dentist cleans teeth and checks for cavities about every 6 months.' Sort: tooth-friendly — apple, cheese, carrots, milk; sticky/sugary — candy, raisins, soda, crackers.

weeks.prep: Paper for a routine chart and a sleep log (bedtime, wake time). A bedtime picture book (e.g., 'Goodnight Moon').
misconceptions: Thinking kids need the same sleep as adults: 6–12-year-olds need about 9–12 hours.
Thinking screens before bed help you relax: screen light can make it harder to fall asleep.
Thinking you can 'catch up' on sleep easily: regular bedtimes are best.

days.guide: Learn that 6-year-olds need about 9–12 hours of sleep and why.

questions.q: How much sleep do you need?
questions.a: About 9–12 hours each night.
Body rests, grows, and brain stores learning.

days.guide: Start a sleep log.

questions.a: 11 hours.
10 hours.

days.guide: Make a picture chart for a calm bedtime routine.

questions.a: Bath, pajamas, brush teeth, story, lights out.
Screen light can keep you awake.

days.guide: Read a bedtime picture book; discuss rest.

questions.q: How does the book show getting ready for sleep?
questions.a: Answers vary by book (e.g., 'Goodnight Moon' — saying goodnight to things in the room as it gets darker).
Dark, quiet, calm routine.

days.guide: Review the log; explain how you feel with good sleep.

questions.q: How do you feel after good sleep?
questions.a: Energetic, happy, able to focus.
Tired, grumpy.

weeks.assessment_key: Rubric: 4 = complete 7-day log with hours calculated (goal 9–12 hours) and routine chart with 4+ calm steps; 3 = log mostly complete; 2 = incomplete; 1 = missing.

weeks.prep: Poster board, markers, a recycling bin, and a 5-day habit tracker (handwashing, brushing, sleep).
misconceptions: Thinking healthy habits are only about yourself: clean spaces and recycling help everyone.
Teaching handwashing steps out of order: follow the poster.
Stopping the tracker after one day: habits form with daily practice.

days.guide: Make a handwashing poster for the bathroom.

questions.a: The handwashing steps and 20 seconds.
Near the sink.

days.guide: Teach a younger sibling or friend handwashing.

questions.a: Show each step and sing 'Happy Birthday' twice.

questions.q: How do you check they did it right?
questions.a: Watch for soap, all surfaces, 20 seconds.

days.guide: Sort recycling; discuss how clean places keep us healthy.

questions.a: Paper, cardboard, plastic bottles, cans (check local rules).

questions.q: How do clean places help health?
questions.a: Less trash means fewer germs and pests.

days.guide: Track handwashing, brushing, sleep for 5 days.

questions.q: How many brushing checks in 5 days (twice a day)?

questions.a: To see if you're building the habit.

days.guide: Give the Unit 2 assessment.

questions.q: How long should you scrub hands?
questions.a: 20 seconds.

questions.q: How much sleep do you need?
questions.a: About 9–12 hours.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 2 test (suggested): 1) Germs are too small to see 2) Stop germs: wash hands, sneeze in elbow, hands away from face 3) Scrub 20 seconds 4) Wash before eating and after bathroom 5) Brush teeth 2 minutes twice a day 6) Floss once a day 7) Visit dentist about every 6 months 8) Sleep 9–12 hours. Proficient 7–8.

weeks.prep: A MyPlate printout (myplate.gov), grocery ads, scissors, glue, a paper plate divided into 5 sections, and 15 food cards.
misconceptions: Putting potatoes or corn in the grains group: they're vegetables (starchy).
Thinking beans are only vegetables: beans count as vegetables or protein.
Thinking cheese and yogurt are protein only: they're in the dairy group.

days.guide: Look at MyPlate; name 5 food groups and their colors.

questions.a: Fruits, vegetables, grains, protein, dairy.

questions.q: What color is vegetables on MyPlate?
questions.a: Green.

days.guide: Cut foods from ads and sort them on a paper-plate MyPlate.

questions.a: Grains.
Protein.

days.guide: Find one food from each group in the kitchen.

questions.a: Milk, yogurt, cheese.
Rice, oatmeal, pasta.

days.guide: Check today's lunch for food groups.

questions.q: A turkey sandwich, apple, milk — which groups?
questions.a: Grains (bread), protein (turkey), fruit (apple), dairy (milk).
Vegetables.

days.guide: Sort 15 food cards.

questions.a: Fruit.
Vegetable.

weeks.assessment_key: Sort key (suggested 15): Fruits — apple, banana, orange; Vegetables — carrot, broccoli, corn; Grains — bread, rice, oatmeal; Protein — chicken, eggs, beans (also accepted as vegetables); Dairy — milk, cheese, yogurt. Proficient 14–15.

weeks.prep: 4 fruits/vegetables of different colors (e.g., red strawberries, orange carrots, green cucumber, purple grapes — cut grapes for young children), a colander, a rainbow chart, and 'Eating the Alphabet' by Lois Ehlert (library). Check for food allergies.
misconceptions: Thinking fruits and vegetables are all the same nutritionally: different colors give different vitamins.
Washing produce with soap: rinse under running water only.
Thinking you dislike a food after one taste: it can take many tries.

days.guide: Taste 4 colorful fruits/vegetables; describe them.

questions.a: Crunchy, sweet, orange.
Answers vary.

days.guide: Wash produce properly.

questions.a: Rinse under cool running water and rub with hands; no soap.
To remove dirt and germs.

days.guide: Track eating red, orange, yellow, green, purple foods this week.

questions.a: Grapes, eggplant, plums, purple cabbage.
Banana, corn, yellow pepper.

days.guide: Read 'Eating the Alphabet.'

questions.a: Fruits and vegetables for every letter A to Z.

questions.q: Name a fruit or vegetable for A.
questions.a: Apple, apricot, artichoke, avocado, asparagus.

days.guide: Your child explains why we eat many colors.

questions.a: Different colors have different vitamins and nutrients that help our bodies.

questions.q: How many colors did you eat this week?
questions.a: Read from chart.

weeks.assessment_key: Rainbow chart: proficient = at least one food in each of the 5 colors during the week, plus explanation 'Different colors give our bodies different vitamins/nutrients.'

weeks.prep: Sugar cubes (each about 4 grams), a can of soda, a carton of milk, a water bottle, snack items (pairs: apple vs. candy, yogurt vs. cookies), celery, peanut/sun butter, raisins. Check allergies.
misconceptions: Thinking juice and soda are healthy because they're drinks: they often have lots of sugar; water is best.
Skipping breakfast: breakfast gives energy to learn.
Thinking 'healthy' means tasteless: many healthy snacks are delicious.

days.guide: Count sugar cubes in soda vs. milk vs. water.

questions.q: About how many sugar cubes in a 12-ounce can of soda?
questions.a: About 10 (about 39 grams of sugar).
Zero.

days.guide: Discuss why breakfast fuels the brain; plan a healthy breakfast.

questions.a: It gives energy to think, learn, and play.
Example: oatmeal, banana, milk.

days.guide: Use 'stop, think, choose' between snack pairs.

questions.a: Apple — it has vitamins and fiber.
Water.

days.guide: Make ants-on-a-log or fruit-and-yogurt.

questions.q: What food groups are in ants-on-a-log?
questions.a: Vegetable (celery), protein (nut/seed butter), fruit (raisins).
Yes — fruit and dairy.

days.guide: Your child chooses 3 healthy snacks and explains why.

questions.a: Apple slices, carrot sticks, cheese, yogurt.
They come from food groups and don't have lots of added sugar.

weeks.assessment_key: Rubric: 4 = names 3 healthy snacks from food groups and explains (vitamins, energy, low added sugar); 3 = 2 snacks; 2 = 1; 1 = sugary choices with no reasons.

weeks.prep: Cereal boxes, magazine ads, a recorded kids' food commercial, and paper and markers.
misconceptions: Believing everything in ads: ads try to make you want to buy.
Thinking cartoon characters mean a food is good for you: check the food, not the character.
Thinking family food traditions are unhealthy: many traditional foods are healthy; balance is key.

days.guide: Look at cereal boxes for cartoons and colors.

questions.a: To attract kids.

questions.q: Where is the cereal placed in stores?
questions.a: Often at kids' eye level.

days.guide: Watch a kid's food commercial; discuss tricks.

questions.a: Fun music, toys, cartoons, kids having fun.

questions.q: Does the ad say if the food is healthy?
questions.a: Not always.

days.guide: Interview a family member about family foods and traditions.

questions.q: Ask: what food did you eat growing up?
questions.a: Answers vary.

questions.q: Why do families have food traditions?
questions.a: To celebrate, remember culture, share.

days.guide: Make an ad for a fruit or vegetable.

questions.a: Bright picture, catchy words, reasons to eat it.
Crunch into carrots — super snack for super eyes!

days.guide: Your child explains one influence on food choices.

questions.a: Ads, family, friends, culture, taste.
Example: I wanted cereal because of the cartoon.

weeks.assessment_key: Ad rubric: 4 = ad for a fruit/vegetable with picture, catchy slogan, and a true health reason (e.g., 'carrots have vitamins for healthy eyes'), plus explanation of one influence; 3 = missing reason; 2 = unclear; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Kitchen tools, a recipe card for a simple wrap or salad, a refrigerator thermometer (optional), and produce. Adult handles knives and stove.
misconceptions: Leaving milk or meat out on the counter: cold foods go back in the fridge quickly (within 2 hours).
Touching knives or hot pans: these are adult jobs.
Skipping handwashing before cooking: always wash first.

days.guide: Wash hands and produce before cooking.

questions.a: Wash hands with soap.
Rinse under running water.

days.guide: Learn some foods must stay cold.

questions.q: Name a food that stays cold.
questions.a: Milk, yogurt, meat, cheese.
Germs grow fast in warm food.

days.guide: Make a simple MyPlate wrap or salad with an adult.

questions.q: What groups are in a turkey-cheese-lettuce wrap?
questions.a: Grain, protein, dairy, vegetable.

questions.q: What can you add for fruit?
questions.a: Apple slices on the side.

days.guide: Learn knife, stove, and hot-pan rules.

questions.a: Adults (or kids only with close adult help and a kid-safe knife).

questions.q: What do you do near a hot stove?
questions.a: Stay back; let adults handle it; turn pot handles inward.

days.guide: Your child explains 3 kitchen safety rules.

questions.a: Wash hands, adults handle knives/stove, keep cold foods cold.
Tell an adult and clean it up so no one slips.

weeks.assessment_key: Rubric: 4 = explains 3 correct rules (wash hands/produce; adults use knives, stove, hot pans; refrigerate cold foods; wipe spills) with reasons; 3 = 2 rules; 2 = 1; 1 = none.

weeks.prep: A goal chart, stickers, a MyPlate printout for menu planning, and paper for a grocery list.
misconceptions: Picking a goal that's too big: start small ('eat a vegetable at dinner').
Giving up after a missed day: keep going the next day.
Menus with no vegetables: check each meal for food groups.

days.guide: Choose a healthy eating goal.

questions.a: Eat a vegetable at every dinner.
Easier to do and stick with.

days.guide: Track the goal with stickers.

questions.a: You met the goal that day.

questions.q: What if you miss a day?
questions.a: Try again tomorrow.

days.guide: Plan one day's meals using MyPlate.

questions.a: Chicken, rice, broccoli, milk, orange slices.
Protein, grain, vegetable, dairy, fruit.

days.guide: Write a grocery list with foods from each group.

questions.a: Apples, carrots, bread, eggs, yogurt.
To buy healthy foods and not forget.

days.guide: Give the Unit 3 assessment.

questions.a: Fruits, vegetables, grains, protein, dairy.
Count stickers.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 3 test: sort 10 foods (apple-fruit, carrot-vegetable, rice-grain, fish-protein, yogurt-dairy, grapes-fruit, spinach-vegetable, bread-grain, beans-protein/vegetable, cheese-dairy) and label a blank MyPlate with 5 groups. Proficient 14–15 of 15 plus a goal reflection ('I met my goal 5 of 7 days').

weeks.prep: A timer, a jump rope, paper for an activity log.
misconceptions: Thinking only sports count as activity: dancing, walking, playing tag count.
Thinking a faster heartbeat is bad: it shows the heart is working and getting stronger.
Thinking 60 minutes must be all at once: it can be added up through the day.

days.guide: Feel heartbeat and breathing before and after 1 minute of jumping.

questions.a: It got faster.
Muscles need more oxygen, so the heart pumps faster.

days.guide: List how activity helps heart, muscles, bones, mood.

questions.q: How does activity help the heart?
questions.a: Makes it stronger.
Makes you feel happier and calmer.

days.guide: Learn kids need 60 minutes of activity daily; brainstorm.

questions.q: How many minutes of activity daily?
questions.a: At least 60.
Biking, dancing, tag, swimming, jumping rope.

days.guide: Start an activity log with drawings and minutes.

questions.q: You biked 20 minutes and played tag 15 minutes. Total?
questions.a: 35 minutes.

days.guide: Your child explains 3 benefits.

questions.a: Strong heart, strong muscles and bones, better mood/sleep.

questions.q: Which activity makes your heart beat fastest?
questions.a: Answers vary — e.g., running.

weeks.assessment_key: Rubric: 4 = names 3 correct benefits (stronger heart/lungs, stronger muscles and bones, better mood, better sleep, healthy weight) with an example; 3 = 2; 2 = 1; 1 = none.

weeks.prep: Activity log, a timer, and a list of active swaps.
misconceptions: Thinking all screen time is bad: balance matters; choose active play often.
Not counting all screens: TV, tablets, phones, and video games all count.
Thinking activity must be outside: indoor dancing and stretching count.

days.guide: Count screen minutes for a day.

questions.a: TV, tablets, phones, computers, video games.

questions.q: If you watched 30 minutes of TV and played 20 minutes of games, total?
questions.a: 50 minutes.

days.guide: Make a list of active swaps.

questions.a: Dance party, bike ride, jump rope, build a fort.

questions.q: When can you use a swap?
questions.a: When you feel bored or want a screen.

days.guide: Play outside 30 minutes with a family member.

questions.a: Answers vary.
Answers vary — often happy, tired.

days.guide: Take a family walk after dinner.

questions.a: Helps digestion and is family time.
Answers vary.

days.guide: Compare active and screen minutes.

questions.a: Answers vary — aim for more active.
Use active swaps.

weeks.assessment_key: Rubric: 4 = log records screen and active minutes for at least 3 days, compares them correctly, and names 2 active swaps; 3 = mostly complete; 2 = partial; 1 = missing.

weeks.prep: A goal chart with 7 boxes, crayons, and equipment for a new activity (scooter, hopscotch chalk, swimming access).
misconceptions: Choosing a goal you can't control: choose something you can do daily.
Forgetting to record: color the box right after the activity.
Only doing favorite activities: trying new ones builds skills.

days.guide: Choose a goal like 'play outside 30 minutes every day.'

questions.a: Play outside 30 minutes every day.
To remember and track it.

days.guide: Color a box each day you meet the goal; note the activity.

questions.q: If you colored 5 of 7 boxes, how many days did you miss?
What activity did you do today?
questions.a: Answers vary.

days.guide: Try a new activity.

questions.a: Answers vary.

questions.q: Was it hard or easy at first?
questions.a: Answers vary; new skills take practice.

days.guide: Invite a family member to join.

questions.a: Makes it more fun and helps you remember.
Answers vary.

days.guide: Count boxes; tell if you met the goal; name 3 benefits.

questions.a: Based on boxes.
Strong heart, strong muscles, good mood.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 4 rubric: 4 = goal chart with boxes colored and activities named, honest reflection on meeting the goal, and 3 correct benefits; 3 = 2 benefits; 2 = incomplete chart; 1 = missing.

weeks.prep: A blindfold (or closed eyes), spices (cinnamon, garlic powder, mint, vanilla), a box with 6 textured objects (sponge, spoon, pinecone, cotton ball, rock, feather), and sweet/salty/sour foods (honey, pretzels, lemon). Check allergies.
misconceptions: Thinking the tongue is the only part used for flavor: smell helps us taste too.
Smelling strong spices too close: waft gently toward your nose.
Thinking skin is not a sense organ: skin senses touch, heat, cold, pain.

days.guide: Name the five senses and body parts.

questions.q: Name the senses and body parts.
questions.a: Sight–eyes, hearing–ears, smell–nose, taste–tongue, touch–skin.
Skin.

days.guide: Guess spices by smell with eyes closed.

questions.a: Wave the smell toward your nose; don't sniff deeply.
Smell.

days.guide: Identify 6 objects by touch; describe textures.

questions.a: Rough, bumpy, pointy.
Soft, fluffy.

days.guide: Taste sweet, salty, sour foods.

questions.a: Sour.
Salty.

days.guide: Label a body diagram with sense organs.

questions.a: Ears.
Skin.

weeks.assessment_key: Diagram key: eyes — sight; ears — hearing; nose — smell; tongue — taste; skin — touch. Proficient 5/5 labels correct.

weeks.prep: Butcher paper, crayons, a plastic bottle, two balloons, a rubber band, scissors (adult cuts the bottle), and tape.
misconceptions: Thinking the heart is on the left side of the chest like a valentine: it's near the center, tilted slightly left, and shaped like a fist.
Thinking the stomach is where your belly button is: it's higher, under the left ribs.
Thinking the brain only thinks: it controls everything — moving, breathing, heartbeat, feelings.

days.guide: Trace your child's body on butcher paper.

questions.a: To draw organs in the right places.

questions.q: Where is your head on the outline?
questions.a: At the top.

days.guide: Draw and label heart, lungs, brain, stomach.

questions.a: In the chest, between the lungs, slightly left.
In the chest, on both sides of the heart.

days.guide: Make a lung model with a bottle and balloons; pull the bottom balloon.

questions.q: What happens when you pull the bottom balloon?
questions.a: The balloon inside fills with air, like lungs breathing in.

questions.q: What does the bottom balloon act like?
questions.a: The diaphragm muscle.

days.guide: Learn the brain sends messages; play a reaction game (drop and catch a ruler).

questions.a: Controls the body, thinks, sends messages through nerves.

questions.q: How did the brain help you catch the ruler?
questions.a: Eyes saw it drop; brain told hand to catch.

days.guide: Your child points to each organ and tells its job.

questions.a: Pumps blood around the body.
Breaks down (digests) food.

weeks.assessment_key: Outline rubric: 4 = brain (head; controls body), heart (chest; pumps blood), lungs (chest, both sides; breathe air in and out), stomach (upper belly, left side; digests food) drawn in correct places with correct jobs; 3 = one error; 2 = two; 1 = several.

weeks.prep: Your child's baby photos and current photos, a measuring tape, and paper for a timeline.
misconceptions: Thinking growing only means getting taller: we also grow skills, teeth, and abilities.
Comparing growth with others in a hurtful way: everyone grows at their own pace.
Thinking growth stops at 6: you'll keep growing until you're grown up.

days.guide: Compare baby photos and current photos.

questions.a: Taller, more hair, more teeth, can walk and talk.
Answers vary — e.g., eye color.

days.guide: Measure height and hand size; compare with family.

questions.a: Answers vary.
Yes — as you grow.

days.guide: Make a life timeline: baby, toddler, now, grown-up.

questions.a: Cry, drink milk, sleep.
Drive, work, take care of others.

days.guide: List things you can do now you couldn't as a baby.

questions.a: Walk, talk, read, ride a bike.
Answers vary.

days.guide: Your child explains 3 ways they've grown and changed.

questions.a: Taller, can read, lost baby teeth.
Answers vary.

weeks.assessment_key: Timeline rubric: 4 = 4 stages in order (baby, toddler, now, grown-up) with drawings and 3 accurate growth changes explained; 3 = 2 changes; 2 = out of order; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: The body outline from week 21, sunglasses, a list of healthy habits, and a Unit 5 assessment sheet.
misconceptions: Thinking loud music can't hurt ears: very loud sounds can damage hearing.
Looking at the sun with sunglasses on: never look directly at the sun.
Thinking growth foods are only meat: protein and dairy come from many foods (beans, eggs, milk, yogurt).

days.guide: Add healthy habits around the body outline.

questions.a: Brush twice a day.
Move 60 minutes a day.

days.guide: Discuss protecting eyes and ears.

questions.q: How do you protect your eyes?
questions.a: Sunglasses, don't look at the sun, safety goggles.

questions.q: How do you protect your ears?
questions.a: Keep volume low; cover ears near very loud noises.

days.guide: Connect protein and dairy to growing.

questions.a: Strong bones and teeth (calcium).
Build muscles.

days.guide: Present the body outline to family.

questions.q: Name a sense and a habit.
questions.a: Eyes — sunglasses.

questions.q: Name an organ and a habit.
questions.a: Heart — exercise.

days.guide: Give the Unit 5 assessment.

questions.a: Eyes, ears, nose, tongue, skin.
Get taller.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 5 test: label 5 sense organs (eyes, ears, nose, tongue, skin) and 4 inner organs (brain, heart, lungs, stomach) and describe one way bodies grow (taller, bigger hands/feet, lose baby teeth). Proficient 9–10 of 10.

weeks.prep: Chalk to draw a crosswalk, a booster seat, and a walk route with crosswalks and a signal.
misconceptions: Looking only one way before crossing: look left, right, then left again.
Crossing between parked cars: drivers can't see you; cross at corners and crosswalks.
Thinking a seat belt alone is safe for a 6-year-old: use a booster seat in the back until the belt fits (usually about 4'9").

days.guide: Practice stop, look left-right-left, listen, and hold an adult's hand.

questions.q: What do you do at the curb?
questions.a: Stop.
Left, right, left.

days.guide: Learn walk/don't walk signals and stop signs.

questions.q: What does the walking person mean?
questions.a: You may cross (still look).

questions.q: What does the flashing hand mean?
questions.a: Don't start crossing.

days.guide: Practice buckling into a booster seat.

questions.q: Where should the lap belt go?
questions.a: Low across the hips/upper thighs, not the tummy.

questions.q: Where should the shoulder belt go?
questions.a: Across the chest and shoulder, not the neck.

days.guide: Walk with an adult and use crosswalks.

questions.a: At crosswalks or corners.
You and the adult.

days.guide: Your child demonstrates safe crossing.

questions.a: Stop at curb, look left-right-left, listen, cross with an adult, keep looking.
To hear cars you can't see.

weeks.assessment_key: Demonstration checklist: stops at curb; looks left, right, left; listens; holds adult's hand; crosses at crosswalk; walks (doesn't run) and keeps looking. Proficient 6/6.

weeks.prep: A bike helmet, a bike or scooter, 2 raw eggs and foam (or a sponge) for an egg 'helmet,' and a park.
misconceptions: Wearing the helmet tipped back: it should sit low on the forehead, two fingers above the eyebrows.
Loose straps: they should form a V under each ear, with one finger of space under the chin strap.
Thinking you only need a helmet for long rides: always wear one.

days.guide: Practice the 2-V-1 helmet fit test.

questions.a: 2 fingers between eyebrows and helmet.
Straps make a V under each ear.
1 finger fits under the chin strap.

days.guide: Drop an egg with and without a foam helmet (outside, low height).

questions.q: What happened to the egg without a helmet?
questions.a: It cracked.
Cushions and protects your head.

days.guide: Ride with a helmet in a safe area.

questions.q: Where is a safe place to ride?
questions.a: Driveway, park path, empty lot with an adult watching.
Closed-toe shoes.

days.guide: List playground rules and practice at a park.

questions.a: Go down the slide feet first; walk around swings; take turns.
So you don't hit your head.

days.guide: Your child puts on the helmet alone and passes 2-V-1; names 2 rules.

questions.a: Two fingers, V under ears, one finger under chin strap.
Take turns; slide feet first.

weeks.assessment_key: Helmet check: 2 fingers above brows ✓, V under each ear ✓, 1 finger under chin strap ✓, buckled snug ✓. Proficient = all 4 done independently plus 2 correct playground rules.

weeks.prep: Your home's smoke alarm (adult tests it), a blanket held up for 'smoke,' paper for a floor plan, and a timer.
misconceptions: Hiding under a bed or in a closet during a fire: get out and stay out.
Going back in for a toy or pet: never go back inside; tell firefighters.
Standing up in smoke: crawl low where the air is cleaner.

days.guide: Listen to the smoke alarm test; learn what to do.

questions.q: What do you do when you hear the alarm?
questions.a: Get out fast and go to the meeting place.

questions.q: How often should adults test alarms?
questions.a: Monthly.

days.guide: Practice stop, drop (cover face), roll, and crawling low.

questions.a: Stop, drop, cover your face, and roll.
Cleaner air is near the floor.

days.guide: Draw a floor plan with two exits from each room and a meeting place.

questions.q: How many ways out of each room?
questions.a: Two (usually a door and a window).
A safe spot outside, like the mailbox or a neighbor's tree.

days.guide: Hold a family fire drill; time it.

questions.q: How fast should everyone get out?
questions.a: As fast as possible — aim for under 2 minutes.

questions.q: Before opening a door, what do you check?
questions.a: Feel it with the back of your hand; if hot, use the other exit.

days.guide: Your child explains the escape plan.

questions.q: Two ways out of your bedroom?
questions.a: Answers vary — door and window.
Go back inside.

weeks.assessment_key: Rubric: 4 = floor plan with 2 exits from each room and a named meeting place; drill completed; explains 'two ways out, meet at ___, never go back inside'; 3 = minor gaps; 2 = only one exit; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: A toy phone, an address card, and situation cards (fire, someone not breathing, a stranger trying to get in vs. a scraped knee, lost toy).
misconceptions: Calling 911 for non-emergencies: 911 is for fires, serious injuries, and danger.
Hanging up early: stay on the line until the operator says to hang up.
Not knowing your address: practice it every day.

days.guide: Sort situations into emergency and not.

questions.a: Emergency — call 911 after getting out.
Not an emergency.

days.guide: Memorize home address and a parent's phone number.

questions.a: Answers vary — check accuracy.
Answers vary.

days.guide: Practice a pretend 911 call.

questions.a: Your name, your address, what's wrong.
The 911 dispatcher/operator.

days.guide: Learn to tell an adult when someone is hurt.

questions.q: Your friend falls and is bleeding. What do you do?
questions.a: Get a trusted adult right away.

questions.q: Who do you call if no adult is around and someone won't wake up?

days.guide: Your child recites address and role-plays a 911 call.

questions.a: When the operator says to.

questions.q: Is calling 911 for a joke okay?
questions.a: No — it can keep help from people who need it.

weeks.assessment_key: Role-play checklist: knows when to call (real emergency); dials 911; says name; says full address; explains the problem; stays on the line. Proficient = all 6 plus correct address and phone number.

weeks.prep: The trusted adults hand from Unit 1 and scenario cards. Parent preview: this week covers body safety and unsafe touch. Use calm, matter-of-fact language and correct names for body parts. If your child shares something concerning, stay calm, thank them, and contact your pediatrician or the Childhelp National Child Abuse Hotline (1-800-422-4453).
misconceptions: Thinking strangers are the only danger: most important rule is 'No, Go, Tell' with anyone who makes you feel unsafe.
Thinking secrets about touching should be kept: surprises (like a gift) are okay; secrets about touching must be told.
Thinking a child is in trouble if they tell: they will never be in trouble for telling.

days.guide: Discuss safe touches (hugs from family, high fives) and unsafe touches.

questions.a: A hug from family, a high five, a doctor's checkup with a parent there.
A touch that hurts or touches private parts (parts covered by a swimsuit), or makes you feel scared or uncomfortable.

days.guide: Practice 'No, Go, Tell.'

questions.a: Say No, Go away, Tell a trusted adult.
A trusted adult from your hand.

days.guide: Discuss what to do if a stranger offers a ride or treat.

questions.q: A stranger offers you candy to get in a car. What do you do?
questions.a: Say No, run away, tell a trusted adult.

questions.q: Should you go with someone who says your mom sent them?
questions.a: No — only with people your family has told you about (or who knows your family password).

days.guide: Discuss that your body belongs to you and secrets about touching should be told.

questions.q: Who is the boss of your body?
questions.a: You are.

questions.q: Surprise or secret: a birthday gift?
questions.a: A surprise — okay to keep for a short time.

days.guide: Role-play 'No, Go, Tell' in 3 scenarios; name 3 trusted adults.

questions.q: Someone wants you to keep a touching secret. What do you do?
questions.a: Say No, Go, and Tell a trusted adult.
Answers vary — e.g., Mom, Dad, Grandma.

weeks.assessment_key: Rubric: 4 = uses No–Go–Tell correctly in all 3 scenarios (firm 'No,' leaves, names a trusted adult to tell) and names 3 trusted adults; 3 = 2 scenarios; 2 = 1; 1 = cannot demonstrate.

weeks.prep: Construction paper (dark colors fade well), small objects (keys, leaves), sunscreen (SPF 30+), a hat, a life jacket (if available), and paper for a safety mini-book.
misconceptions: Thinking you only need sunscreen at the beach: you need it whenever you're in the sun, even on cloudy days.
Thinking floaties keep you safe: only life jackets (Coast Guard approved) and adult supervision do.
Running near pools: walk — wet surfaces are slippery.

days.guide: Place objects on construction paper in the sun; check fading after a few hours.

questions.a: It faded except where objects blocked the sun.

questions.q: What does this show about our skin?
questions.a: The sun's rays can damage skin, so we protect it.

days.guide: Practice applying sunscreen and wearing a hat.

questions.a: About every 2 hours and after swimming.
Hat, sunglasses, shade, long sleeves.

days.guide: Learn water rules.

questions.a: No — always with an adult watching.

questions.q: What keeps you safe in a boat?
questions.a: A life jacket.

days.guide: Make a safety mini-book with one rule per page.

questions.a: Always swim with an adult.
Wear sunscreen and a hat.

days.guide: Give the Unit 6 assessment.

questions.a: Left, right, left.

questions.q: What do you do if your clothes catch fire?
questions.a: Stop, drop, cover your face, and roll.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 6 test: sort safe/unsafe pictures (helmet on/off, crossing at crosswalk/between cars, swimming with adult/alone, sunscreen/no sunscreen) and explain: road — stop, look left-right-left, hold hands; fire — get out, stay out, meeting place, stop-drop-roll; 911 — real emergencies, give name and address; touch — No, Go, Tell; sun — sunscreen, hat, shade. Proficient = 90%+.

weeks.prep: Empty medicine bottles (rinsed, caps on), pictures of look-alike candy and pills (e.g., candy-coated chocolates vs. pills), and a medicine label. Keep real medicine locked away.
misconceptions: Thinking medicine is candy: some medicines look and taste like candy, but too much can make you very sick.
Thinking you can take medicine on your own if you feel sick: only a trusted adult gives medicine.
Thinking more medicine works faster: the right dose matters.

days.guide: Learn medicines can help when sick but only trusted adults give them.

questions.a: A parent or trusted adult (or a nurse/doctor).
Yes, if you take the wrong kind or too much.

days.guide: Compare pictures of look-alike candy and pills.

questions.q: Can you always tell candy and pills apart?
questions.a: No — they can look alike.

questions.q: What should you do if you find a pill?
questions.a: Don't touch it; tell an adult.

days.guide: Look at a medicine label with an adult.

questions.a: How much to take, how often, and warnings.
An adult.

days.guide: Practice saying 'I need to ask my mom/dad first.'

questions.q: A friend offers you a vitamin gummy. What do you say?
questions.a: No thanks, I need to ask my mom/dad first.
Only trusted adults give medicine or vitamins.

days.guide: Your child explains who can give medicine.

questions.a: A parent, trusted adult, nurse, or doctor.
You could take the wrong one or too much.

weeks.assessment_key: Rubric: 4 = explains that only a trusted adult gives medicine, that medicine can look like candy, and that you never take it on your own; 3 = 2 points; 2 = 1; 1 = incorrect.

weeks.prep: Empty, rinsed cleaning bottles, poison symbol stickers (skull-and-crossbones, Mr. Yuk), and product cards. Keep real products locked up during the hunt.
misconceptions: Thinking only things labeled 'poison' are dangerous: cleaners, medicines, batteries, and some plants can be too.
Thinking you can smell or taste a product to check it: never smell, taste, or touch unknown products.
Thinking bright-colored products are drinks: some cleaners look like juice.

days.guide: Learn skull-and-crossbones and Mr. Yuk.

questions.a: Poison — dangerous; don't touch.

questions.q: What does Mr. Yuk's face mean?
questions.a: No! Poison — stay away.

days.guide: With an adult, find products under the sink with warning labels.

questions.q: Name a product with a warning.
questions.a: Bleach, dish detergent, drain cleaner.

questions.q: What do you do if you see one?
questions.a: Don't touch; tell an adult.

days.guide: Help put dangerous products up high or locked.

questions.a: So young children can't reach them.
Adults (child can help with empty ones).

days.guide: Learn the Poison Control number.

questions.q: What is the Poison Control number?
When would an adult call it?
questions.a: If someone swallowed or touched something poisonous.

days.guide: Sort product cards: safe to touch vs. ask an adult.

questions.a: Ask an adult.
Safe to touch.

weeks.assessment_key: Sort key (suggested): Safe to touch — apple, crayons, book, water cup, toothbrush; Ask an adult — bleach, dish soap pods, medicine, batteries, bug spray, window cleaner. Proficient 10–11 of 11.

weeks.prep: The balloon lung model from week 21, refusal skill cards, and poster paper.
misconceptions: Thinking only the smoker is harmed: secondhand smoke hurts others nearby.
Thinking vapes are just water: they usually contain nicotine and chemicals that harm the body.
Thinking saying no is rude: it's a healthy choice.

days.guide: Revisit the balloon lung model; discuss what smoke does.

questions.a: Bring air into the body.

questions.q: What does smoke do to lungs?
questions.a: Damages them so breathing is harder.

days.guide: Learn that breathing others' smoke harms health.

questions.a: Smoke from someone else's cigarette that you breathe in.
Move away and ask for smoke-free spaces.

days.guide: Practice saying 'No thanks' and walking away.

questions.q: Someone offers you a vape. What do you say?
questions.a: No thanks — and walk away and tell a trusted adult.
To stay safe.

days.guide: Make a smoke-free home poster.

questions.a: Example: Smoke-free home — healthy lungs live here!
To protect everyone's lungs.

days.guide: Give the Unit 7 assessment.

questions.a: Poison.
A trusted adult.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 7 test: 1) Identify the poison symbol (skull-and-crossbones/Mr. Yuk) 2) Explain only trusted adults give medicine 3) Poison Control: 1-800-222-1222 (with adult) 4) Model saying 'No thanks' to smoke/vape and walking away 5) Secondhand smoke hurts people nearby. Proficient 5/5.

weeks.prep: A toy doctor kit, a community map, interview questions, and matching cards for 6 health helpers (doctor, nurse, dentist, pharmacist, eye doctor, school nurse/EMT).
misconceptions: Being scared of doctors: they help keep us healthy.
Thinking a dentist treats tummy aches: each helper has a special job.
Thinking pharmacists are cashiers: they prepare medicines and explain how to take them.

days.guide: Learn about doctors, nurses, dentists, pharmacists.

questions.a: Prepares medicine the doctor orders and explains how to take it safely.
Cares for patients, checks temperature, gives shots, helps doctors.

days.guide: Role-play a doctor checkup with a toy kit.

questions.a: Listens to the heart and lungs.
To make sure you're growing healthy.

days.guide: Interview a health helper about their job.

questions.a: What do you do every day? How do you help people?
Answers vary.

days.guide: Find clinics, pharmacies, hospitals on a community map.

questions.q: Where would you go for medicine?
questions.a: A pharmacy.
A hospital emergency room.

days.guide: Match helpers to jobs; tell who to visit for a toothache.

questions.a: Dentist.
Eye doctor (optometrist).

weeks.assessment_key: Matching key: doctor — checks health and treats illness; nurse — cares for patients; dentist — teeth; pharmacist — medicine; eye doctor — eyes/vision; EMT/paramedic — emergency help in an ambulance. Toothache → dentist. Proficient 6/6.

weeks.prep: Trash bags, gloves (adult picks up sharp or unknown items), card supplies, and a healthy snack to share.
misconceptions: Picking up sharp or unknown trash: only adults handle glass, needles, or unknown items.
Thinking one person can't help a community: small acts add up.
Thinking encouragement is only for winners: encourage effort.

days.guide: Do a family clean-up.

questions.a: Wear gloves, don't touch sharp things, tell an adult.
Less trash means fewer germs and safer places to play.

days.guide: Make a healthy-habits card for a neighbor.

questions.a: Example: Wash your hands for 20 seconds!
To help others be healthy.

days.guide: Share a healthy snack with friends.

questions.a: Answers vary — e.g., fruit.
Helps friends eat well.

days.guide: Encourage a friend learning something new.

questions.a: You can do it! Keep trying!
Makes people feel confident.

days.guide: Your child explains how they helped the community.

questions.a: Cleaned up the park, shared healthy messages.

questions.q: How does a healthy community help you?
questions.a: Clean, safe places to live and play.

weeks.assessment_key: Rubric: 4 = describes 2+ community actions and explains how each helps health (clean park = fewer germs/safer; healthy card = reminds neighbors); 3 = 1 action explained; 2 = action named only; 1 = none.

weeks.prep: Trackers and charts from the year, a goal sheet (eating, activity, hygiene), and a water bottle.
misconceptions: Setting a goal without steps: break goals into small steps.
Forgetting to track: use a chart on the fridge.
Setting goals that depend on others: choose things you control.

days.guide: Review trackers from the year.

questions.q: Which habit did you do best?
questions.a: Answers vary.
Answers vary.

days.guide: Choose summer goals in eating, activity, hygiene.

questions.a: Drink water instead of juice.
Brush 2 minutes twice a day.

days.guide: Write or draw 2 steps for each goal.

questions.a: Keep a water bottle in the fridge; drink a glass at each meal.
Bike after lunch; walk after dinner.

days.guide: Share goals with family; choose a goal buddy.

questions.q: What does a goal buddy do?
questions.a: Reminds and encourages you.
Answers vary.

days.guide: Your child explains one goal, steps, and tracking.

questions.a: Goal: play outside daily. Steps: after lunch, ride bike; after dinner, walk. Track: sticker chart.

questions.q: How will you know you met it?
questions.a: Check the chart.

weeks.assessment_key: Goal sheet rubric: 4 = 3 goals (eating, activity, hygiene), each with 2 specific steps and a tracking method; 3 = 2 goals complete; 2 = goals without steps; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Jeopardy-style question cards (feelings, hygiene, food, activity, safety), paper for a 'My Healthy Me' book, and healthy party foods.
misconceptions: Rushing through review: talk through any wrong answers.
Forgetting earlier units (feelings): review all five areas.
Making a party with only sweets: include healthy foods from MyPlate.

days.guide: Play a health Jeopardy game.

questions.q: How long do you scrub hands?
questions.a: 20 seconds.
Fruits, vegetables, grains, protein, dairy.

days.guide: Make a 'My Healthy Me' book (feelings, hygiene, food, activity, safety).

questions.a: When I feel angry I take 3 belly breaths.
I wear a helmet when I ride my bike.

days.guide: Teach a family member a health skill.

questions.a: Handwashing, belly breathing, 2-V-1 helmet check.

questions.q: How do you know they learned it?
questions.a: They can do it alone.

days.guide: Plan and prepare a healthy snack party.

questions.a: Fruit kabobs, veggie sticks with dip, cheese cubes, water.
Fruit, vegetables, dairy.

days.guide: Present the book at the party.

questions.a: Answers vary.

questions.q: What will you keep doing this summer?
questions.a: Answers vary.

weeks.assessment_key: Year-end review (suggested): 1) Name 4 feelings 2) Calm-down strategy 3) No–Go–Tell 4) Handwashing 20 seconds 5) Brush 2 minutes twice daily 6) 9–12 hours sleep 7) 5 food groups 8) 60 minutes activity 9) 5 senses and organs 10) Look left-right-left 11) Two ways out in a fire 12) Only trusted adults give medicine; Poison Control 1-800-222-1222. Proficient 11–12. Book: 5 accurate pages.

HSS.overview: Teach HSS through stories, primary-source photos, maps, and hands-on projects. Use 'See, Think, Wonder' with every photo and document, connect each topic to your child's own family and community, and let them explain ideas aloud before writing. Preview the read-aloud books — several touch on history topics like segregation and immigration that may prompt questions — and answer honestly at a first-grade level.

weeks.prep: A simple board game, chart paper and markers, picture cards of community signs (stop sign, crosswalk, library 'quiet,' park rules), and 'What If Everybody Did That?' by Ellen Javernick (library).
misconceptions: Thinking rules are only to keep kids from having fun: show how rules keep people safe and make things fair.
Thinking rules only exist at home or school: point out community rules (traffic signs, park hours).
Confusing rights with doing whatever you want: rights come with responsibilities.

days.guide: Play a board game for two minutes with no rules (anyone can move anywhere). Then stop and ask what went wrong and why rules matter.

questions.a: Answers vary: arguing, confusion, unfair play, no one knew who won.
To make play fair and help everyone know what to do.

days.guide: Walk the neighborhood. Your child draws or photographs 5 signs and says what each keeps safe.

questions.q: What does a stop sign keep safe?
questions.a: Drivers, walkers, and bikers — cars stop so no one crashes.
To show people a safe place to cross where drivers expect them.

days.guide: Write 5 home/homeschool rules together and illustrate each.

questions.q: Give a good home rule and its reason.
questions.a: Example: Put toys away — so no one trips and things don't get lost.
Everyone in the family.

days.guide: Read 'What If Everybody Did That?' and match 3 rights with 3 responsibilities.

questions.q: What does the book ask about small actions like dropping litter?
questions.a: What would happen if everybody did that — small actions add up to big problems.

questions.q: Match: the right to use the park.
questions.a: Responsibility to keep it clean.

days.guide: Your child explains one home rule and one community rule and what could happen without each.

questions.q: What would happen without traffic lights?
questions.a: Cars could crash and people could get hurt.

questions.q: Why do we have a rule to wash hands before eating?
questions.a: To keep germs away so we don't get sick.

weeks.assessment_key: Rubric: 4 = states a home rule and a community rule, explains the purpose of each (safety, fairness, order), and what could happen without it; 3 = two rules with one clear purpose; 2 = names rules without purposes; 1 = cannot name a rule.

weeks.prep: 'The Golden Rule' by Ilene Cooper (library), role-play cards (someone cuts in line; a friend is left out; someone takes your toy; a sibling is sad), and a kindness log (paper with 3 boxes).
misconceptions: Thinking the Golden Rule means 'do what others do to you': it means treat others the way you want to be treated.
Thinking disagreeing is always rude: you can disagree politely and respectfully.
Thinking kindness must be big: small acts (holding a door, sharing) count.

days.guide: Read 'The Golden Rule.' Your child says the rule in their own words.

questions.a: Treat others the way you want to be treated.

questions.q: According to the book, is the Golden Rule found in only one religion or culture?
questions.a: No — versions of it are found in many religions and cultures around the world.

days.guide: Act out 4 situations and show a Golden Rule choice for each.

questions.q: A friend is left out of a game. What's a Golden Rule choice?
questions.a: Invite them to join.

questions.q: Someone cuts in line. What can you do?
questions.a: Calmly say 'The line starts back there, please,' or tell an adult.

days.guide: Survey family on favorite food; practice saying 'I see it differently because...' politely.

questions.q: Your brother says pizza is the best food; you like tacos. What can you say?
questions.a: 'I see it differently because I like tacos more.'

questions.q: Is it okay to have different opinions?
questions.a: Yes, as long as we're respectful.

days.guide: Your child does 3 kind acts this week and draws each in the log.

questions.a: Example: helping set the table, sharing a toy.

questions.q: How do kind acts follow the Golden Rule?
questions.a: We're kind because we'd like others to be kind to us.

days.guide: Your child draws a comic strip of someone following the Golden Rule and explains it.

questions.a: Example: A girl shares her snack with a boy who forgot his, because she'd want help if she forgot hers.

questions.q: Why is that the Golden Rule?
questions.a: She treats him the way she'd want to be treated.

weeks.assessment_key: Rubric: 4 = comic clearly shows a Golden Rule choice and explanation names how the character treats someone the way they'd want to be treated; 3 = clear comic, partial explanation; 2 = comic unclear; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: A simple outdoor game (tag, kickball) or board game, scenario cards (fair/unfair), and a T-chart (Good Sport / Poor Sport).
misconceptions: Thinking 'fair' always means 'exactly the same': fair means everyone gets what they need (e.g., glasses for someone who can't see).
Thinking good sports only win: good sportsmanship is how you act whether you win or lose.
Bragging when winning: say 'good game' and thank the other player.

days.guide: Discuss whether fair always means the same. Sort scenario cards into fair and unfair.

questions.q: Is it fair if only one child gets to choose the game every day?
questions.a: No — taking turns is fair.

questions.q: Is it fair that a child who needs glasses gets them and others don't?
questions.a: Yes — fair means getting what you need.

days.guide: Play a backyard game; practice taking turns, following rules, and shaking hands at the end.

questions.q: What do you say at the end of a game?
questions.a: 'Good game!'
So everyone gets a chance.

days.guide: Role-play good and poor ways to win and lose. Fill a T-chart of sportsmanlike words.

questions.a: 'Good game, you played well.'
Yelling, quitting, bragging, or blaming others.

days.guide: Your child writes and signs a 3-line good-sport pledge.

questions.a: I will follow the rules.
I will say 'good game' whether I win or lose.

days.guide: Your child tells how a good sport acted in a game this week.

questions.q: How did you act like a good sport?
questions.a: Answers vary — e.g., I took turns and congratulated my sister.

questions.q: What does a good sport do if a game feels unfair?
questions.a: Calmly talk about it or ask an adult.

weeks.assessment_key: T-chart: proficient lists at least 3 good-sport words/actions (take turns, follow rules, say 'good game,' encourage others) and 3 poor-sport ones (cheat, brag, quit, yell). Pledge: 3 positive lines, signed.

weeks.prep: 'Duck for President' by Doreen Cronin (library), paper ballots, a box for a ballot box, and a tally chart.
misconceptions: Thinking the majority means everyone agrees: some people still voted for the other choice.
Thinking voting is only for presidents: we can vote in families and clubs.
Thinking the losing side should sulk: we respect the result.

days.guide: Read 'Duck for President.' Talk about why the animals voted.

questions.q: Why did Duck want an election?
questions.a: He was tired of doing chores for Farmer Brown and wanted to be in charge.

questions.q: What did Duck learn about being a leader?
questions.a: Running things (the farm, the state, the country) was hard work, so he went back to the farm.

days.guide: Hold a family vote on Friday's movie or snack with paper ballots. Count tallies.

questions.a: Everyone voted, and we counted the votes.
So people can vote how they want without pressure.

days.guide: Count votes; explain that the most votes wins; discuss feelings.

questions.q: Popcorn 3 votes, fruit 2 votes. Which wins?
questions.a: Popcorn.

questions.q: How should the fruit voters act?
questions.a: Accept the result kindly; there will be other votes.

days.guide: Propose a new household rule and let everyone vote.

questions.q: What happens if the rule gets more yes votes than no?
questions.a: It becomes a rule.
Yes — everyone votes on the rule.

days.guide: Your child explains direct democracy in one sentence and gives the example.

questions.a: Everyone votes directly on a decision or rule.
Our family voted on the Friday movie.

weeks.assessment_key: Rubric: proficient = 'In direct democracy, everyone votes on the decision' plus an accurate example (e.g., the family movie vote where the choice with the most votes won).

weeks.prep: Your city's website or newspaper (to find mayor and city council), paper for campaign posters, two stuffed animals, and ballots.
misconceptions: Thinking leaders can make any rule they want: they must follow laws and voters can choose new leaders.
Mixing up direct and representative democracy: direct = everyone votes on the rule; representative = people elect leaders who make rules.
Thinking only adults' voices matter: kids can share ideas with leaders by writing letters.

days.guide: Explain that in big places, people elect a small group (city council, mayor) to make rules for everyone.

questions.a: A person elected to make decisions for a group of people.

questions.q: Why can't everyone in a city vote on every rule?
questions.a: There are too many people and too many rules.

days.guide: Look up your mayor and city council; find one rule they made.

questions.a: Name from city website.
Examples: park hours, speed limits, leash laws, recycling rules.

days.guide: Make campaign posters for two stuffed-animal candidates; hold an election for 'family representative.'

questions.q: What does a campaign poster tell?
questions.a: The candidate's name and what they promise to do.
The voters (family).

days.guide: Make a T-chart comparing direct and representative democracy.

questions.a: Family votes on a movie.
City council makes a park rule after people elect them.

days.guide: Give the Unit 1 assessment.

questions.q: People elect a mayor. Direct or representative?
questions.a: Representative.
Treat others the way you want to be treated.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 1 test (suggested): Sort — 1) Family votes on dinner: direct 2) Voters elect a mayor who makes rules: representative 3) Class votes on a game: direct 4) City council passes a law: representative 5) Club members vote on a name: direct. 6) Golden Rule: treat others as you want to be treated. 7) Why rules? safety and fairness. Proficient 6–7.

weeks.prep: Blocks or small boxes, a toy, a camera/phone, and paper.
misconceptions: Thinking maps must show everything: maps show the important things from above using symbols.
Drawing a side view instead of bird's-eye view: imagine you're a bird looking straight down.
Thinking a photo and a map are the same: a photo shows what something looks like; a map shows where things are.

days.guide: Look at a toy from above and from the side; draw both.

questions.a: Looking straight down from above.

questions.q: What does a cup look like from above?
questions.a: A circle.

days.guide: Build a 3-D model of your bedroom with blocks and boxes.

questions.q: What could stand for your bed?
questions.a: A rectangular block or box.
A small copy of something real.

days.guide: Photograph the room and compare with the model.

questions.q: What does the photo show that the model doesn't?
questions.a: Real colors, details, objects.

questions.q: What does the model show better?
questions.a: Where things are compared to each other, from any side.

days.guide: Draw a bird's-eye map of the room with simple symbols.

questions.q: How would you draw a bed on the map?
questions.a: A rectangle.

questions.q: How would you draw a round rug?
questions.a: A circle.

days.guide: Your child explains one thing a model shows better and one thing a picture shows better.

questions.a: Where things are in the room and their size from all sides.
Real colors and details.

weeks.assessment_key: Map rubric: 4 = bird's-eye view, main furniture placed correctly with simple symbols, plus clear model-vs-picture comparison; 3 = mostly correct; 2 = side views or major misplacements; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: A compass (or phone compass), sticky notes labeled N, S, E, W, a park map with a key, and a small 'treasure.'
misconceptions: Thinking north is always 'up' in real life: north is a direction; on most maps it's at the top.
Mixing up east and west: 'Never Eat Soggy Waffles' (N, E, S, W clockwise).
Ignoring the map key: the key explains what each symbol means.

days.guide: Use a compass to label walls N, S, E, W. Follow directions like 'take 3 steps north.'

questions.q: What are the four cardinal directions?
questions.a: North, south, east, west.
West.

days.guide: Study a park map's key; find 5 symbols.

questions.a: A box that explains what the symbols mean.

questions.q: What might a tree symbol mean?
questions.a: A wooded area or trees.

days.guide: Draw a compass rose and add it to the room map.

questions.q: What does a compass rose show?
questions.a: Directions (N, S, E, W).

questions.q: Where is north usually on a map?
questions.a: At the top.

days.guide: Follow a family-made map with symbols and directions to find hidden treasure.

questions.q: How did you use the map?
questions.a: Followed symbols and directions.

questions.q: If the map says go east from the couch, which way?
questions.a: Toward the side labeled E.

days.guide: Your child makes a yard/street map with a key of 4 symbols and a compass rose.

questions.a: Answers vary — e.g., house, tree, mailbox, driveway.

questions.q: Where is your house compared to the street?
questions.a: Answers use directions.

weeks.assessment_key: Rubric: 4 = map with 4 symbols explained in a key, compass rose with N/S/E/W correct, and features placed accurately; 3 = one part missing; 2 = no key or compass rose; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Large paper, a printed street map of your area (or online map), colored pencils.
misconceptions: Drawing landmarks in the wrong order along the route: walk or check the online map.
Directions without landmarks: add 'turn left at the park.'
Making the map too small to read: plan space before drawing.

days.guide: Walk your neighborhood and list landmarks.

questions.a: An important or easy-to-see place that helps you find your way.
Example: the library, park, fire station.

days.guide: Find your home on a printed or online map.

questions.q: How did you find your street?
questions.a: By its name on the map.
Answers vary.

days.guide: Draw a community map with home, 4 landmarks, key, compass rose.

questions.a: The symbols for each landmark.

questions.q: Where does the compass rose go?
questions.a: In a corner of the map.

days.guide: Draw a route from home to the library; describe it with directions.

questions.a: Example: Go north on Oak Street, turn east at the park, the library is on the left.
The path you take from one place to another.

days.guide: Your child gives a family member directions to a landmark using the map.

questions.a: Using directions (N/S/E/W), street names, and landmarks.

questions.q: Did the listener reach the landmark?
questions.a: Check by following on the map.

weeks.assessment_key: Rubric: 4 = map with home, 4 landmarks, key, compass rose, and accurate route described with cardinal directions; 3 = one element missing; 2 = route unclear; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: A globe, a U.S. map, a California map, blank outline maps, and paper for nesting circles.
misconceptions: Thinking California is a country: it is a state in the United States.
Thinking the capital is Los Angeles or San Francisco: the capital is Sacramento.
Thinking globes and flat maps show different places: both show Earth; the globe is round like Earth.

days.guide: Make nesting circles: home → city → California → United States → North America → Earth.

questions.q: Which is bigger: California or the United States?
questions.a: The United States.

questions.q: What continent is the U.S. on?
questions.a: North America.

days.guide: Find your city, Sacramento, and the Pacific Ocean on a California map.

questions.a: Sacramento.
The Pacific Ocean.

days.guide: Find California on a U.S. map; name the bordering states.

questions.a: Oregon (north), Nevada (east), Arizona (southeast).

questions.q: What country borders California to the south?
questions.a: Mexico.

days.guide: Find the U.S. and California on a globe; compare to a flat map.

questions.q: How is a globe different from a flat map?
questions.a: A globe is round like Earth; a flat map shows Earth flat.
The globe.

days.guide: Label your city, California, and the U.S. on blank maps.

questions.q: Label California on a U.S. map.
questions.a: On the west coast, along the Pacific.
In northern-central California.

weeks.assessment_key: Labeled maps: proficient = city in the right area of California, Sacramento marked, Pacific Ocean labeled, California correctly shaded on the U.S. map, and the U.S. labeled on a North America/world outline.

weeks.prep: A globe, a world map, paper continent cut-outs, a blue world map outline, animal pictures, and a blank world map.
misconceptions: Thinking there is one big ocean: there are named oceans (Pacific, Atlantic, Indian, Arctic, and often the Southern Ocean).
Confusing countries and continents: a continent is a huge land area with many countries.
Mixing up Antarctica and the Arctic: Antarctica is the frozen continent at the bottom (south); the Arctic Ocean is at the top (north).

days.guide: Learn a continents song and point to each continent.

questions.a: North America, South America, Europe, Asia, Africa, Australia, Antarctica.
Asia.

days.guide: Find the Pacific, Atlantic, Indian, Arctic Oceans; trace them.

questions.a: Pacific.

questions.q: Which ocean is between North America and Europe?
questions.a: Atlantic.

days.guide: Cut out continents and glue them in the right places.

questions.a: Southeast of Asia, between the Indian and Pacific Oceans.

questions.q: What continent is south of North America?
questions.a: South America.

days.guide: Place animals on their continents.

questions.a: Australia.
Antarctica (and other southern lands).
Africa.

days.guide: Your child labels 7 continents and 4 oceans.

questions.q: Which ocean is at the very top of the globe?
questions.a: Arctic.

questions.q: Which continent do we live on?
questions.a: North America.

weeks.assessment_key: Labeling key: North America, South America, Europe, Asia, Africa, Australia, Antarctica; Pacific, Atlantic, Indian, Arctic Oceans (Southern Ocean accepted if added). Proficient 10–11 of 11.

weeks.prep: Photos of an igloo, a stilt house, an adobe home, and an apartment (Library of Congress/Smithsonian), clothing cards (snow, rain, hot, desert), and images of California beach, Sierra Nevada, and desert.
misconceptions: Thinking people everywhere live the same way: environment shapes homes, food, clothing, and travel.
Thinking igloos are where most Arctic people live today: they were traditional temporary shelters; most people live in modern houses now.
Judging other ways of life as 'weird': they make sense for the place.

days.guide: Compare homes; tell how each fits its environment.

questions.q: Why are stilt houses on stilts?
questions.a: To stay above floods, water, or wet ground.

questions.q: Why are adobe homes good in hot places?
questions.a: Thick mud-brick walls keep the inside cool.

days.guide: Sort clothing cards by place.

questions.q: What do people wear in snowy places?
questions.a: Warm coats, boots, mittens, hats.
Light, loose clothing and hats to block the sun.

days.guide: Compare life at the beach, in the Sierra Nevada, and in the desert.

questions.q: A fun winter activity in the Sierra Nevada?
questions.a: Skiing or sledding in snow.

questions.q: What do people need in the desert?
questions.a: Water, shade, sun protection.

days.guide: Compare transportation in snowy places, islands, and cities.

questions.q: How do people travel between islands?
questions.a: By boat or plane.
They move easily over snow.

days.guide: Give the Unit 2 assessment.

questions.q: Find California on a U.S. map.
questions.a: On the west coast.

questions.q: How does living near snow affect clothing?
questions.a: People wear warm, waterproof clothes.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 2 test (suggested): 1) Find California on U.S. map 2) Mark the Pacific Ocean 3) Name 4 directions on a compass rose 4) Use a map key to find a park symbol 5) Point to your continent (North America) 6) Explain: people in snowy places wear warm coats and build homes to keep heat in (or similar accurate example). Proficient 5–6 with a clear environment explanation.

weeks.prep: A U.S. flag, printed Pledge of Allegiance, lyrics to 'My Country 'Tis of Thee' (Samuel Francis Smith) and 'America the Beautiful' (Katharine Lee Bates), and photos of American landscapes (mountains, wheat fields, coasts).
misconceptions: Saying the Pledge without knowing the words' meanings: discuss each key word.
Thinking 'indivisible' means invisible: it means cannot be divided — one nation together.
Thinking patriotic songs are only for holidays: they express love for the country any time.

days.guide: Read the Pledge line by line; discuss allegiance, liberty, justice.

questions.a: Loyalty — promising to be faithful.
Freedom.
Fairness.

days.guide: Draw a picture for liberty, justice, indivisible.

questions.a: Cannot be divided; we stay united as one nation.
Example: a balance scale or people being treated fairly.

days.guide: Learn the first verse of 'My Country 'Tis of Thee'; talk about 'sweet land of liberty.'

questions.q: What does 'sweet land of liberty' mean?
questions.a: A country we love where people are free.

questions.q: What is the last line of the first verse?
questions.a: 'Let freedom ring!'

days.guide: Learn the first verse of 'America the Beautiful'; match lines to landscape photos.

questions.a: Golden wheat fields.
Tall mountains that look purple from far away.

days.guide: Your child recites the Pledge, sings one song, and explains one idea.

questions.a: I pledge allegiance to the Flag of the United States of America, and to the Republic for which it stands, one Nation under God, indivisible, with liberty and justice for all.
Example: 'Liberty and justice for all' means everyone should be free and treated fairly.

weeks.assessment_key: Recitation rubric: 4 = recites the Pledge accurately and explains a key word (liberty = freedom; justice = fairness; indivisible = can't be divided; allegiance = loyalty); 3 = 1–2 prompts; 2 = several prompts; 1 = cannot recite.

weeks.prep: Library of Congress photos of veterans, card-making supplies, a children's nonfiction book on the 1621 harvest feast, and 'Thank You, Sarah: The Woman Who Saved Thanksgiving' by Laurie Halse Anderson (library).
misconceptions: Confusing Veterans Day and Memorial Day: Veterans Day (Nov. 11) honors everyone who served; Memorial Day honors those who died serving.
Thinking the first Thanksgiving was only the Pilgrims: the Wampanoag people, led by Massasoit, were there too and had helped the Pilgrims.
Thinking Thanksgiving was always a national holiday: Sarah Josepha Hale worked for years until President Lincoln made it national in 1863.

days.guide: Learn what a veteran is and why we honor them on November 11. View LOC photos.

questions.a: Someone who served in the armed forces.
November 11.

days.guide: Your child writes a thank-you card to a veteran.

questions.q: What could you thank a veteran for?
questions.a: Serving and protecting our country.
A family member, neighbor, or local VA.

days.guide: Learn about the 1621 harvest feast of the Wampanoag and the Pilgrims.

questions.a: The Pilgrims (English colonists at Plymouth) and the Wampanoag people.

questions.q: How had the Wampanoag helped the Pilgrims?
questions.a: Taught them to grow corn and find food (Tisquantum/Squanto helped them plant corn and fish).

days.guide: Read 'Thank You, Sarah'; learn how Sarah Hale helped make Thanksgiving national.

questions.q: How did Sarah Hale try to make Thanksgiving a national holiday?
questions.a: She wrote many letters to presidents and leaders for many years.
Abraham Lincoln, in 1863.

days.guide: Your child makes a two-panel poster explaining Veterans Day and Thanksgiving.

questions.q: What goes on the Veterans Day panel?
questions.a: Honoring people who served in the military, on November 11.
Giving thanks; harvest feast of 1621; Sarah Hale; fourth Thursday of November.

weeks.assessment_key: Poster rubric: 4 = Veterans Day honors people who served in the armed forces on Nov. 11; Thanksgiving is a day of giving thanks, recalling the 1621 harvest feast of the Wampanoag and Pilgrims and Sarah Hale's work (national holiday since Lincoln, 1863); 3 = both correct, few details; 2 = one holiday correct; 1 = incorrect.

weeks.prep: Smithsonian/LOC images of the flag, bald eagle, Great Seal (on the back of a $1 bill), Statue of Liberty, and Liberty Bell; construction paper; a quarter dated 1998 or earlier (eagle on back) if available.
misconceptions: Thinking the flag always had 50 stars: stars were added as states joined; there are 13 stripes for the 13 original colonies.
Thinking the Statue of Liberty was built in America by Americans: it was a gift from the people of France (dedicated in 1886).
Thinking the Liberty Bell is still rung: it cracked and is no longer rung.

days.guide: Count stars and stripes; learn their meaning; make a paper flag.

questions.q: How many stars, and what do they stand for?
questions.a: 50, one for each state.
13, for the 13 original colonies (7 red, 6 white).

days.guide: Learn why the bald eagle is the national bird; find it on the Great Seal (back of the $1 bill) and older quarters.

questions.q: Why was the bald eagle chosen?
questions.a: It is native to North America and stands for strength and freedom.

questions.q: Where can you see the eagle?
questions.a: On the Great Seal (on the back of the $1 bill) and on many quarters from 1998 and earlier.

days.guide: View LOC photos of the Statue of Liberty being built; discuss what it welcomes.

questions.q: Who gave the Statue of Liberty to the U.S.?
questions.a: The people of France.
Immigrants and visitors arriving by ship in New York Harbor; it stands for freedom.

days.guide: Find the crack in a Liberty Bell photo and learn its story.

questions.a: Philadelphia, Pennsylvania.
It cracked, and the crack grew too large (by the 1840s).

days.guide: Match 6 symbols to names and meanings.

questions.a: Freedom and welcome.
Strength and freedom.
