weeks.assessment_key: Quiz (suggested): 23 = 2t 3o; 45 = 4t 5o; 60 = 6t 0o; 18 = 1t 8o; 92 = 9t 2o; 37 = 3t 7o; 81 = 8t 1o; 50 = 5t 0o; 74 = 7t 4o; 99 = 9t 9o. Proficient 9–10 built and recorded correctly.

weeks.prep: Base-ten blocks, index cards for a match game (e.g., 47 / 40 + 7 / 4 tens 7 ones), mystery-number riddle cards, and pictures of blocks for day 4.
misconceptions: Saying 'eleven is one and one': build 11 as a ten and one.
Writing expanded form as 4 + 7 instead of 40 + 7: point to the tens digit and ask 'What is it worth?'
Writing 'sixty-three' as 603: build 6 tens 3 ones and write 63.

days.guide: Build 11–19 one at a time with a ten rod and ones. Your child says 'Fourteen is one ten and four ones' for each.
Show 47 with blocks and write 47 = 40 + 7. Play a matching game pairing standard form, expanded form, and tens/ones cards.
Read riddles aloud: 'I have 6 tens and 3 ones. What am I?' Let your child build and answer, then make riddles for you.
Say numbers in words ('fifty-eight') and show pictures of blocks; your child writes the numeral.
Give a place-value quiz with teen and two-digit numbers.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz (suggested): 1) 13 = 1 ten 3 ones 2) 19 = 10 + 9 3) 52 = 50 + 2 4) 7 tens 8 ones = 78 5) 30 + 4 = 34 6) 'eighty-six' = 86 7) 'forty' = 40 8) riddle 5 tens 1 one = 51 9) blocks 2 rods 9 cubes = 29 10) 1 ten 1 one = 11. Proficient 9–10.

weeks.prep: Base-ten blocks, symbol cards (>, <, =), a deck of cards 0–9 (Ace = 1, paper 0s), and the 12-item comparison quiz.
misconceptions: Comparing ones first (thinking 38 > 42 because 8 > 2): always compare tens first.
Reversing < and >: 'the open mouth eats the bigger number' or 'the small point points to the smaller number.'
Reading 52 < 61 backward: read left to right: '52 is less than 61.'

days.guide: Build 42 and 38 with blocks. Compare the rods first: 4 tens vs 3 tens, so 42 is greater even though 8 ones > 2 ones.

questions.a: 42; 4 tens is more than 3 tens.
56; same tens, 6 ones < 9 ones.

days.guide: Teach the symbols: > means greater than, < means less than, = means equal. Your child writes comparisons for 10 pairs and reads each aloud.
Each player flips 2 cards and makes a 2-digit number. Compare and record with a symbol (e.g., 73 > 46). Bigger number wins the round.

questions.q: You make 35, I make 53. Record it.
With cards 6 and 2, what is the biggest number you can make?

days.guide: Your child orders 5 two-digit numbers from least to greatest by sorting tens first, then ones.
Give the 12-item comparison quiz.

weeks.prep: 120 chart, base-ten blocks, a list of 20 numbers for mental 10 more/10 less, plus-shaped chart pieces, and a Unit 6 test (see key).
misconceptions: Thinking 10 more than 47 is 48 (adding 1): show on the chart that 10 more is straight down, not to the right.
Changing the ones digit when finding 10 less: only the tens digit changes; the ones stay the same.
Forgetting that 10 more than 95 is 105 (not 96 or 15): count it on the 120 chart.

days.guide: Put a finger on 34. Move down one row: 44 (10 more). Move up: 24 (10 less). Practice with 6 numbers.
Build 56 with blocks. Add a ten rod: 66. Remove a rod: 46. Ask which digit changed.

questions.a: 66 — the tens digit changes from 5 to 6.

days.guide: Say 20 numbers quickly and your child says 10 more or 10 less without the chart. If stuck, picture the blocks.
Give plus-shaped pieces with only the center filled. Your child fills up (10 less), down (10 more), left (1 less), right (1 more).

questions.q: Center 67: fill up, down, left, right.
questions.a: Up 57, down 77, left 66, right 68.
Up 90, down 110, left 99, right 101.

days.guide: Give the Unit 6 test, reading aloud as needed.

weeks.prep: Base-ten blocks (at least 10 rods and 20 units), a hundred or 120 chart, and a quiz of 10 addition problems (see key).
misconceptions: Adding the ones digit of 30 + 20 as '5' or writing 32: 3 tens + 2 tens = 5 tens = 50.
Adding tens to ones (34 + 20 = 36): line up tens with tens and ones with ones.
In 38 + 6, writing 314 (3 tens and 14 ones written side by side): trade 10 ones for a ten: 4 tens 4 ones = 44.

days.guide: Show 30 + 20 with 3 rods and 2 rods: 5 rods = 50. Say 'three tens plus two tens is five tens.' Practice 40 + 50, 10 + 60.
Build 34 and add 2 rods: 54. Then show on the chart: start at 34 and move down 2 rows.
Build 42, add 5 units: 4 tens 7 ones = 47. No new ten needed because 2 + 5 is less than 10.
Build 38 + 6. 8 ones + 6 ones = 14 ones, so trade 10 ones for a rod. Or think: 38 + 2 = 40, then 40 + 4 = 44.
Your child solves mixed problems by drawing tens as sticks and ones as dots.

weeks.prep: Base-ten blocks, paper for open number lines, and a strategy quiz (see key).
misconceptions: Jumping by ones on an open number line for +30: show one big jump of 10 three times (47 → 57 → 67 → 77).
Drawing ten-sticks and dots but miscounting the new ten: circle 10 dots and turn them into a stick.
Writing an explanation that only restates the answer ('it is 63'): prompt with 'First I…, then I…'.

days.guide: Draw an open number line. For 47 + 30, mark 47 and draw three jumps of 10: 57, 67, 77. For 56 + 8, jump 4 to 60 then 4 more to 64.
Use quick drawings: a line for a ten, a dot for a one. 25 + 7: 2 sticks 5 dots + 7 dots = 12 dots, circle 10 to make a stick: 3 sticks 2 dots = 32.
Read problems like 'A farm has 46 chickens and 8 ducks. How many birds?' Your child chooses a strategy and writes an equation.

questions.q: 46 chickens and 8 ducks. How many birds?
A farm has 35 cows; 40 more come. How many cows?

days.guide: Your child solves 59 + 4 and writes one sentence telling how: e.g., 'I added 1 to make 60 and then 3 more to get 63.'

questions.a: 33; e.g., 'I added 2 to get 30, then 3 more is 33.'

days.guide: Give the strategy quiz; each problem needs an answer and a drawing or sentence.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz (suggested): 1) 36+40=76 2) 58+7=65 3) 44+5=49 4) 27+60=87 5) 69+3=72 6) 15+9=24. Explanation rubric: 4 = correct answer plus clear steps (make a ten, jumps, or tens/ones); 3 = correct with partial explanation; 2 = some errors but sensible strategy; 1 = no strategy shown.

weeks.prep: Ten rods, a 120 chart, 10 real dimes (or paper), and a quiz of 10 subtracting-tens problems.
misconceptions: Subtracting 3 from 70 when asked 70 − 30 (getting 67): say 'seven tens take away three tens.'
Moving down the chart instead of up to subtract tens: up = 10 less.
Thinking dimes are worth 1 each: a dime is 10¢, so count dimes by tens.

days.guide: Lay out 7 rods (70). Take away 3 rods. Count: 4 rods = 40. Write 70 − 30 = 40.
For 90 − 60, ask '60 plus what makes 90?' Count up by tens: 70, 80, 90 = 3 tens = 30.
On the chart, start at 80 and jump up 3 rows to subtract 30: 70, 60, 50.
Count 8 dimes: 10, 20 ... 80¢. Take away 5 dimes: 30¢ left. Write 80¢ − 50¢ = 30¢.

questions.q: You have 6 dimes and spend 4. How much is left?

days.guide: Your child solves 10 subtracting-tens problems with rods or the chart.

weeks.prep: Base-ten blocks, open-number-line paper, 120 chart, a die, Khan Academy login, 5 worked problems with errors (see day 4), and the Unit 7 test.
misconceptions: Adding tens and ones together as if both were ones (40 + 3 = 7): build both numbers before adding.
When an error is found, erasing without explaining: ask your child to tell what went wrong.
Racing to 100 by adding without tracking regrouping: keep the running total on blocks.

days.guide: Set up three stations (blocks, number line, 120 chart). Give one problem per station (e.g., 46 + 20, 38 + 5, 70 − 40); your child solves each a different way.
Sit with your child for Khan Academy 'add within 100' and 'subtract tens' practice. Ask them to explain one problem aloud.
Race to 100: roll a die and choose to add that many tens or ones to your total. Record each move as an equation (e.g., 34 + 5 = 39). First to exactly 100 (or closest without going over) wins.

questions.q: You're at 74 and roll 2. If you add tens, where are you? Ones?
questions.a: 94 with tens; 76 with ones.

days.guide: Show 5 worked problems with mistakes, e.g., 45 + 30 = 48; 36 + 7 = 313; 80 − 20 = 78; 29 + 4 = 23; 54 + 20 = 56. Your child finds and fixes each and says what went wrong.

questions.a: 75; 30 is 3 tens, not 3 ones.
43; 13 ones = 1 ten 3 ones, so 4 tens 3 ones.
60; take away 2 tens, not 2 ones.

days.guide: Give the Unit 7 test.

weeks.prep: Pencils and crayons of different lengths, string or yarn, scissors, 3 ribbons of different lengths, household objects.
misconceptions: Comparing without lining up ends (an object looks longer because it sticks out on one side): always line up the ends on a table edge.
Thinking the string must be the same length as both objects: the string 'stands in' for the first object; cut or mark it, then compare to the second.
Ordering by thickness or size instead of length: point along the long side only.

days.guide: Give 3 pencils or crayons. Line up their bottom ends on the table edge and order shortest to longest. Ask your child to use the words shortest, longer, longest.

questions.q: Which is longest, and how do you know?
questions.a: The one that sticks out farthest when the ends are lined up.

questions.q: If A is longer than B and B is longer than C, which is shortest?
questions.a: C.

days.guide: Compare pairs of household objects (spoon vs fork, book vs remote) by lining up ends. Your child says '___ is longer than ___.'

questions.q: Why must you line up the ends?
questions.a: So you only compare how far each one reaches; otherwise the comparison isn't fair.

questions.q: Which is longer, a spoon or a crayon (usually)?
questions.a: A spoon.

days.guide: You can't move the door or table, so stretch string along the table's length and cut/mark it. Hold the string against the door width. Ask which is longer.

questions.a: It copies the table's length so we can compare it with the door.

questions.q: The string is longer than the door's width. What does that mean?
questions.a: The table is longer than the door is wide.

days.guide: Your child finds 3 things longer and 3 shorter than their arm by holding them alongside their arm, and draws them.

questions.q: Name something longer than your arm.
questions.a: Example: a broom, a couch, a bed.
Example: a spoon, a crayon.

days.guide: Your child orders 3 ribbons and uses a string to compare a couch and a bed, explaining their method.

questions.q: Explain how you compared the couch and the bed.
questions.a: Stretch string along the couch, mark it, then hold it along the bed; whichever is longer than the string is longer.

questions.q: Which ribbon goes first in shortest to longest?
questions.a: The shortest one.

weeks.assessment_key: Performance task rubric: 4 = lines up ends to order 3 ribbons correctly AND uses string to compare couch and bed with a clear explanation ('the string was the couch's length; the bed was longer than the string'); 3 = correct ordering and comparison with prompting; 2 = orders ribbons but cannot do indirect comparison; 1 = does not line up ends.

weeks.prep: A box of same-size paper clips, connecting cubes, a book, spoon, shoe, pictures of measurements with gaps/overlaps (draw 3), and a recording sheet.
misconceptions: Leaving gaps or overlapping units: line units end to end, touching, starting exactly at the edge.
Mixing unit sizes (big and small paper clips): every unit must be the same size.
Thinking a bigger number always means a longer object even with different units: more cubes than clips doesn't mean the object grew — smaller units give bigger counts.

days.guide: Show how to measure a book: start the first clip at the edge, line clips end to end with no gaps, and count. Record each measurement as 'The book is __ paper clips long.'

questions.q: Where must the first paper clip start?
questions.a: Exactly at the end of the object.

questions.q: If 7 clips fit along the spoon, how long is it?
questions.a: 7 paper clips long.

days.guide: Show drawings with gaps between clips, overlapping clips, and one correct. Your child circles the mistakes and explains.

questions.q: Why is a gap a mistake?
questions.a: The gap is part of the length but not counted, so the number is too small.
You count more clips than fit, so the number is too big.

days.guide: Measure the same book, spoon, and shoe with cubes. Compare: 'The book was 6 clips but 9 cubes.' Ask why.

questions.q: Why did the book measure more cubes than clips?
questions.a: Cubes are shorter than paper clips, so it takes more of them.
No — only the unit changed.

days.guide: Measure the hallway with heel-to-toe steps. Then a family member measures it. Compare the numbers and discuss why they're different.

questions.q: Why did Dad need fewer steps?
questions.a: His feet are longer, so each step covers more distance.

questions.q: How could we get the same number?
questions.a: Use the same unit, like the same paper clips or a ruler.

days.guide: Your child measures 5 objects with clips, records each, and circles any measurement where gaps/overlaps happened.

questions.q: A pencil is 5 clips and a crayon 3 clips. How much longer is the pencil?
questions.a: 2 clips longer.
Same-size units, end to end, no gaps or overlaps.

weeks.assessment_key: Recording sheet: answers vary by object; check that each entry has a number and the unit ('6 paper clips'). Proficient (4) = all 5 measured with units touching end to end, starting at the edge, counts within 1 of your own check, and any gap/overlap correctly circled; 3 = one error; 2 = several gaps or no units named; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Connecting cubes, 10 toys of different lengths, grid paper, and a Unit 8 test (see key).
misconceptions: Putting a toy in the wrong category because the boundaries are unclear: decide rules first, e.g., short = 1–4 cubes, medium = 5–8, long = 9 or more.
Graph bars not starting at zero: draw a baseline and color from the bottom.
Answering how-many-more by adding the bars: subtract or count up from the shorter bar.

days.guide: Your child decides 3 length categories and writes cube ranges for each (e.g., short 1–4, medium 5–8, long 9+).

questions.q: Why do we need number rules for each category?
questions.a: So every toy fits in exactly one category.

questions.q: A toy is 6 cubes. With our rules, which category?
questions.a: Medium (5–8).

days.guide: Your child measures 10 toys with cubes and records each length and category.

questions.q: A toy car is 4 cubes long. Category?
questions.a: Short (1–4).
Long (9+).

days.guide: Make a bar graph with 3 bars (short, medium, long), one square per toy, with a title and labels.

questions.q: If 4 toys are short, how tall is that bar?
questions.a: 4 squares.
Example: 'How Long Are My Toys?'

days.guide: Ask how-many-more questions about the graph.

questions.q: Short 4, medium 4, long 2. How many more short than long?

days.guide: Give the Unit 8 test.

questions.q: A pencil is 8 cubes, a crayon is 5 cubes. Which is longer, and by how much?
questions.a: The pencil, by 3 cubes.

questions.q: Rope A is longer than rope B; rope B is longer than rope C. Is A longer than C?
questions.a: Yes.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 8 test (suggested): 1) Order 3 pictured strips shortest to longest (check order). 2) A is longer than string; string is longer than B → A is longer than B. 3) Measure a pictured line with paper clips drawn end to end (count shown, e.g., 6). 4) Circle the picture with a gap → the gapped one. 5) Graph short 3, medium 5, long 2: most = medium; how many more medium than long = 3; total = 10. Proficient: all correct or one error.

weeks.prep: Paper plate, brass fastener, construction paper hands (short hour hand, long minute hand), markers, a real analog clock, and 10 clock pictures for Friday.
misconceptions: Mixing up the hour and minute hands: the short hand tells the hour; the long hand tells minutes.
At half past, reading the hour as the next number (2:30 read as 3:30) because the hour hand is near 3: the hour hand is between 2 and 3, so it's still 2-something.
Writing 3:00 as 3:0 or 30:0: show digital clocks — hours, colon, two digits for minutes.

days.guide: Write 1–12 around a paper plate (12, 3, 6, 9 first so spacing is even). Attach a short and a long hand with a fastener. Your child shows 'clock face parts' and names each hand.

questions.a: The hour hand.

questions.q: What number is at the top of a clock?

days.guide: Show times on the hour: long hand on 12, short hand on the hour. Your child shows and writes 3:00, 7:00, 12:00.

questions.q: The short hand is on 8 and the long hand on 12. What time?

questions.a: Short hand on 5, long hand on 12.

days.guide: Move the long hand to 6 and show that the hour hand slid halfway between two numbers. Read it as 'half past' or ':30'.

questions.q: Long hand on 6, short hand halfway between 4 and 5. Time?
questions.a: 4:30, half past four.

questions.q: Where is the hour hand at 9:30?
questions.a: Halfway between 9 and 10.

days.guide: Your child draws 4–5 parts of their day (breakfast, lessons, lunch, play, bed) with a clock time for each, on the hour or half hour.

questions.q: If lunch is at 12:30, draw the hands.
questions.a: Long hand on 6, short hand halfway between 12 and 1.

days.guide: Your child reads 10 clock pictures and writes each time.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz (suggested 10 clocks): 1:00, 3:00, 6:00, 9:00, 12:00, 2:30, 5:30, 7:30, 10:30, 12:30 — your child should write each as shown. Proficient 9–10; watch especially for half-past times read one hour too late.

weeks.prep: Real pennies, nickels, dimes, and quarters; a magnifying glass; a coin chart sheet; play-store toys with price tags under 50¢; a Unit 9 test.
misconceptions: Thinking bigger coins are worth more (nickel more than dime): the dime is smallest but worth 10¢.
Counting all coins by ones: count dimes by tens first, then pennies by ones.
Mixing up penny and nickel names: penny is copper-colored, 1¢; nickel is silver, bigger, 5¢.

days.guide: Let your child examine each coin with a magnifier: color, size, edge (dimes and quarters have ridges), and the pictures. Sort into four piles and name them.

questions.a: The penny.
The dime.

days.guide: Make a coin chart: penny 1¢, nickel 5¢, dime 10¢, quarter 25¢. Tape or draw each coin next to its value.

questions.q: How much is a nickel worth?
Which is worth more, a dime or a nickel?
questions.a: A dime (10¢ vs 5¢).

days.guide: Lay out 3 dimes and 4 pennies. Count dimes by tens (10, 20, 30) then pennies by ones (31, 32, 33, 34): 34¢. Connect to 3 tens and 4 ones.
Price toys under 50¢ with tags. Your child 'buys' them by counting out dimes and pennies (and nickels if ready).

questions.q: A toy costs 23¢. Which dimes and pennies pay exactly?
questions.a: 2 dimes and 3 pennies.

questions.q: You buy a 15¢ toy. Pay with a dime and what?
questions.a: A nickel (or 5 pennies).

days.guide: Give the Unit 9 test: read and write 6 clock times, and name and value 8 coins.

questions.q: Name and value of the silver coin with ridges, biggest of the 4.
questions.a: Quarter, 25¢.

questions.q: Short hand between 6 and 7, long hand on 6.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 9 test (suggested): Times: 4:00, 8:00, 11:00, 1:30, 3:30, 9:30. Coins (show real coins): penny 1¢, nickel 5¢, dime 10¢, quarter 25¢, penny 1¢, dime 10¢, nickel 5¢, quarter 25¢. Proficient: 13–14 of 14 correct.

weeks.prep: Cut-out paper shapes (triangles, squares, rectangles, hexagons, circles, trapezoids in different sizes and colors), straws cut into pieces, playdough, and a geoboard or Math Learning Center Geoboard app.
misconceptions: Thinking a 'tipped' triangle or rotated square isn't the same shape: turn the paper shape and recount sides and corners.
Using color or size to name a shape: say 'shape names come from sides and corners, not color or size.'
Thinking a square isn't a rectangle: a square has 4 straight sides and 4 square corners, so it is a special rectangle.

days.guide: Your child sorts shapes into groups by number of sides and corners (3, 4, 6, 0) and names each group.

questions.q: How many sides and corners does a triangle have?
questions.a: 3 sides and 3 corners.

questions.q: How many does a hexagon have?
questions.a: 6 sides and 6 corners.

days.guide: Show a big red triangle and a small blue triangle. Ask why both are triangles. Guide to 'both have 3 straight sides and 3 corners and are closed.'

questions.q: Are these both triangles: a big red one and a small blue one?
questions.a: Yes — both have 3 straight sides and 3 corners; color and size don't matter.

questions.q: Is a shape with 3 sides but a gap a triangle?
questions.a: No — it must be closed.

days.guide: Your child builds shapes from straws joined by playdough balls: a triangle, a square, a rectangle, a hexagon. Count straws (sides) and balls (corners).

questions.q: How many straws for a square?
questions.a: 4, all the same length.

questions.q: How many playdough balls for a hexagon?

days.guide: Give attribute challenges on the geoboard: 'Make a shape with 4 sides that's not a square,' 'Make a triangle that touches 5 pegs on its sides.'

questions.q: Make a shape with 4 sides and 4 square corners but not all sides equal. What is it?
questions.a: A rectangle (not a square).

questions.q: Make a closed shape with 3 sides.
questions.a: A triangle.

days.guide: Give the attribute quiz: circle triangles/rectangles in a mixed set and write why color/size do not matter.

questions.q: Why do color and size not matter?
questions.a: Shapes are named by sides and corners; a triangle is a triangle in any color or size.

questions.q: Is a circle a polygon with sides?
questions.a: No — a circle has no straight sides or corners.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz rubric: Circle all triangles (3 sides, 3 corners, closed) and rectangles (4 sides, 4 square corners, including squares) in the set; do not circle open shapes, circles, or shapes with curved sides. Explanation: 'Shapes are named by sides and corners; color and size don't change that.' Proficient: all shapes sorted correctly and explanation names sides/corners.

weeks.prep: Household boxes, cans, balls, a cone (party hat or ice-cream cone), paper and crayons for tracing, pattern blocks (or the free Pattern Shapes app), and a hexagon outline.
misconceptions: Calling a cube a square or a sphere a circle: flat shapes are 2-D; solids you can hold are 3-D.
Thinking a cylinder's face is a rectangle: trace the end of a can — it's a circle.
Thinking there's only one way to fill a hexagon: try 2 trapezoids, 6 triangles, 3 rhombuses, or mixed.

days.guide: Hunt for 3-D shapes at home: cube (dice), cylinder (can), cone (party hat), sphere (ball), rectangular prism (cereal box). Your child labels or draws each.

questions.q: A soup can is what solid shape?
questions.a: A cylinder.
A rectangular prism.

days.guide: Trace the flat faces of a box, can, and cube on paper. Name the 2-D shape each makes.

questions.q: Trace the end of a can. What shape?
questions.a: A circle.

questions.q: What shape are the faces of a cube?
questions.a: Squares (6 of them).

days.guide: Your child fills a hexagon with pattern blocks: 2 trapezoids, then 6 triangles, then 1 trapezoid + 3 triangles. Count blocks each time.

questions.q: How many triangles make a hexagon?
How many trapezoids make a hexagon?

days.guide: Build a castle from boxes and cans. Your child names each solid used (cylinder towers, cube blocks, cone roofs).

questions.q: What solid makes a good tower that can roll on its side?
questions.a: A cylinder.

questions.q: Which solid has no flat faces?
questions.a: A sphere.

days.guide: Your child fills a hexagon outline three ways, records each by drawing or tracing, and names 5 solid shapes.

questions.q: Name 3 ways to fill a hexagon.
questions.a: 2 trapezoids; 6 triangles; 3 rhombuses (or 1 trapezoid + 3 triangles; 2 rhombuses + 2 triangles).
Cube, cylinder, cone, sphere, rectangular prism.

weeks.assessment_key: Composition task: any 3 different correct fillings, e.g., (a) 2 trapezoids, (b) 6 triangles, (c) 3 rhombuses, (d) 1 trapezoid + 3 triangles, (e) 2 rhombuses + 2 triangles, (f) 1 trapezoid + 1 rhombus + 1 triangle. Solids: cube, cylinder, cone, sphere, rectangular prism. Proficient: 3 correct fillings recorded and all 5 solids named.

weeks.prep: Paper circles and rectangles to fold, scissors, crayons, a tortilla or sandwich, pictures of shapes cut into equal and unequal parts, and a Unit 10 test (see key).
misconceptions: Calling any 2 pieces 'halves': halves must be the same size.
Thinking more pieces means bigger pieces (fourths are bigger than halves): compare by laying a fourth on top of a half.
Thinking a 'fourth' and a 'quarter' are different: they're two names for the same thing.

days.guide: Fold a paper rectangle and circle in half. Unfold and check if the two parts match by folding again. Color one half.

questions.q: How many halves make a whole?

questions.a: The two parts are equal in size.

days.guide: Fold a rectangle and circle in half and in half again to get 4 equal parts. Label each part 'one fourth' or 'one quarter.'

questions.q: How many fourths make a whole?
What's another name for a fourth?
questions.a: A quarter.

days.guide: Show pictures of shapes cut into parts. Your child sorts into 'equal shares' and 'not equal shares' and explains.

questions.q: A circle is cut into 2 different-sized pieces. Are they halves?
questions.a: No — the pieces must be equal.

questions.q: A rectangle is cut into 4 equal strips. What is each called?
questions.a: A fourth (quarter).

days.guide: Cut a tortilla in halves, then another in fourths. Compare: which piece is bigger, a half or a fourth? Then enjoy the snack.

questions.q: Which is bigger: one half or one fourth of the same tortilla?
questions.a: One half.

questions.q: If you share a sandwich equally with 3 friends (4 people), what does each person get?
questions.a: One fourth.

days.guide: Give the Unit 10 test.

questions.q: How many sides does a trapezoid have?
Draw a line to cut a circle into halves.
questions.a: A line straight through the center.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 10 test (suggested): 1) Triangle: 3 sides, 3 corners 2) Rectangle: 4 sides, 4 square corners 3) Circle the rectangles (including a square) 4) Pattern blocks to make a hexagon: e.g., 2 trapezoids 5) Name the solid: can = cylinder, ball = sphere 6) Shade one half of a rectangle 7) Shade one fourth of a circle 8) Which picture shows equal shares? 9) Which is bigger, a half or a fourth of the same pizza? half 10) How many quarters in a whole? 4. Proficient 9–10.

weeks.prep: Flash cards within 20, base-ten blocks, symbol cards, 6 story problems (see day 3), favorite games (cards, dice), and a 20-item cumulative review.
misconceptions: Forgetting earlier strategies (make ten, doubles) under pressure: post a strategy reminder chart.
Mixing up 10 more and 1 more on place value problems: build with blocks to check.
Reading compare stories as add problems: ask 'Are we finding a total or a difference?'

days.guide: Give the final within-10 fluency check (30 facts in 2 minutes) and practice within 20 with flash cards. Note which strategies your child uses.
Your child builds 5 two-digit numbers, finds 10 more/10 less for each, and compares pairs with >, <, =.
Your child solves 6 mixed story problems and writes an equation for each: add to, take from, compare, three addends.

questions.q: Mia had 12 shells and found 5 more. How many?
Raj has 15 cards; Sam has 9. How many more does Raj have?

days.guide: Play favorite math games from the year (Make Ten Go Fish, War, Race to 100). Ask your child to say each fact aloud.

questions.q: In Go Fish for 10, you hold a 4. What do you ask for?

days.guide: Give the 20-item cumulative review part 1.

weeks.prep: Printed end-of-year assessment part 2 (see key), a math journal or folded paper booklet, a clipboard for the scavenger hunt, and favorite game materials.
misconceptions: Rushing through a long test: break it into short sessions and read aloud.
Forgetting half-hour clock reading: review the hour hand 'between two numbers' before the test.
Confusing nickel and dime values: review the coin chart.

days.guide: Give the end-of-year assessment part 2 over 1–2 sittings, reading every item aloud.

questions.q: Short hand between 3 and 4, long hand on 6. Time?

days.guide: Your child makes a journal page about a favorite thing they learned, with a drawing and an example problem they solved.

questions.q: What was your favorite math topic? Show one example.
questions.a: Answers vary; the example must be correct (e.g., 9 + 4 = 13 by making ten).
Make ten: 9 + 1 = 10, plus 5 = 15.

days.guide: Take a walk outside to find shapes (circles, rectangles), numbers (house numbers, signs), and things to compare by length. Record findings on a clipboard.

questions.q: Find a rectangle outside. How do you know?
questions.a: Example: a door — 4 sides, 4 square corners.

questions.q: Read a house number. How many tens and ones?
questions.a: Answers vary; e.g., 47 = 4 tens 7 ones.

days.guide: Your child teaches a family member a favorite game and explains the math in it ('In Go Fish for 10, you need partners that make 10').

questions.q: What math do you practice in Make Ten Go Fish?

questions.a: Comparing numbers and how many more.

days.guide: Hold a math fair: your child shows projects (survey graph, clock, journals) and explains one thing they learned.

questions.q: Tell how your survey graph works.
questions.a: Each square/bar shows how many people chose that answer; the tallest bar is the most popular.

questions.q: What's one thing you got better at?
questions.a: Answers vary — encourage specific examples.

weeks.assessment_key: End-of-year part 2 (suggested) with answers: 1) 30+40=70 2) 52+7=59 3) 38+5=43 4) 61+20=81 5) 90−40=50 6) Order 3 pictured objects by length (check) 7) A shoe measured with cubes drawn → count shown 8) Clocks: 7:00, 10:30, 2:30 9) 3 dimes 4 pennies = 34¢ 10) Name & value: quarter 25¢, nickel 5¢ 11) Graph (apples 5, pears 2, grapes 4): most = apples, total 11, apples − pears = 3 12) Circle the shape with 3 sides & 3 corners (triangle) 13) Shade one fourth of a square. Proficient: 90% or better; review any weak strand over the summer.

PE.overview: PE 1 is about 30 minutes a day of active play outdoors or in a cleared room. Start every session with a short warm-up, teach one skill with 2-4 simple cues, let your child practice it through a game, and end by asking them to say or show the cues. Praise effort and correct form more than winning or speed; check shoes, water and a clear, safe space before each lesson. Keep the fitness journal from week 14 so your child can compare progress in week 33.

weeks.prep: Hula hoop and 6-8 cones or plastic cups; clear a yard or room space free of furniture and tripping hazards. Choose a clear 'Stop' signal (word or whistle).
misconceptions: Thinking personal space means standing still: you can move arms and legs, you just stay in your own bubble.
Running too fast to stop safely: practice slow-to-fast and stop on the signal with feet planted and hands to self.

days.guide: Warm up with 10 arm circles each way. Lay the hoop down; your child stands in it and reaches high, low, and wide while you say 'Your bubble is your personal space.' Call out body parts to stretch toward the edge without stepping out.

questions.a: The space all around your body that you can reach without moving from your spot (your bubble).

questions.q: Can you move in your personal space?
questions.a: Yes, you can stretch, twist and reach as long as your feet stay in your spot.

days.guide: Set cones around the yard. Have your child walk, then jog, among them without touching cones or people, freezing when you say 'Stop.' Point out that the whole shared area is general space.

questions.a: The open shared area everyone can move in.

questions.q: What do you do when you hear 'Stop'?
questions.a: Freeze right away with feet still and balanced.

days.guide: Play red light/green light. Before playing, model a safe stop: slow down, bend knees, feet apart. Send back anyone who slides or falls past the line to start over.

questions.q: How do you make a safe stop?
questions.a: Slow down, bend your knees, put feet apart and keep your balance.
So you don't bump into people or objects and get hurt.

days.guide: Together write or draw 3 rules: stay in your space, listen for stop, take care of equipment. Play a gentle tag game (two-finger touches only) and stop the game to praise rule-following.

questions.a: Stay in your space / listen for stop / take care of equipment.
Gentle touch with fingers on the back or arm, no pushing.

days.guide: Call 'personal space' and 'general space' and have your child show each. Ask why we warm up first; check that the answer mentions getting muscles and heart ready.

questions.q: Show personal space, then general space.
questions.a: Personal: stays in one spot and reaches; general: moves around the open area safely.

questions.q: Why do we warm up first?
questions.a: To get our muscles warm and heart pumping so we move better and don't get hurt.

weeks.assessment_key: Observation checklist: stops within 2 seconds of the signal with balanced feet; keeps a safe distance from people and cones; shows personal space (stays in one spot reaching high/low/wide) vs. general space (moves in open area). Proficient = all three most of the time; developing = needs reminders; beginning = bumps or does not stop.

weeks.prep: Sidewalk chalk and a jump rope or long string; a paved area or driveway. Preview your child's name letters for Day 3.
misconceptions: Calling a curved path 'zigzag': zigzag has sharp corners; curved is smooth and round like a snake.
Only walking pathways: show that any movement (skip, jog, gallop) can follow any pathway.

days.guide: Draw a straight line, a curvy line, and a zigzag line in chalk. Name each, then have your child walk, skip and jog along each one.

questions.q: What does a zigzag pathway look like?
questions.a: Sharp corners going back and forth, like a lightning bolt.

questions.q: What does a curved pathway look like?
questions.a: Smooth bends, like a snake or a letter S.

days.guide: Lead your child around the yard on a mix of pathways while they copy you; then switch so they lead. Ask them to name the pathway as they go.

questions.q: What pathway did I just use?
questions.a: Answer matches the path you led, e.g., 'straight' for a line with no turns.

questions.q: Make a curved path for me to follow.
questions.a: Leads you in a smooth, rounded path without sharp turns.

days.guide: Have your child walk the letters of their name in big shapes on the grass or pavement. Discuss which letters use straight lines (L, T), curves (C, S) or zigzags (Z, W).

questions.q: Which pathway is in the letter S?
questions.a: Curved.

questions.q: Which pathway is in the letter Z?
questions.a: Zigzag (straight lines with sharp corners).

days.guide: Set up a course with a straight rope line, a curved chalk path and a zigzag of cones. Run it twice, then time a third try for fun.

questions.q: Which part of the course was zigzag?
questions.a: The cones you weaved back and forth through with sharp turns.

days.guide: Call out a pathway and a movement (e.g., 'zigzag gallop'). Check each is shown correctly.

questions.a: Straight, curved and zigzag.

weeks.assessment_key: Pathway demonstration rubric: names and moves on straight (no turns), curved (smooth bends) and zigzag (sharp corners) on command. 3 correct = proficient; 2 = developing; 0-1 = beginning.

weeks.prep: Music player and 2-3 scarves (or plastic grocery bags). Clear space for moving freely.
misconceptions: Confusing level with direction: level is how high or low your body is; direction is which way you move.
Walking backward without looking: teach a quick look over the shoulder and slow speed.

days.guide: Play music; when it pauses, call 'high' (on tiptoes, arms up), 'medium' (standing, bent), or 'low' (close to the ground). Have your child freeze in that level.

questions.a: Body close to the ground: crouching, crawling, or lying.

questions.q: What level is standing on tiptoes with arms up?
questions.a: High level.

days.guide: Toss a scarf high, then catch it as low as possible (crouching). Repeat, catching at medium and high levels.

questions.q: Where did you catch the scarf when it was at a low level?
questions.a: Near the ground, crouched down.

days.guide: Play Simon Says with 'walk forward,' 'walk backward,' 'step sideways.' Remind your child to look over their shoulder when going backward.

questions.q: How do you move backward safely?
questions.a: Go slowly and look over your shoulder.
Toward your side, left or right, with your body facing the front.

days.guide: Model a gallop forward at medium level, then a crab walk backward at low level. Let your child copy and then invent a new combo.

questions.q: A crab walk is at which level?
questions.a: Low level.

questions.q: What direction does a crab walk go in our game?
questions.a: Backward.

days.guide: Have your child build and perform a 4-move sequence with two levels and two directions, saying each as they do it.

questions.q: Tell me the levels and directions in your sequence.
questions.a: Names two levels and two directions that match what they performed.

weeks.assessment_key: Sequence rubric: performs 4 moves using two different levels (high/medium/low) and two different directions (forward/backward/sideways) and can name them. Proficient = 4 correct moves named; developing = mixes up levels or directions once; beginning = needs help to create moves.

weeks.prep: Sturdy table or chairs, broomstick, hula hoop, blanket, beanbag or ball. Build a safe course with soft landing areas.
misconceptions: Mixing up left and right: put a sticker or bracelet on the right hand as a reminder.
Thinking 'through' and 'around' are the same: through goes inside/across the middle; around goes along the outside.

days.guide: Build a course: crawl under a table, step over a broomstick, go through a hoop, walk around a chair. Say each word as your child does it, then have them say it.

questions.q: Did you go over or under the broomstick?
questions.a: Over.

questions.q: Did you go through or around the hoop?
questions.a: Through.

days.guide: Call positions for a beanbag: behind you, in front of you, next to you, on your right, on your left. Your child places it there.

questions.a: Places it at their back.

questions.q: Put it on your left side.
questions.a: Places it beside the left hand side.

days.guide: Face your child as a mirror; raise your right hand and have them mirror. Explain mirrors flip sides: your right is their left. Then practice 'right hand up, left foot out.'

questions.a: Raises the right hand (check sticker/bracelet).

days.guide: Have your child design a new course using 6 position words and draw a simple map. Run it together.

questions.q: Name the 6 position words in your course.
questions.a: Six of: over, under, through, around, next to, behind, in front of, up, down, left, right.

days.guide: Have your child run their course while calling each position word aloud. Use the rubric.

questions.q: What did you do at the chair?
questions.a: Matches their course, e.g., 'went around it.'

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 1 check rubric: completes the course while correctly saying each position word (over, under, through, around, next to, behind/in front). 6/6 words correct = proficient; 4-5 = developing; 3 or fewer = beginning. Also note safe movement and stopping.

weeks.prep: 6 cones, music with a steady beat; a yard or park loop for jogging. Water.
misconceptions: Swinging arms across the body when jogging: arms bent, swinging forward and back like pulling a rope.
Galloping without keeping the same foot in front: the lead foot stays in front the whole time; the back foot chases it.

days.guide: Model jogging with arms bent at 90 degrees swinging front to back. Jog 3 easy laps together; stop if your child is gasping and walk instead.

questions.q: Where do your arms go when you jog?
questions.a: Bent, swinging forward and back by your sides.
A little faster than walking but slow enough to keep going and talk.

days.guide: Gallop like a horse: step forward with the lead foot, bring the back foot up to it, repeat. Switch the lead foot after 10 gallops.

questions.q: In a gallop, which foot stays in front?
questions.a: The lead foot always stays in front.

questions.q: Can you gallop with the other foot leading?
questions.a: Shows the switch with the other foot forward.

days.guide: Set a cone 15 feet away. Gallop to it with one lead, switch leads at the cone, gallop back. Repeat 4 times.

questions.a: You switch your lead foot.

days.guide: Play music; jog for 8 beats, then gallop for 8 beats, switching on your call. Keep it playful.

questions.q: What is the difference between a jog and a gallop?
questions.a: A jog alternates feet one at a time; a gallop keeps one foot leading with a step-together rhythm.

days.guide: Have your child gallop with each lead foot and say the cues. Use the cue check.

questions.a: Lead foot in front, back foot catches up, keep the rhythm.

weeks.assessment_key: Cue check: Jog = bent arms swinging front to back, light steps on balls of feet, eyes forward. Gallop = same lead foot in front, back foot catches up (step-together), arms relaxed; can switch to other lead foot. Proficient = shows both gallop leads and says 2+ cues for each skill.

weeks.prep: Chalk for a hopscotch board and lily pads, beanbag (or small stone). Flat surface.
misconceptions: Using both feet (a jump) instead of one (a hop): a hop takes off and lands on the same one foot.
Landing stiff-legged: bend the knee and land on the ball of the foot softly.

days.guide: Show a hop: take off and land on the same foot, knee bent, arms out. Hop 5 on the right, then 5 on the left.

questions.a: Take off and land on the same one foot.
Bend your knee and land on the ball of your foot.

days.guide: Draw a hopscotch board. Toss the beanbag into square 1, hop over it on one foot in single squares, land with two feet in double squares, then hop back and pick it up.

questions.q: In hopscotch, how do you land in a single square?
questions.a: On one foot.

questions.q: Do you hop in the square with your beanbag?
questions.a: No, you skip over it.

days.guide: Model right-right-left-left hops. Have your child say the pattern aloud while hopping.

questions.a: Left-left.

days.guide: Draw chalk circles as lily pads a short hop apart. Your child hops from pad to pad on one foot, switching feet halfway.

questions.q: Why do your arms go out when you hop?
questions.a: To help you balance.

days.guide: Count hops in a row on each foot without the other foot touching. Record on the checklist.

questions.q: Which foot is easier to hop on?
questions.a: Answers vary; encourage practice on the weaker foot.

weeks.assessment_key: Hop count: record consecutive hops on right and left foot (goal 10 each without the other foot touching). 10/10 both feet = proficient; 5-9 = developing; under 5 = beginning. Note soft landings and arms used for balance.

weeks.prep: 2 cones about 15 feet apart, chalk line, music.
misconceptions: Crossing feet during a slide: the feet come together but never cross.
Turning to face the direction of travel: in a slide, your body faces forward and you move sideways.

days.guide: Model a slide: face forward, step sideways, bring the other foot to it, never cross. Slide cone to cone leading right, then return leading left.

questions.q: Do your feet cross in a slide?
questions.a: No, they come together but don't cross.

questions.q: Which way does your body face in a slide?
questions.a: Forward, while you move sideways.

days.guide: Play slide tag along a chalk line: everyone may only slide sideways. Switch the tagger each round.

questions.q: What is the only way to move in slide tag?
questions.a: Sliding sideways.

days.guide: Practice step-hop slowly: step on right, hop on right, step on left, hop on left. Speed it up until it becomes a skip.

questions.q: What two moves make a skip?
questions.a: A step and a hop, switching feet each time.

days.guide: Play music. Each time it stops, call a new skill (walk, jog, gallop, slide, hop, step-hop).

questions.q: Show me a slide, then a gallop.
questions.a: Slide goes sideways; gallop goes forward with a lead foot.

days.guide: Have your child demonstrate the slide and step-hop, then cheer on a family member trying it.

questions.q: What is something kind you can say to someone learning?
questions.a: Example: 'Nice try! Keep your feet together, you're getting it!'

weeks.assessment_key: Slide demonstration: body faces forward, moves sideways; step-together without crossing feet; leads with both right and left side; brief moment with both feet off the ground. Proficient = all cues on both sides; developing = 2-3 cues; beginning = feet cross or turns body.

weeks.prep: 4 station signs (jog, hop, gallop, slide), cones, timer. Print or write a simple cue checklist for Day 5.
misconceptions: Rushing the skill and losing form: slower with good form is better than fast and sloppy.
Mixing up gallop and slide: gallop moves forward, slide moves sideways.

days.guide: Set 4 stations. Do jog, hop, gallop, slide for 1 minute each, resting 20 seconds between stations.

questions.q: What do you do at the slide station?
questions.a: Move sideways with step-together, feet not crossing.

days.guide: Call animal moves: bunny hop (two-foot hops), horse gallop, crab slide (sideways on all fours). Let your child invent one.

questions.q: Which skill does a horse use?
questions.a: Gallop.

days.guide: Play tag where the tagger calls the movement everyone must use. Switch taggers.

questions.q: If I call 'slide,' how do you move?
questions.a: Sideways with step-together feet.

days.guide: Have a family member gallop while your child watches and gives one cue as feedback.

questions.q: What cue could you give someone galloping?
questions.a: 'Keep the same foot in front' or 'back foot catches up.'

days.guide: Use the cue checklist to check hop, gallop, jog and slide.

questions.a: Bent arms swinging front to back / light steps / eyes forward.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 2 checklist (1 point per cue): Hop - same foot, soft landing, arms for balance. Gallop - lead foot stays front, step-together. Jog - arms bent swinging, light feet. Slide - sideways, feet don't cross, body faces forward. Proficient = at least 2 cues on each of the 4 skills.

weeks.prep: A mat or carpeted rug; soft surface for balances.
misconceptions: Counting the hand as one 'part' when the knee also touches: count every body part touching the floor.
Wobbling because of looking around: fix the eyes on one spot and tighten the tummy.

days.guide: Model balances on 2 feet, 1 foot, 2 hands + 1 foot, then 5 body parts (2 hands, 2 knees, 1 foot). Count touching parts out loud.

questions.q: How many body parts are touching in a balance on hands and knees?
questions.a: Four (2 hands, 2 knees).
Look at one spot, tighten your tummy, arms out.

days.guide: Play music; when it stops, call a number and your child freezes balancing on that many body parts.

questions.q: Show a balance on 3 body parts.
questions.a: Example: 2 feet and 1 hand.

days.guide: Press palms together with a partner and lean to make a shared balance. Try one-foot balances holding hands.

questions.q: How does a partner help you balance?
questions.a: They give support so you can lean or stand on fewer parts.

days.guide: Hold three balances for 5 seconds each while you count.

questions.q: Is it easier to balance on more or fewer body parts?
questions.a: More body parts is easier; a wider base of support is more stable.

days.guide: Have your child show balances on 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 body parts while you check.

questions.q: What is a base of support?
questions.a: The body parts touching the ground that hold you up.

weeks.assessment_key: Balance demonstration: holds a still balance for about 3 seconds on 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 body parts (e.g., 1 foot; 2 feet; 2 feet + 1 hand; 2 hands + 2 feet; 2 hands + 2 knees + 1 foot). Proficient = all five held still.

weeks.prep: Masking tape line, a 2x4 board laid flat on the ground (or a low curb), beanbag. Keep the beam at ground level.
misconceptions: Looking at the feet: eyes on the end of the beam keeps you steadier.
Crossing feet when walking sideways: step out, then bring feet together.

days.guide: Walk forward on a tape line, arms out like airplane wings, eyes on the end. Repeat 4 times.

questions.a: At the end of the line, not your feet.

days.guide: Walk forward on the 2x4 on the ground. Spot by walking beside, but don't hold unless needed.

questions.a: Stretch out to the sides to help balance.

days.guide: Walk sideways along the board: step out, bring feet together, arms out, eyes on the far end.

questions.q: Do your feet cross when walking sideways on the beam?
questions.a: No, step apart then together.

days.guide: Walk the board with a beanbag on the head. Go slowly; restart if it falls.

questions.q: Why go slowly with the beanbag?
questions.a: Slow, smooth steps keep your balance and the beanbag on.

days.guide: Have your child walk forward then sideways the full length. Count step-offs.

questions.q: Name two tips for beam walking.
questions.a: Arms out, eyes forward, slow steps, tight tummy.

weeks.assessment_key: Beam walk check: walks the length forward and sideways without stepping off; arms out; eyes forward; sideways uses step-together without crossing. Proficient = both directions with no step-offs; developing = 1-2 step-offs; beginning = needs a hand.

weeks.prep: Mat, rug, or soft grass. Clear area with no hard objects nearby.
misconceptions: Rolling with the head lifted on the rocking chair: tuck chin to chest to protect the neck.
Log roll with bent body: keep body straight and long like a log, arms overhead.

days.guide: Lie long with arms overhead and roll sideways like a log. Roll across the mat and back.

questions.q: How does a log roll look?
questions.a: Body straight and long, arms over your head, rolling sideways.

days.guide: Tuck knees to chest, hug shins, and roll sideways like an egg.

questions.q: What shape is your body in an egg roll?
questions.a: A small tucked ball.

days.guide: Sit, hug knees, tuck chin, rock back on a rounded back and forward again.

questions.q: Why do you tuck your chin?
questions.a: To protect your head and neck.

days.guide: Practice each roll 5 times. Watch for chin tucks and control.

questions.q: Which roll keeps your body straight?
questions.a: Log roll.

days.guide: Have your child demonstrate two rolls with control.

questions.a: Log roll, egg roll, rocking chair.

weeks.assessment_key: Roll demonstration: performs two of log roll (straight body, arms overhead, rolls sideways in a line), egg roll (knees tucked, holding shins, rolls sideways), rocking chair (rounded back, chin tucked, rocks back and forth). Proficient = two rolls with control and no neck strain.

weeks.prep: Mat; paper and crayons to draw the routine plan.
misconceptions: Rushing transitions: moves should flow smoothly, not with long pauses.
Forgetting the still start/end shape: a routine needs a clear beginning and ending.

days.guide: Help your child choose two rolls and one balance and draw them in order on paper.

questions.q: What three moves are in your routine?
questions.a: Two rolls and one balance that match their plan.

days.guide: Practice moving from one move to the next without stopping long.

questions.a: The way you move from one part to the next.

days.guide: Add a still starting shape and a still ending shape (like arms up in a 'ta-da').

questions.q: Why have a still shape at the beginning and end?
questions.a: To show clearly when the routine starts and ends.

days.guide: Practice 5 times, holding the balance for a 5-count each time.

questions.q: How long do you hold your balance?
questions.a: 5 counts.

days.guide: Have your child perform the routine for family. Score with the rubric.

questions.q: What was the order of your routine?
questions.a: Start shape, moves in planned order, end shape.

weeks.assessment_key: Routine rubric: still beginning shape; two different rolls; one balance held for 5 counts; smooth transitions; still ending shape. 4 = all parts with control; 3 = all parts, one wobble; 2 = missing a part; 1 = needs prompting throughout.

weeks.prep: Stopwatch or phone timer, a toilet paper tube to use as a stethoscope, paper and crayons.
misconceptions: Thinking the heart is on the far left side: it's in the middle of the chest, tilted a little to the left.
Thinking the heart only works during exercise: it beats all the time, just faster when we move.

days.guide: Have your child place a hand in the middle of the chest, a little to the left, and feel the heartbeat. Listen with the paper tube on each other's chests.

questions.a: In the middle of the chest, tilted a little to the left.
Pumps blood all around your body.

days.guide: Feel the heartbeat sitting still, then after 1 minute of jumping jacks. Compare.

questions.q: Did your heart beat faster or slower after jumping jacks?
questions.a: Faster.

days.guide: Play freeze tag for 10 minutes; check heartbeats at the end.

questions.q: What happened to your breathing during tag?
questions.a: It got faster/heavier.

days.guide: Draw a heart and list or draw activities that make it pump (running, swimming, biking, dancing).

questions.q: Name an activity that makes your heart pump fast.
questions.a: Examples: running, jumping rope, dancing, swimming, biking.

days.guide: Ask your child to explain why the heart beats faster when we move.

questions.q: Why does your heart beat faster when you move?
questions.a: Your muscles need more blood and oxygen, so the heart pumps faster.

weeks.assessment_key: Expected explanation: 'When I move, my muscles need more oxygen (air) and energy, so my heart beats faster to pump more blood to them.' Proficient = mentions muscles needing more blood/oxygen; developing = 'because I'm moving' only.

weeks.prep: Monkey bars or a sturdy low bar, mat, and a notebook to start a fitness journal.
misconceptions: Thinking bones move by themselves: muscles pull on bones to move them.
Sagging hips in push-ups: keep a straight line from head to knees.

days.guide: Have your child bend the elbow and feel the biceps tighten. Explain muscles pull bones to make us move.

questions.a: Muscles pull on them.

questions.q: What does your arm muscle do when you bend your elbow?
questions.a: It gets tight and bunches up (contracts).

days.guide: Do bear crawls, crab walks and frog jumps across the yard.

questions.q: Which animal walk uses your arms most?
questions.a: Bear crawl and crab walk use arms a lot (accept either).

days.guide: Teach knee push-ups (straight line head to knees) and curl-ups (knees bent, lift shoulders).

questions.q: What should your back look like in a push-up?
questions.a: Straight like a board, no sagging.

days.guide: Hang from a bar with both hands; spot underneath and count seconds.

questions.a: Hands, arms and shoulders (grip strength).

days.guide: Record push-ups, curl-ups and hang time in the journal.

questions.a: So you can see how you improve later.

weeks.assessment_key: Strength baseline: record number of knee push-ups with good form (straight back, chest near floor), curl-ups (knees bent, shoulders lift), and seconds of hang. No passing score: proficient = completes all three with correct form and records them in the journal for week 33.

weeks.prep: Mat; a kids yoga video (e.g., Cosmic Kids or GoNoodle); a ruler or yardstick and tape.
misconceptions: Bouncing in stretches: hold each stretch still and gently for about 10-15 seconds.
Stretching cold muscles: warm up first, then stretch.

days.guide: Lead a 3-minute warm-up: jog in place and arm circles forward and back.

questions.a: Warm muscles stretch better and are less likely to get hurt.

days.guide: Teach butterfly, toe touch, cat-cow, arm cross and side reach. Hold each 10-15 seconds with no bouncing.

questions.q: Should you bounce when you stretch?
questions.a: No, hold it still and gently.

days.guide: Follow a kids yoga video together.

questions.q: How did your body feel after yoga?
questions.a: Answers vary: calm, stretched, relaxed.

days.guide: After a warm-up, sit with legs straight and reach toward a ruler at the toes; measure and record.

questions.a: Flexibility of the back of your legs and lower back.

days.guide: Have your child lead the family in a warm-up and stretch.

questions.q: What comes first: warm-up or stretch?
questions.a: Warm-up.

weeks.assessment_key: Leadership rubric: leads a 3-minute warm-up (jog in place, arm circles) then at least 3 of the 5 stretches (butterfly, toe touch, cat-cow, arm cross, side reach), holding each still. Proficient = correct order (warm up before stretching), clear instructions, no bouncing.

weeks.prep: Water bottle, timer, a park or safe loop. Fitness journal.
misconceptions: Thinking you should never walk: walk-jog is fine; endurance grows by keeping moving.
Waiting until very thirsty to drink: sip water before, during and after activity.

days.guide: Walk-jog for 8 minutes: jog until tired, walk to recover, jog again.

questions.a: Being able to keep moving for a long time without stopping.

days.guide: Talk about energy foods (fruits, whole grains, vegetables, milk) and why water matters.

questions.a: Your body loses water when you sweat, and water helps you keep going.

questions.q: Name a food that gives good energy.
questions.a: Examples: banana, oatmeal, apple, whole-grain bread.

days.guide: Walk-jog for 10 minutes with water breaks.

questions.a: Usually yes, because it is longer; practice builds endurance.

days.guide: Discuss why sleep helps muscles grow and repair (about 9-12 hours for kids).

questions.q: Why is sleep important for active kids?
questions.a: Sleep lets muscles rest, repair and grow, and gives energy for tomorrow.

days.guide: Record jog time, push-ups and stretch in the journal.

questions.q: What three things help your body have energy?
questions.a: Healthy food, water and sleep.

weeks.assessment_key: Fitness journal entries: jog minutes, push-up count and sit-and-reach distance recorded with date. Proficient = all three recorded and child can say one way to get more energy (healthy food, water, sleep).

weeks.prep: Beanbags (or rolled socks), laundry basket, hula hoop; tape to mark 6 and 8 feet.
misconceptions: Stepping with the same foot as the throwing hand: step with the opposite foot.
Stopping the arm at release: follow through toward the target.

days.guide: Teach cues: swing back, step with the opposite foot, release, follow through. Say them as you model.

questions.q: Which foot do you step with if you toss with your right hand?
questions.a: Left foot (opposite foot).

questions.q: Where does your hand point after the toss?
questions.a: At the target (follow through).

days.guide: Toss beanbags into a basket from 6 feet.

questions.a: Look at the target and follow through toward it.

days.guide: After 3 successful tosses, step back one big step.

questions.q: Do you need to swing harder from farther away?
questions.a: Yes, a bit more swing, but keep the same cues.

days.guide: Toss underhand to a partner's ready hands from 8 feet; step back after every 3 good tosses.

questions.a: Hands up in front, fingers spread, ready to catch.

days.guide: Make 10 tosses at the basket from 8 feet and record how many land in.

questions.a: Swing back, step opposite, release, follow through.

weeks.assessment_key: Toss accuracy: record number of 10 underhand tosses landing in the basket from 8 feet. 6+ = proficient; 3-5 = developing; 0-2 = beginning. Also check form: arm swings back, opposite-foot step, follow-through to target.

weeks.prep: A scarf, a beach ball, and a playground ball.
misconceptions: Trapping the ball against the chest: catch with hands only, fingers spread.
Closing eyes or turning away: watch the ball all the way into the hands.

days.guide: Toss a scarf up and catch it with two hands. Then clap once before catching.

questions.q: What do your eyes do when you catch?
questions.a: Watch the object all the way into your hands.

days.guide: Toss the beach ball gently from 5 feet. Remind 'ready hands.'

questions.a: Hands up and out in front, fingers spread.

days.guide: Bounce the ball once to your child, who catches it after the bounce.

questions.q: If the ball is low, which way do your pinkies point?
questions.a: Pinkies together, fingers down (thumbs together for high balls).

days.guide: Count catches in a row from 6 feet; try 3 times to beat your record.

questions.q: What was your best number in a row?
questions.a: Record the child's number.

days.guide: Do 10 gentle tosses; count catches made with hands only.

questions.q: Should you catch against your chest?
questions.a: No, catch with your hands.

weeks.assessment_key: Catching count: catches out of 10 gentle tosses with hands only. 5+ = proficient (meets goal); 3-4 = developing; 0-2 = beginning. Check: ready hands, eyes on ball, gives with the catch.

weeks.prep: Tennis balls or yarn balls; chalk target on a wall; plastic cups.
misconceptions: Facing the target squarely: turn your side to the target.
Stepping with the same foot as the throwing arm: step with the opposite foot.

days.guide: Teach cues: side to target, arm back, step opposite, throw. Model slowly, then practice without a ball.

questions.q: How do you stand for an overhand throw?
questions.a: With your side (non-throwing shoulder) toward the target.

questions.q: Which foot steps forward when you throw with your right arm?
questions.a: Your left foot.

days.guide: Throw at a chalk target on a wall from 10 feet.

questions.q: Where does your throwing arm finish?
questions.a: Across your body toward the opposite hip.

days.guide: Stack cups and knock them down with overhand throws.

questions.q: Did stepping help your throw go farther?
questions.a: Yes, stepping adds power.

days.guide: Throw and catch with a partner, taking turns with one ball.

questions.q: How do you share the ball fairly?
questions.a: Take turns and throw gently so your partner can catch.

days.guide: Have your child throw 5 times while you check cues.

questions.a: Side to target, arm back, step opposite, throw.

weeks.assessment_key: Overhand cue checklist (5 throws): side to target, arm back (T or L shape), step with opposite foot, throw and follow through across body. Proficient = 3-4 cues on at least 4 of 5 throws.

weeks.prep: Several soft balls, a large ball (beach ball), cones; family members to play.
misconceptions: Throwing too hard in close games: match throw strength to distance and partner.
Hogging the ball: in team games everyone gets a turn.

days.guide: Pass a ball quickly around a circle of family members like a hot potato.

questions.a: So everyone can catch it and the game moves fast.

days.guide: Place a big ball between two lines. Throw small balls at it to push it over the other line.

questions.q: Which throw makes the ball go hardest?
questions.a: Overhand throw with a step.

days.guide: Partner catch: step back after each good catch; step forward after a miss.

questions.q: What happens after a good catch?
questions.a: Both partners take a step back.

days.guide: Throw overhand at a cone, run to get the ball, and hand it to the next player.

questions.q: What is teamwork in a relay?
questions.a: Everyone does their part and helps the team, handing off carefully.

days.guide: Check toss, throw and catch with the cue checklist.

questions.q: What is the difference between underhand and overhand?
questions.a: Underhand swings below the waist; overhand starts with the arm back above the shoulder.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 5 skill check: Underhand toss (swing back, step opposite, follow through); overhand throw (side to target, arm back, step opposite); catch (ready hands, eyes on ball, hands only). Proficient = 2+ cues on each skill.

weeks.prep: Soccer ball (or playground ball), cones for a goal; tape mark at 10 feet.
misconceptions: Kicking with the toes: use the inside of the foot for accuracy.
Plant foot too far from the ball: place it right beside the ball, toes pointing at target.

days.guide: Teach: plant foot beside the ball pointing at the target, swing the kicking leg, contact with the inside of the foot.

questions.q: Where does your plant foot go?
questions.a: Right beside the ball, pointing at the target.

questions.q: Which part of the foot do you kick with for aim?
questions.a: The inside of the foot.

days.guide: Kick into a cone goal from 10 feet.

questions.q: What do you look at when kicking?
questions.a: The ball as you kick it.

days.guide: Kick a stationary ball for distance 3 times; mark the best with a cone.

questions.q: What part of the foot kicks a ball far?
questions.a: The laces (top of the foot).

days.guide: Pass back and forth with a partner 10 feet apart using the inside of the foot; count passes.

questions.q: How do you stop a pass coming to you?
questions.a: Put your foot on or against the ball (trap it).

days.guide: 10 kicks at the target; count goals.

questions.a: Plant foot beside ball, inside of foot, eyes on ball.

weeks.assessment_key: Kick accuracy: goals out of 10 from 10 feet. 6+ = proficient; 3-5 = developing; 0-2 = beginning. Form: plant foot beside ball, inside of foot, eyes on ball.

weeks.prep: Soccer ball, cones.
misconceptions: Kicking a moving ball without stopping it first: trap, then kick, until timing improves.
Kicking the ball far ahead while dribbling: use small, soft touches so it stays close.

days.guide: Roll the ball slowly; your child stops it with the sole or inside of the foot, then kicks.

questions.q: How do you trap a rolling ball?
questions.a: Put the sole or inside of your foot on it to stop it.

days.guide: Roll the ball slowly to your child, who kicks it without stopping it.

questions.q: Where do you put your plant foot for a rolling ball?
questions.a: Beside the ball as it arrives.

days.guide: Dribble around cones with small, soft taps using both feet.

questions.a: Small, gentle taps so the ball stays close.

days.guide: Play 5 minutes of gentle 1-on-1 soccer with cone goals.

questions.a: No pushing, no hands, take turns starting.

days.guide: Roll the ball slowly 5 times; your child kicks toward the cone goal.

questions.a: Moving the ball with small kicks while you walk or run.

weeks.assessment_key: Rolling kick check (5 tries): moves to the ball, plants beside it, kicks with inside of foot toward cone goal. Proficient = 3+ solid contacts toward the goal; developing = 1-2; beginning = misses.

weeks.prep: Balloons, paper plates, paint stirrers or rulers, tape, markers. Supervise balloons (choking hazard if popped).
misconceptions: Swinging wildly: use a flat, firm surface and gentle upward taps.
Watching the paddle instead of the balloon: eyes on the balloon.

days.guide: Keep a balloon in the air with open hands, then one hand, then elbows; count taps.

questions.a: Hitting an object with a body part or tool.

days.guide: Tape a paper plate to a paint stirrer or ruler to make a paddle; decorate it.

questions.q: Why should the paddle face be flat?
questions.a: A flat surface sends the balloon straight.

days.guide: Tap the balloon up with the paddle; count taps.

questions.a: Gently, just enough to send it up.

days.guide: Hit the balloon back and forth with a partner.

questions.a: On the balloon.

days.guide: Count consecutive paddle taps; record best of 3 tries.

questions.q: What was your best number of taps?
questions.a: Record child's count.

weeks.assessment_key: Record the best of 3 tries of consecutive paddle taps. 10+ = proficient; 5-9 = developing; under 5 = beginning. Form: flat paddle, gentle upward taps, eyes on balloon.

weeks.prep: Playground ball or small basketball; chalk lines.
misconceptions: Slapping the ball with a flat palm: push with fingertips.
Bouncing too high: keep the ball about waist high.

days.guide: Bounce and catch with two hands 10 times.

questions.q: How high should the ball bounce?
questions.a: About waist high.

days.guide: Dribble in place with one hand using fingertip pushes.

questions.q: What part of the hand do you dribble with?
questions.a: Fingertips (finger pads), not a slap of the palm.

days.guide: Dribble while walking along a straight chalk line, then a curved line.

questions.q: Where should the ball be as you walk?
questions.a: Out in front and to the side of your dribbling hand.

days.guide: Play dribble tag: everyone dribbles while trying to tag others.

questions.q: Why try to look up while dribbling?
questions.a: To see where you're going and avoid others.

days.guide: Check kick, strike and dribble skills.

questions.a: Push with fingertips / waist high / eyes up.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 6 skill check: Kick - plant foot beside, inside of foot; Strike - flat paddle, controlled taps; Dribble - fingertip push, waist-high, eyes up when possible. Proficient = 2 cues on each of the three skills.

weeks.prep: Long rope (8-12 feet), chalk; two turners (family members).
misconceptions: Landing on flat, stiff feet: land softly on balls of feet with bent knees.
Running in when the rope is at the top: enter when the rope just passed the bottom and is going away.

days.guide: Jump forward with two feet and land softly with knees bent.

questions.a: On the balls of your feet with bent knees.

days.guide: Wiggle a rope on the ground like a snake; your child jumps over it.

questions.q: Do you jump with one foot or two?
questions.a: Two feet together.

days.guide: Two turners swing a long rope; your child stands in the middle and jumps each time it reaches the feet.

questions.a: When the rope comes near your feet.

days.guide: Jump to 'Teddy Bear, Teddy Bear, turn around…' doing the actions.

questions.q: What helps you keep the rhythm?
questions.a: Saying the rhyme and jumping on the beat.

days.guide: Count best long-rope jumps in a row from 3 tries.

questions.a: Record child's count.

weeks.assessment_key: Record the best number of consecutive long-rope jumps out of 3 tries. 10+ = proficient; 5-9 = developing; under 5 = beginning.

weeks.prep: Jump rope sized to child: standing on the middle, handles reach armpits.
misconceptions: Turning with whole arms: turn with wrists close to hips.
Jumping too high or double bouncing: small single jumps once per turn.

days.guide: Size the rope: stand on its middle, handles reach armpits. Turn it over your head and step over it.

questions.q: How do you know the rope is the right size?
questions.a: Standing on the middle, handles reach your armpits.

days.guide: Turn the rope over, let it stop at the toes, jump over. Repeat one at a time.

questions.a: Near your hips, turning with wrists.

days.guide: Try continuous jumps, one small jump per turn; count your best streak.

questions.a: Just a little, enough for the rope to pass.

days.guide: Talk about frustration and pride while learning; practice a calm breath and 'I can try again.'

questions.q: What can you do when you feel frustrated?
questions.a: Take a deep breath, rest, and try again; say 'I'm still learning.'

days.guide: Count consecutive self-turned jumps.

questions.a: Record child's count.

weeks.assessment_key: Record consecutive self-turned jumps. 5+ = proficient for grade 1; 2-4 = developing; 0-1 = beginning. Note effort and good attitude.

weeks.prep: Music with clear beats; GoNoodle video access.
misconceptions: Moving off the beat: clap the beat first, then step to the claps.
Doing a different number of counts per move: count out loud '1-2-3-4-5-6-7-8.'

days.guide: Clap and step side to side to the beat, then march and clap together.

questions.a: The steady pulse in music you can clap or tap to.

days.guide: Learn the Hokey Pokey and the Chicken Dance.

questions.q: In the Hokey Pokey, what do you do with your right foot?
questions.a: Put it in, take it out, put it in, shake it all about.

days.guide: Follow a GoNoodle dance; repeat with bigger, cleaner moves.

questions.a: Clear, strong and on the beat.

days.guide: Create an 8-count dance with 4 different moves (2 counts each).

questions.q: How many counts in your dance?
questions.a: 8 counts.

days.guide: Perform the 8-count dance 4 times to music.

questions.a: Moves done in a set order.

weeks.assessment_key: Dance rubric: 8-count dance with 4 moves (step, clap, turn, jump), performed 4 times in a row on the beat. 4 = on beat all 4 times; 3 = mostly on beat; 2 = moves present but off beat; 1 = needs prompting.

weeks.prep: Music, jump rope, space for a family show.
misconceptions: Thinking a show must be perfect: focus on trying your best and finishing.
Losing count: count out loud or in your head during rehearsal.

days.guide: Build a 16-count dance by joining two 8-counts of favorite moves.

questions.a: Two.

days.guide: Practice jumping rope fast, then slow.

questions.a: Turn the rope faster with wrists and use smaller jumps.

days.guide: Rehearse the dance and a 20-second rope routine together.

questions.a: Practice helps you remember and do it better.

days.guide: Perform for family; end with a bow.

questions.q: What does a performer do at the end?
questions.a: Takes a bow.

days.guide: Reflect on feelings and growth since starting rope and dance.

questions.a: Answers vary, e.g., more rope jumps in a row.

weeks.assessment_key: Show rubric: 16-count dance performed in order; 20-second jump-rope routine (fast and slow jumping); bow at the end. Proficient = completes both parts with few stops and good effort.

weeks.prep: Cones, a playground ball, chalk for a four-square court.
misconceptions: Thinking rules only matter when winning: rules keep games fair and safe for everyone.
Arguing calls: use rock-paper-scissors or a redo.

days.guide: Play Duck Duck Goose; everyone gets a turn to be 'it.'

questions.a: So everyone gets a fair chance to play.

days.guide: Play Simon Says with locomotor and balance commands; let your child lead a round.

questions.q: What do you do if Simon doesn't say it?
questions.a: Don't move.

days.guide: Draw four squares; teach a slow-bounce version: let the ball bounce once in your square, then hit it into another square.

questions.q: How many bounces in your square before you hit it?
questions.a: One.

days.guide: Invent a backyard game with 3 rules and one safety rule; write or draw them.

questions.a: Example: 'Tag with gentle touches only.'

days.guide: Your child teaches and plays their game with family, enforcing rules fairly.

questions.a: It is the same for everyone.

weeks.assessment_key: Rule-following observation: takes turns, follows game rules, uses the safety rule, accepts calls calmly. Proficient = all four during the invented game; developing = 2-3; beginning = 0-1.

weeks.prep: Bath towel, ball, balloons.
misconceptions: Thinking cooperation means doing all the work yourself: partners share the job.
Pulling unevenly on the towel: count '1-2-3, toss!' together.

days.guide: Two people hold a towel and toss a ball up and catch it together.

questions.q: How did you and your partner toss together?
questions.a: Counted together and lifted at the same time.

days.guide: Keep a balloon up with a partner, alternating taps; count your record.

questions.a: So both partners help and it's fair.

days.guide: Wheelbarrow walk 10 feet: partner holds ankles (or knees for easier), then switch.

questions.q: What does the person holding the legs need to do?
questions.a: Go slowly and listen to the walker.

days.guide: Practice encouraging words during a simple game.

questions.a: 'Nice try!' 'You can do it!' 'Great job!'

days.guide: Do a partner challenge (e.g., towel toss 10 in a row).

questions.a: Talking, taking turns, encouraging each other.

weeks.assessment_key: Cooperation check: communicates with partner, takes turns, uses encouraging words, and keeps trying after mistakes. Proficient = all four.

weeks.prep: Bedsheet as a parachute, small soft balls, a sock 'flag' for each team.
misconceptions: Thinking a good sport only matters when you lose: win or lose, be kind.
Pouting or bragging: practice 'good game' and a high five.

days.guide: Hold the sheet's edges; toss balls on it and shake it to make 'popcorn.'

questions.a: Everyone holds and moves the sheet at the same time.

days.guide: Play simplified capture the flag with a sock flag in each half of the yard.

questions.q: What is the goal of capture the flag?
questions.a: Take the other team's flag back to your side without being tagged.

days.guide: End every game with a high five and 'good game' and name one thing the other player did well.

questions.q: What do you say at the end of a game?
questions.a: 'Good game!'

days.guide: Talk about feelings when winning and losing.

questions.q: What can you do if you lose?
questions.a: Take a breath, congratulate the winner, and try again.

days.guide: Self-rate sportsmanship on a 3-face scale; set one goal.

questions.a: Playing fair and being kind whether you win or lose.

weeks.assessment_key: Self-rating: child circles a face (great / OK / needs work) for following rules, taking turns and kind words, and writes or tells one goal. Proficient = honest rating plus a specific goal (e.g., 'say good game even when I lose').

weeks.prep: Chalk, a playground ball (kickball), 3 bases (paper plates), access to a playground.
misconceptions: Freezing incorrectly in freeze tag: stay frozen until a teammate unfreezes you.
Unsafe playground use: go down the slide feet first and one at a time.

days.guide: Play freeze tag, then shadow tag (tag by stepping on someone's shadow).

questions.q: How do you tag in shadow tag?
questions.a: Step on the other person's shadow.

days.guide: Draw a hopscotch board and play, hopping on one foot in single squares.

questions.q: How do you land in a double square?
questions.a: With one foot in each square.

days.guide: Play mini kickball: kick a rolled ball and run 3 bases.

questions.q: Which way do you run the bases?
questions.a: First base, then second, then third, then home (counterclockwise).

days.guide: Visit a playground; practice safe play rules.

questions.q: How do you go down a slide safely?
questions.a: Sitting, feet first, one at a time, after the slide is clear.

days.guide: Your child leads a family game and teaches the rules.

questions.q: What did you need to explain first?
questions.a: The goal and rules of the game.

weeks.assessment_key: Leadership rubric: explains the game's rules clearly, demonstrates, keeps it safe, and plays fairly. Proficient = family can play after the explanation.

weeks.prep: Fitness journal with week 14-16 records, stopwatch, ruler.
misconceptions: Being upset if one number didn't improve: bodies grow at different rates; look at effort and other gains.
Comparing with others: compare only with your own past scores.

days.guide: Record push-ups, curl-ups and hang time.

questions.q: How many push-ups did you do?
questions.a: Record child's count.

days.guide: Walk-jog 10 minutes; record laps.

questions.q: How many laps did you finish?
questions.a: Record child's count.

days.guide: Warm up, then measure sit-and-reach.

questions.a: Warm muscles stretch farther and safely.

days.guide: Compare scores with week 14 records.

questions.a: Based on the journal entries.

days.guide: Set a summer fitness goal and write 2 ways to practice.

questions.q: Give an example of a fitness goal.
