questions.a: Hang 20 seconds; practice by hanging at the park twice a week and doing push-ups.

weeks.assessment_key: Fitness comparison: child lists week 14 vs. now for push-ups, hang time, sit-and-reach and jog laps and says which improved. Proficient = accurate comparison + a goal with 2 practice ideas.

weeks.prep: Balls, cones, a 2x4 board, timer; cue checklist.
misconceptions: Forgetting cues under time pressure: slow down and say cues aloud.
Practicing only favorite skills: rotate through all.

days.guide: Circuit of hop, gallop, slide and skip.

questions.a: Step-hop, alternating feet.

days.guide: Throw overhand and catch from 10 feet, saying cues aloud.

questions.a: Side to target, arm back, step opposite, throw.

days.guide: Kick at a target; dribble around cones.

questions.q: Which part of the foot do you use for an accurate kick?
questions.a: Inside of the foot.

days.guide: Rotate 5 stations (hop, beam, throw, kick, dribble), 3 minutes each.

questions.a: Answers vary.

days.guide: Complete the skill checklist with a parent.

questions.a: Ready hands, watch the ball, catch with hands.

weeks.assessment_key: Skill checklist (cues): Hop - same foot, soft landing. Gallop - lead foot front. Throw - side to target, step opposite. Catch - ready hands, eyes on ball. Kick - plant beside, inside of foot. Dribble - fingertips, waist high. Proficient = 2 cues on 5 of 6 skills.

weeks.prep: Cones, pillowcases, spoons and plastic eggs, baton (paper towel tube), poster paper.
misconceptions: Rushing the egg and spoon: steady, careful walking is faster than dropping.
Running at the handoff: the receiver gets ready and grabs the baton smoothly.

days.guide: Choose 5 field-day events and draw a poster for each.

questions.a: List of 5, e.g., sack race, egg and spoon, relay, beanbag toss, obstacle course.

days.guide: Practice a pillowcase sack race: two-footed jumps.

questions.q: How do you move in a sack race?
questions.a: Jump with both feet together while holding the sack.

days.guide: Walk a 15-foot egg-and-spoon course with a plastic egg.

questions.q: What do you do if the egg falls?
questions.a: Stop, pick it up, and continue from that spot.

days.guide: Practice a hop-gallop-slide relay with a baton handoff.

questions.q: How do you hand off a baton?
questions.a: Place it in your teammate's hand; they grab it and go.

days.guide: Make a schedule with event times; invite family.

questions.a: So everyone knows what happens and when.

weeks.assessment_key: Field day plan: 5 events with a poster for each and a schedule with times and invited guests. Proficient = all 5 events chosen, posters made, schedule complete.

weeks.prep: All field-day equipment, water, sunscreen, shade; prizes/paper for awards.
misconceptions: Thinking only winners matter: field day celebrates effort and encouragement.
Skipping water breaks on hot days: drink often.

days.guide: Run the sack race and locomotor relay; cheer for others.

questions.q: What do you say to cheer someone on?
questions.a: 'Go, go, go!' 'You can do it!'

days.guide: Beanbag toss and family kickball.

questions.q: Which toss cues help in beanbag toss?
questions.a: Swing back, step opposite, follow through.

days.guide: Obstacle course and tug-of-war (pull steadily; no sudden letting go).

questions.q: How do you stay safe in tug-of-war?
questions.a: Hold with both hands, never wrap the rope around you, and don't let go suddenly.

days.guide: Make awards for effort and encouragement.

questions.q: What award would you give and why?
questions.a: Example: 'Best Cheerleader' for encouraging everyone.

days.guide: Share favorite activities and feelings from the year.

questions.q: What was your favorite PE activity this year?
questions.a: Answers vary.

weeks.assessment_key: Participation: tries every event, cheers for others, follows safety rules, shows good sportsmanship. Proficient = all four.

SCI.overview: Each week follows a hands-on investigation: ask a question, predict, test with household materials, record in a science notebook, and explain using evidence. Let your child do the hands-on work while you ask 'What do you notice? How do you know?' Emphasize safety (never look at the sun, never shine lights into eyes, no tasting outdoors) and keep the notebook as the record of learning.

weeks.prep: A magnifying glass, a science notebook (composition book), pencils/crayons, a leaf, rock and shell, a paper bag with 4 household objects (e.g., spoon, cotton ball, key, pinecone), and a jar for 'I wonder' questions.
misconceptions: Mixing up observations and guesses ('the rock is old'): an observation is something you notice with your senses ('the rock is gray and bumpy').
Thinking scientists only work in labs: scientists observe anywhere — backyards, parks, kitchens.
Tasting unknown things on a senses walk: we never taste things outdoors; we use sight, hearing, smell (wafting) and touch.

days.guide: Walk outside for 15 minutes. Stop at 4 spots and ask 'What do you see? hear? smell? feel?' Your child draws or writes one thing per sense in the notebook. Remind them: no tasting outdoors.

questions.q: Which senses did we use on the walk?
questions.a: Sight, hearing, smell, and touch (not taste — we don't taste unknown things outside).

questions.q: Give an observation of something you heard.
questions.a: Example: I heard a bird chirping.

days.guide: Have your child draw the leaf, rock, and shell first without the magnifier, then again with it. Compare: what new details appeared? Label at least two details.

questions.q: What does a magnifying glass do?
questions.a: It makes things look bigger so we can see small details.

questions.q: Name a detail you saw only with the magnifier.
questions.a: Example: tiny veins on the leaf, sparkly bits in the rock, lines on the shell.

days.guide: Your child dictates 5 'I wonder' questions. Sort them: questions we can test ourselves (Does a ball roll farther on carpet or floor?) and questions we look up (How old is the Earth?).

questions.q: Is 'Do plants grow faster with more water?' a can-test or look-up question?
questions.a: Can-test — we could grow plants with different amounts of water.

questions.q: Is 'How far away is the moon?' can-test or look-up?
questions.a: Look-up — we can't measure it ourselves.

days.guide: Put 4 objects in a bag. Your child reaches in, feels one, and describes clues (soft, hard, cold, pointy) before guessing.

questions.q: What clues help you identify a cotton ball by touch?
questions.a: Soft, light, fluffy, squishes.
Touch.

days.guide: Your child explains to a family member how scientists observe and ask questions, using notebook drawings.

questions.a: Observe carefully and ask questions.

questions.q: Why do scientists draw and label?
questions.a: To record exactly what they noticed so they and others can look back later.

weeks.assessment_key: Rubric for notebook entries: 4 = at least 4 dated entries with drawings and 2+ labels each, observations use the senses (color, shape, texture, sound); 3 = entries with 1 label each; 2 = drawings without labels or mostly guesses; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: 'Rosie Revere, Engineer' by Andrea Beaty (library), paper, tape, craft sticks, two books of equal height, a ruler, and a small toy figure.
misconceptions: Thinking engineers only build big things like buildings: engineers design any solution to a problem — even a better spoon.
Building before planning: sketch first, label materials, then build.
Seeing a design that fails as a failure: Rosie learns that failing is how engineers learn what to improve.

days.guide: Read 'Rosie Revere, Engineer.' Talk about what engineers do (design solutions to problems). Your child lists 3 home problems a tool could fix.

questions.q: What happened when Rosie's flying machine crashed?
questions.a: It flew briefly then crashed; her great-great-aunt Rose cheered because Rosie's first try was a success and you only fail when you quit.
A person who designs and builds things to solve problems.

days.guide: Set up two books 20 cm apart as river banks. Your child draws the problem: a toy needs to cross the 'river.'

questions.a: The toy needs a way to cross a 20 cm gap between two books.
The toy can get across without the bridge falling.

days.guide: Your child sketches two bridge designs with labeled materials (paper, sticks, tape).

questions.q: Why sketch more than one design?
questions.a: To compare ideas and choose the best.
What material each part is made of.

days.guide: Your child builds the favorite design.

questions.q: How long must the bridge be?
questions.a: More than 20 cm, so it rests on both books.

questions.q: How can you make paper stronger?
questions.a: Fold it into a beam or accordion shape, or roll it into tubes.

days.guide: Test: can the toy cross? Your child tells what worked and what to change.

questions.q: If the bridge sagged, what could you change?
questions.a: Add folds, more craft sticks, or supports.
To see if the design solves the problem and find what to improve.

weeks.assessment_key: Rubric: 4 = sketch with labeled materials, clearly states the problem (the toy needs to cross a 20 cm gap) and explains how the solution solves it and one improvement; 3 = sketch and problem stated, explanation partial; 2 = sketch without labels or unclear problem; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Aluminum foil (two 15 cm squares per test), about 100 pennies, a tub of water, tape, and a data table (boat, pennies before sinking).
misconceptions: Changing several things at once when improving: change only one feature so you know what made the difference.
Thinking heavier boats always sink: boats float when their shape spreads out and pushes aside lots of water.
Dumping pennies in one spot: place them carefully and evenly, the same way for every test, to keep it fair.

days.guide: Your child shapes one foil square into a flat raft and another into a tall-sided tub, and sketches each.

questions.q: How are the two boats different?
questions.a: One is flat with low/no sides; the other has tall sides.

questions.q: Why use the same size foil for both?
questions.a: So the test is fair — only the shape is different.

days.guide: Float each boat and add pennies one at a time until it sinks. Record counts.

questions.q: Why add one penny at a time?
questions.a: To count exactly how many it holds before sinking.
The number of pennies each boat held.

days.guide: Compare data: which held more and why?

questions.a: A boat with a wide, flat bottom and sides tall enough to keep water out.

questions.q: Why might the flat raft sink sooner?
questions.a: Water spills over the low edges.

days.guide: Your child changes one feature on the weaker boat and retests.

questions.a: So you know which change made the difference.

questions.q: Did it improve? How do you know?
questions.a: Compare the new penny count to the old count.

days.guide: Your child draws the engineering cycle (ask, imagine, plan, create, improve) using the boat as the example.

questions.q: Name the steps of the engineering cycle.
questions.a: Ask, imagine, plan, create, improve.

questions.q: Which step was the penny test?
questions.a: Testing as part of create/improve.

weeks.assessment_key: Data table: two boats with penny counts recorded; proficient includes the redesign count. Cycle drawing: 4 = all 5 steps in order with a boat example for each; 3 = all steps, few examples; 2 = steps missing; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Rubber bands, an empty tissue box, a 30 cm ruler, a pot and wooden spoon, and paper for labeled drawings.
misconceptions: Thinking sound comes from 'nowhere' or only from mouths: all sounds come from something vibrating.
Thinking vibration and sound are unrelated: when vibrating stops, sound stops — hold the ruler still to show this.
Believing louder means faster vibration: louder means bigger vibration; faster vibration makes a higher pitch.

days.guide: Your child hums with fingers on their throat — loud, then soft — and describes the buzzing.

questions.q: What did you feel when you hummed?
questions.a: A buzz — my throat (vocal cords) vibrating.

questions.q: Did loud humming feel different from soft?
questions.a: Yes — loud humming had stronger vibrations.

days.guide: Hold a ruler on a table edge with part hanging off. Twang it at long and short lengths. Record observations.

questions.q: What do you see when the ruler makes sound?
questions.a: It moves back and forth fast — it vibrates.

questions.q: What happens to the sound when the hanging part is shorter?
questions.a: The pitch gets higher because it vibrates faster.

days.guide: Stretch rubber bands over a tissue box. Pluck and watch.

questions.a: The band vibrates and makes a sound.

questions.q: What happens if you touch the band to stop it?
questions.a: The vibration stops and the sound stops.

days.guide: List 10 sounds around the house and what vibrates for each.

questions.q: What vibrates when a dog barks?
questions.a: Its vocal cords.

questions.q: What vibrates when you knock on a door?
questions.a: The door (wood).

days.guide: Your child draws and labels how a sound is made using the word vibrate.

questions.q: Explain how a drum makes sound.
questions.a: Hitting it makes the drum skin vibrate, which makes sound.

questions.q: Can there be sound without vibration?
questions.a: No — sound is made by vibrations.

weeks.assessment_key: Rubric: 4 = drawing of an object (e.g., drum) with labels showing what vibrates and a sentence like 'The drum skin vibrates and makes sound'; 3 = drawing with vibrate label; 2 = drawing without the word vibrate; 1 = no connection to vibration.

weeks.prep: Plastic wrap, a bowl, rubber band, uncooked rice, a pan and spoon, a metal spoon and a glass of water, and a PBS LearningMedia clip on how ears hear.
misconceptions: Thinking sound can't move objects: the rice jumps because sound vibrations shake the plastic.
Thinking our ears 'catch' sound like a net: sound makes the eardrum vibrate, and nerves send signals to the brain.
Changing more than loudness when testing: keep distance and pan the same; only change how hard you bang.

days.guide: Stretch plastic wrap tightly over a bowl, sprinkle rice, bang a pan nearby. Watch the rice.

questions.a: The sound vibrations make the plastic wrap vibrate, which bounces the rice.

questions.q: What happens when the pan sound stops?
questions.a: The rice stops jumping.

days.guide: Strike a metal spoon on a hard surface and touch it to water. Look for ripples.

questions.a: The spoon's vibrations moving the water.

questions.q: What happens if you touch the spoon to your hand first?
questions.a: It stops vibrating, so no ripples or sound.

days.guide: Watch the PBS clip about ears. Model an eardrum with plastic wrap.

questions.q: What part of the ear vibrates when sound enters?
questions.a: The eardrum.

questions.q: Where does the signal go next?
questions.a: To the brain, which tells us what we heard.

days.guide: Plan how to test whether louder sounds make rice jump higher. Keep distance the same; bang soft then loud.

questions.a: Only how loud the sound is.
Distance, pan, bowl, and amount of rice.

days.guide: Your child explains their evidence.

questions.q: What is your evidence that sound makes things vibrate?
questions.a: When I banged the pan, the rice jumped; louder sounds made it jump higher.

questions.q: Predict: what happens to rice if the sound is very soft?
questions.a: It barely moves or doesn't move.

weeks.assessment_key: Plan: proficient lists what changes (loudness), what stays the same (distance, pan, bowl), and what to observe (how high rice jumps). Evidence statement: 'When the pan was louder, the rice jumped higher, so sound makes materials vibrate.' Rubric 4–1 on completeness.

weeks.prep: 4–5 glass jars with different water levels, a metal spoon, rubber bands of different thickness, a tissue box, and picture cards (lion roar, whisper, bird tweet, tuba, siren, mouse squeak).
misconceptions: Mixing pitch and volume: pitch is high/low (like a bird vs. a tuba); volume is loud/soft.
Thinking more water always means higher sound: when you TAP the glass, more water makes a lower pitch.
Thinking a thick band is louder: thicker bands make lower pitch; plucking harder makes louder.

days.guide: Tap jars with different water levels and order from high to low pitch.

questions.q: Which jar makes the highest pitch when tapped?
questions.a: The one with the least water.
The fullest one.

days.guide: Pluck thick and thin bands. Record pitch.

questions.q: Which band makes a lower sound?
questions.a: The thick band.
It vibrates more slowly.

days.guide: Pluck gently and strongly. Compare vibration size.

questions.q: What changes when you pluck hard?
questions.a: The band vibrates in bigger movements and the sound is louder.
No — mostly only loudness changes.

days.guide: Play a short tune (e.g., 'Hot Cross Buns') on the jar xylophone.

questions.q: Which jars play the low notes?
questions.a: The fuller ones.

questions.q: How can you make a note higher?
questions.a: Pour out some water.

days.guide: Sort picture cards by pitch and volume.

questions.q: Is a mouse squeak high or low?
questions.a: High.

questions.q: Is a whisper loud or soft?
questions.a: Soft.

weeks.assessment_key: Sort key: high pitch — bird tweet, mouse squeak, siren (also loud); low pitch — lion roar, tuba. Loud — lion roar, siren, tuba; soft — whisper, mouse squeak, bird tweet. Proficient = all cards sorted correctly on both pitch and volume.

weeks.prep: Paper cups, a sharpened pencil to poke holes, 3 m each of string, yarn, and thin wire, paper clips, and a drum or pot.
misconceptions: Holding the string slack: the string must be pulled tight to carry vibrations.
Thinking sound travels through the cup phone as 'air in a tube': vibrations travel along the string.
Thinking drum codes are random noise: a code needs agreed meanings (3 fast beats = 'come here').

days.guide: Talk about drums, bells, and whistles used long ago to send messages (church bells, ship bells, drum signals, whistles in sports).

questions.q: Why did people use bells and drums?
questions.a: They are loud and carry far, so people far away could hear the message.

questions.q: Name a sound signal used today.
questions.a: Fire alarm, school bell, car horn, referee whistle.

days.guide: Build a cup phone: poke holes in cup bottoms, thread string, tie to paper clips. Pull tight and talk.

questions.q: What must you do with the string?
questions.a: Keep it tight.

questions.q: What happens if the string touches something?
questions.a: The vibrations stop or get weaker.

days.guide: Compare string, yarn, and wire.

questions.a: Usually the tight thin string or wire; fluffy yarn works worst because it soaks up vibrations.

questions.q: How do you make the test fair?
questions.a: Same cups, same length, same words, same voice.

days.guide: Create a 3-beat drum code and test it outside.

questions.a: Example: beat-beat-pause-beat = 'dinner time.'
To know the code ahead of time.

days.guide: Your child explains how vibrations travel in the cup phone.

questions.q: How does the sound get to the other cup?
questions.a: My voice vibrates the cup bottom, the string vibrates, then the other cup vibrates and makes sound.

questions.q: Why doesn't it work with a loose string?
questions.a: A loose string doesn't pass vibrations well.

weeks.assessment_key: Data table: string/yarn/wire with ratings (clear/fuzzy/can't hear). Expected result: tight thin string or wire clearest; yarn weakest. Proficient: table complete with a sentence naming the best material and why.

weeks.prep: A free Mystery Science sound lesson (mysteryscience.com), household materials for instruments (boxes, rubber bands, bottles, rice, paper towel tubes, pots), and the science notebook.
misconceptions: Thinking only the instrument's outside makes the sound: point to the part that actually vibrates (string, skin, air).
Thinking bigger instruments are always louder: loudness depends on how hard you play.
Thinking pitch and loudness can't both change together: you can play a high quiet note or a low loud note.

days.guide: Watch a Mystery Science sound lesson and answer the mystery question.

questions.a: Vibrations.

questions.q: Answer the mystery question in one sentence.
questions.a: Answers vary; must mention vibration.

days.guide: Your child designs and builds an instrument from household materials.

questions.q: What part of your instrument will vibrate?
questions.a: Example: the rubber bands, the rice hitting the bottle, the drum skin.
Pluck, tap, shake, or blow.

days.guide: Compare your instrument with another: louder? higher?

questions.a: The one that makes bigger vibrations.
The one with faster vibrations (shorter, thinner, or tighter parts).

days.guide: Your child plays the instrument and explains what vibrates.

questions.q: How can you make it louder?
questions.a: Pluck or hit it harder.

questions.q: How can you change the pitch?
questions.a: Change length, thickness, or tightness.

days.guide: Give the sound assessment.

questions.a: The strings.

questions.q: Is a tuba high or low?
questions.a: Low.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 2 test (suggested): Draw what vibrates — drum: drum skin; guitar: strings; bell: the metal bell. Questions: 1) What makes sound? vibrations 2) How do you make a drum louder? hit it harder 3) Thin or thick band makes higher pitch? thin 4) Is a whisper loud or soft? soft 5) Which is higher: bird or cow? bird. Proficient 7–8 of 8.

weeks.prep: A shoebox with a small peephole cut in one end and a flap cut in the lid, a small toy, a flashlight, a closet you can darken, and pictures of light sources (sun, lamp, fire, candle) and non-sources (mirror, moon, spoon).
misconceptions: Thinking the moon is a light source: the moon reflects sunlight; it does not make its own light.
Thinking eyes 'send out' light to see: we see when light bounces off objects into our eyes.
Thinking we can see a little in total darkness if we wait long enough: with no light at all, we see nothing.

days.guide: Sort pictures into light sources (make their own light) and non-sources.

questions.q: Is the moon a light source?
questions.a: No — it reflects light from the sun.
Yes — it makes its own light.

days.guide: Look into the closed box through the peephole, then open the flap. Compare.

questions.q: Could you see the toy when the box was closed?
questions.a: No (or barely), because no light got in.

questions.q: What changed when you opened the flap?
questions.a: Light came in, bounced off the toy, and into my eye, so I could see it.

days.guide: Sit in a dark closet; record what you see. Add light gradually (crack the door).

questions.q: What could you see in total darkness?
questions.a: Nothing.

questions.q: What happened as light was added?
questions.a: Shapes then colors became visible.

days.guide: Your child explains why we need light to see, using peep-box observations.

questions.q: Why do we need light to see?
questions.a: Light must bounce off objects and into our eyes.
In the closed box I couldn't see the toy; with light I could.

days.guide: Your child draws what they saw with and without light.

questions.q: What does the 'no light' drawing look like?
questions.a: All dark/black, no toy visible.
The toy, with light coming in through the flap.

weeks.assessment_key: Rubric: 4 = two drawings (dark box: nothing visible; lit box: toy visible) plus explanation 'Light enters, bounces off the toy and goes into my eye'; 3 = drawings and partial explanation; 2 = drawings only; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: A flashlight, plastic wrap, wax paper, cardboard, fabric, foil, tissue paper, and a chart with Predict / Result columns.
misconceptions: Thinking translucent means 'see-through': translucent lets some light through but you can't see clearly through it.
Thinking all fabric is opaque: thin fabric may be translucent — test it.
Thinking colored glass/plastic is opaque: if you can see clearly through it, it's transparent.

days.guide: Your child predicts which materials will let light through.

questions.q: Predict: will light pass through cardboard?
questions.a: No — it's opaque.
Yes — it's transparent.

days.guide: Shine the flashlight through each material onto a wall and record.

questions.a: Let some light through — a dim, fuzzy glow (translucent).
Blocked all light (opaque).

days.guide: Sort materials into transparent, translucent, opaque.

questions.a: Lets almost all light through; you can see clearly through it.
Blocks all light.

days.guide: Find 3 of each kind at home and test each.

questions.a: Window glass, clear water bottle, clear plastic bag.
Wax paper, frosted glass, thin curtain, tissue paper.

days.guide: Your child explains why window glass is transparent and curtains are opaque.

questions.a: So light comes in and we can see outside.

questions.q: Why might bedroom curtains be opaque?
questions.a: To block light so we can sleep.

weeks.assessment_key: Chart key: plastic wrap — transparent; wax paper — translucent; tissue paper — translucent; cardboard — opaque; foil — opaque; fabric — opaque or translucent depending on thickness (accept with test evidence). Proficient = all correct with test results recorded.

weeks.prep: A flashlight, small toys, a ruler, sidewalk chalk, a bedsheet, a lamp, cardboard, and craft sticks.
misconceptions: Thinking a shadow is a reflection or 'copy' of you: a shadow is a dark area where your body blocks light.
Thinking shadows don't change: they change size with distance from the light and direction/length as the sun moves.
Thinking transparent objects make dark shadows: only opaque objects make dark shadows.

days.guide: Make hand-shadow animals with a flashlight. Your child explains that the hand blocks light.

questions.a: My hand blocks the light, so the area behind it is dark.

questions.q: Would a clear plastic bag make a dark shadow?
questions.a: No — it lets light through.

days.guide: Move a toy closer to and farther from the light; measure shadow size.

questions.q: What happens when the toy moves closer to the light?
questions.a: The shadow gets bigger.
The shadow gets smaller.

days.guide: Trace your child's shadow with chalk at 9 a.m. and noon, standing on the same spot.

questions.a: At 9 a.m. — the sun was lower in the sky.

questions.q: Why is it shorter at noon?
questions.a: The sun is high in the sky.

days.guide: Make cardboard puppets on sticks and perform behind a bedsheet lit by a lamp.

questions.a: Behind the puppets, so their shadows fall on the sheet.
It's opaque and blocks light.

days.guide: Your child explains why a shadow forms.

questions.a: An opaque object blocks light, leaving a dark shape behind it.

questions.q: Where is a shadow compared to the light?
questions.a: On the opposite side of the object from the light.

weeks.assessment_key: Record: proficient includes toy shadow measurements (closer = bigger), 9 a.m. vs. noon tracings (morning longer), and the explanation 'An opaque object blocks light.' Rubric 4–1.

weeks.prep: 2 small mirrors, a flashlight, foil (smooth and crumpled), white paper, a target (paper circle), a clean milk carton, tape, and scissors.
misconceptions: Thinking only mirrors reflect: all objects reflect some light; shiny smooth surfaces reflect it clearly.
Thinking light bends around corners on its own: light travels in straight lines; mirrors change its direction.
Looking directly into a flashlight or reflecting sunlight into eyes: never shine light into anyone's eyes.

days.guide: Bounce a flashlight beam off a mirror to hit a target. Safety: never aim at eyes.

questions.q: What happens when light hits a mirror?
questions.a: It bounces off (reflects).

questions.q: How do you change where the light goes?
questions.a: Tilt the mirror.

days.guide: Compare reflection from foil (smooth and crumpled), mirror, and paper.

questions.a: The mirror.
It scatters light in many directions.

days.guide: Build a periscope from a milk carton with two mirrors at angles (help with cutting).

questions.a: Light bounces off the top mirror down to the bottom mirror and into your eye.
Slanted at about 45 degrees, facing each other.

days.guide: Use two mirrors to redirect light around a corner.

questions.q: How many times does the light bounce?
questions.a: Twice — once per mirror.
No, in straight lines between bounces.

days.guide: Your child draws arrows showing light's path.

questions.a: Straight arrows from flashlight to mirror 1, to mirror 2, to target.
Light travels in straight lines.

weeks.assessment_key: Drawing: proficient = straight arrows from the flashlight to each mirror and to the target, with arrows pointing the direction light travels, and the mirrors labeled. Rubric 4–1.

weeks.prep: A flashlight, colored cellophane (red, green), a mirror, a book about lighthouses (e.g., 'Hello Lighthouse' by Sophie Blackall), and a code sheet.
misconceptions: Thinking lighthouses are just decoration: they warn ships about rocks and show where the coast is.
Sending codes too fast: slow, clear blinks are easier to decode.
Thinking colors don't matter: colors can carry meanings (red = stop, green = go).

days.guide: Read about lighthouses.

questions.a: Shines a light to warn ships of rocks and the shore and to help them find their way at night.

questions.q: Why do lighthouses have different flash patterns?
questions.a: So sailors can tell which lighthouse they're seeing.

days.guide: Invent a flashlight code and send messages.

questions.a: Example: 1 blink = yes; 2 blinks = no; 3 = come here.

questions.q: Why must both people know the code?
questions.a: So the message is understood.

days.guide: Use cellophane for colored signals.

questions.a: Stop/danger.
Go/safe.

days.guide: Test the code at dusk across the yard; record decoded messages.

questions.a: Light signals are easier to see in dim light.

questions.q: How do you know your code works?
questions.a: Your partner decodes messages correctly.

days.guide: Give the light assessment and your child explains their signal device.

questions.q: Is wax paper transparent, translucent, or opaque?
questions.a: Translucent.

questions.q: Why can't you see in a dark room?
questions.a: No light bounces off objects into your eyes.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 3 test (suggested): 1) Sort: glass = transparent, wax paper = translucent, cardboard = opaque 2) Draw a lamp, a ball, and its shadow on the far side 3) Explain: you can't see in the dark because there is no light to reflect off things into your eyes 4) Moon a light source? no 5) Mirror reflects light. Signal device explanation: proficient = describes the code and how light carries the message.

weeks.prep: A compass (phone compass works), sidewalk chalk, a fixed spot outside with a landmark (tree, roof, pole), and paper for sky sketches. Safety: teach never to look directly at the sun.
misconceptions: Thinking the sun moves around the Earth: the sun looks like it moves because the Earth spins.
Looking directly at the sun: never — look at landmarks near it or at shadows.
Thinking shadows always point the same way: shadows point away from the sun, so they change direction during the day.

days.guide: Teach sun safety. Stand in the same spot at 9 a.m. and sketch where the sun is relative to a landmark.

questions.q: Why never look at the sun?
questions.a: It can hurt your eyes.

questions.q: Where is the sun in the morning?
questions.a: Low in the eastern sky.

days.guide: Sketch the sun's position at morning, noon, and late afternoon from the same spot, labeling east and west.

questions.q: Where is the sun at noon?
questions.a: Highest in the sky (toward the south in California).

questions.q: Where is it in late afternoon?
questions.a: Lower in the western sky.

days.guide: Your child stands on a chalk X; trace the shadow at 9 a.m., noon, 3 p.m.

questions.a: Around noon.

questions.q: Which way does the morning shadow point?
questions.a: West (away from the sun in the east).

days.guide: Your child describes the pattern in two sentences.

questions.a: The sun rises in the east, is highest at midday, and sets in the west.
They're long in morning and evening and short at midday, pointing away from the sun.

days.guide: Your child predicts and draws where the sun and their shadow will be at noon tomorrow, then checks.

questions.a: Short, pointing north.

questions.q: Was your prediction right? How do you know?
questions.a: Compare with the real shadow tracing.

weeks.assessment_key: Prediction rubric: 4 = drawing shows sun high in the southern sky at noon and a short shadow pointing north, checked against real observation with comments; 3 = mostly correct; 2 = sun or shadow misplaced; 1 = no prediction.

weeks.prep: A paper plate, a pencil, modeling clay, a marker, a clock, a compass, a coin, and a sunny spot that gets sun from 9 a.m. to 3 p.m.
misconceptions: Thinking the shadow moves because the plate turned: keep the plate in the same place; the sun's position changes.
Thinking a sundial works at night or on cloudy days: it needs sunlight to make a shadow.
Thinking the sundial and clock should match exactly: sundial times can be off from clock time (daylight saving time, location).

days.guide: Push a pencil through the plate center, anchor with clay, and point the '12' mark north with a compass.

questions.a: In California, the noon shadow points north.
The pencil blocking sunlight.

days.guide: Every hour from 9 a.m. to 3 p.m., mark the shadow and write the time.

questions.q: Which way does the shadow move during the day?
questions.a: From the west side, around through north, to the east side (clockwise).
Around midday.

days.guide: Predict where tomorrow's 10 a.m. shadow will fall; place a coin; check.

questions.q: Where should you put the coin?
questions.a: On today's 10 a.m. mark.
The sun follows nearly the same path every day.

days.guide: Read time on the sundial and clock at 3 times; record.

questions.a: Daylight saving time and our location can make sundial time differ from clock time.

questions.q: What do you notice about the pattern?
questions.a: The difference stays about the same each time.

days.guide: Your child explains why the shadow moves.

questions.a: Because the sun's position in the sky changes as the Earth spins.

questions.q: Would the sundial work at night?
questions.a: No — there's no sunlight.

weeks.assessment_key: Rubric: 4 = sundial with hourly marks 9–3 labeled, and explanation 'The shadow moves because the sun's position in the sky changes'; 3 = most marks and partial explanation; 2 = few marks; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: A moon journal (calendar page stapled to paper), sandwich cookies and a plastic knife, a paper plate, 'The Moon Book' by Gail Gibbons (library), and 6 moon-phase picture cards.
misconceptions: Thinking the moon changes shape: the moon is always round; we see different amounts of its sunlit side.
Thinking the Earth's shadow causes phases: phases come from how much of the lit half faces us (Earth's shadow causes eclipses, which are rare).
Thinking the moon only comes out at night: it is often visible during the day.

days.guide: Go outside after dinner. Draw the moon's shape and position. Continue nightly for 4 weeks (skip cloudy nights and note them).

questions.q: What shape was the moon tonight?
questions.a: Answers vary — check against a moon calendar.
To see the pattern over time.

days.guide: Read 'The Moon Book' and list 4 moon phases.

questions.a: New moon, crescent, first/last quarter (half), full moon (also gibbous).
Sunlight reflecting off the moon.

days.guide: Scrape frosting from cookies to model new, crescent, half, and full moons; label.

questions.q: What does a new moon look like?
questions.a: Dark — we can't see the lit side.
A completely lit circle.

days.guide: Look for the moon in daytime; record time and shape; discuss why.

questions.q: Why can we see the moon in daytime?
questions.a: It reflects sunlight and is bright enough to see when it's above the horizon during the day.
Not every day at the same time; its rise time changes daily.

days.guide: Order 6 phase cards; compare with the journal.

questions.q: Order: full, new, crescent, half, gibbous.
questions.a: New, crescent, half (first quarter), gibbous, full.
The lit part shrinks (waning).

weeks.assessment_key: Card order (waxing): new moon → waxing crescent → first quarter (half) → waxing gibbous → full moon → waning (gibbous, last quarter, crescent). Proficient = cards in correct order and journal has entries on most clear nights.

weeks.prep: Moon journal, a lamp without a shade, a foam ball on a pencil, a dark room, and NASA Space Place (spaceplace.nasa.gov).
misconceptions: Thinking the pattern is random: it repeats about every 29½ days.
Mixing up waxing and waning: waxing = growing lit part; waning = shrinking.
Thinking clouds cause phases: clouds only hide the moon.

days.guide: Lay out two weeks of drawings; describe whether the lit part is growing or shrinking.

questions.a: The lit part getting bigger each night.
The lit part getting smaller.

days.guide: In a dark room, hold the foam ball at arm's length and turn slowly around the lamp. Watch the lit part change.

questions.q: What does the lamp stand for?
questions.a: The sun.

questions.q: What does your head stand for?
questions.a: The Earth.

days.guide: Explore a NASA Space Place moon activity; add a fact.

questions.a: Example: The moon goes around Earth about once a month; the moon has no air.

questions.q: How long is the moon's cycle?
questions.a: About a month (29½ days).

days.guide: Draw what the moon will look like in 3 nights; check.

questions.q: If the moon is a crescent and growing, what will it look like in 3 nights?
questions.a: A bigger crescent, close to a half moon.
Look at the sky that night and compare.

days.guide: Your child explains the moon pattern repeats about monthly.

questions.q: How often does the pattern repeat?
questions.a: About every month.
My journal shows the moon growing, full, shrinking, and starting again.

weeks.assessment_key: Rubric: 4 = prediction matches the observed moon and explanation says the pattern repeats about every month with journal evidence; 3 = mostly correct; 2 = prediction or explanation incorrect; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: A flashlight, black construction paper, a pushpin, paper cups, a star map showing the Big Dipper (or a free stargazing app), and a clear night. Note: from California in winter evenings, the Big Dipper is low in the northeast/north and rises higher later in the night.
misconceptions: Thinking stars disappear in the daytime: they're still there; sunlight is so bright it hides them.
Thinking stars are tiny: stars are huge suns very far away.
Thinking the Big Dipper is the only constellation: it's one of many patterns (part of the Great Bear).

days.guide: On a clear night, look for 5 minutes and count stars in one window pane's view; record the time.

questions.q: Why look at one window pane?
questions.a: To count a small, fair section.

questions.q: Why see more stars away from city lights?
questions.a: Less light pollution.

days.guide: Shine a flashlight on a wall in a dark room, then in a bright room.

questions.q: Why is the flashlight hard to see in a bright room?
questions.a: The bright light outshines it.

questions.q: How is that like stars in the day?
questions.a: Sunlight is so bright it hides the stars.

days.guide: Poke the Big Dipper pattern (7 stars) into a paper cup's bottom; shine a flashlight through onto the ceiling.

questions.q: How many stars are in the Big Dipper?

questions.a: A dipper or ladle — a bowl with a handle.

days.guide: Search for the Big Dipper in the northern sky; draw it.

questions.a: North.

questions.q: Is it always in the same place in the sky?
questions.a: No — it moves around the North Star during the night and the year.

days.guide: Your child answers: 'Are stars still there during the day?'

questions.q: Are stars there during the day?
questions.a: Yes — sunlight is too bright to see them.
The flashlight was still on in the bright room but hard to see.

weeks.assessment_key: Rubric: 4 = star count recorded with date/time and answer 'Yes, the stars are still there; the sun's light is too bright, like my flashlight in a bright room'; 3 = answer correct, evidence partial; 2 = answer without evidence; 1 = incorrect.

weeks.prep: Science notebook, sun sketches, sundial, moon journal, stapled booklet, and a Mystery Science lesson in the 'Spaceship Earth' or sky unit.
misconceptions: Mixing up daily (sun) and monthly (moon) patterns: the sun pattern repeats every day; the moon's every month.
Thinking stars move like the sun on purpose: Earth's spin makes sun, moon, and stars appear to move.
Leaving out evidence in the book: each page needs a drawing from your data.

days.guide: Your child lists three patterns from their data.

questions.a: The sun rises in the east and sets in the west every day.
The moon's shape changes in a pattern that repeats about every month.

days.guide: Watch a Mystery Science sky lesson; answer the question in a sentence.

questions.q: Why does the sun seem to move across the sky?
questions.a: Because the Earth spins.
Answers vary; must be accurate.

days.guide: Make pages about the sun's daily path and the moon's shapes.

questions.q: What goes on the sun page?
questions.a: Sun rising in the east, high at noon, setting in the west.

questions.q: What goes on the moon page?
questions.a: Drawings of phases in order.

days.guide: Add a page about stars and 'What I predict for tonight.' Share with family.

questions.a: At night when the sky is dark.
Based on the journal; answers vary.

days.guide: Give the sky-pattern assessment.

questions.q: Order the sun: noon, morning, evening.
questions.a: Morning (east), noon (high), evening (west).

questions.q: Why can't we see stars by day?
questions.a: Sunlight is too bright.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 4 test (suggested): 1) Number sun positions: rising east = 1, high at noon = 2, setting west = 3 2) Sequence moon cards: new, crescent, half, gibbous, full 3) Stars aren't seen by day because the sun's light is too bright 4) Shortest shadow: noon 5) The moon's light comes from the sun. Book: proficient = sun, moon, star pages with data drawings.

weeks.prep: Printed sunrise/sunset times (timeanddate.com or a weather site), a paper clock, grid paper. For reference: in much of California, December daylight is about 9½–10 hours and June daylight about 14½–15 hours.
misconceptions: Thinking day and night are always the same length: daylight changes with the seasons.
Counting hours incorrectly from sunrise to sunset: count each hour jump on the clock.
Thinking winter is colder because the sun is farther away: it's mainly because of Earth's tilt — fewer daylight hours and lower sun.

days.guide: Record today's sunrise and sunset; check if it's dark at dinnertime.

questions.q: Is it dark at dinnertime in winter?
questions.a: Usually yes — the sun sets around 5 p.m.
Daylight changes over time.

days.guide: Count daylight hours on a paper clock, hour by hour.

questions.q: If the sun rises at 7 a.m. and sets at 5 p.m., how many hours of daylight?
questions.a: 10 hours.

questions.q: If sunrise is 7 and sunset is 4:45?
questions.a: About 9¾ hours (between 9 and 10).

days.guide: Look up June 21 times; count daylight hours.

questions.q: If June sunrise is 6 a.m. and sunset is 8 p.m., how many hours?
questions.a: 14 hours.

questions.q: Which has more daylight, winter or summer?
questions.a: Summer.

days.guide: Make a 2-bar graph comparing winter and summer daylight.

questions.a: Summer.
About 4–5 hours in California (e.g., 14 − 10 = 4).

days.guide: Your child explains which season has more daylight and how the graph shows it.

questions.a: Summer.

questions.q: How does the graph show it?
questions.a: The summer bar is taller.

weeks.assessment_key: Rubric: 4 = graph with title, labels, accurate bars (e.g., winter about 10 hours, summer about 14–15 hours), and explanation 'Summer has more daylight; its bar is taller'; 3 = minor errors; 2 = inaccurate bars; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: 'Sunshine Makes the Seasons' by Franklyn Branley (library), a globe or ball with a pencil axis, a lamp, monthly sunrise/sunset data, and 8 season cards.
misconceptions: Thinking Earth is closer to the sun in summer: Earth's tilt causes seasons — our half leans toward the sun in summer.
Thinking the tilt changes direction during the year: Earth's axis stays tilted the same way as it travels around the sun.
Thinking every place has seasons at the same time: when it's summer in the northern half, it's winter in the southern half.

days.guide: Read the book; list one daylight fact per season.

questions.a: Earth's tilt as it travels around the sun.

questions.q: Which season has the longest days?
questions.a: Summer.

days.guide: Walk a tilted globe around a lamp, keeping the tilt pointed the same way.

questions.q: When our part leans toward the lamp, what season is it?
questions.a: Summer.
Winter.

days.guide: Make a 4-box chart: daylight, weather, clothing per season.

questions.a: Shortest.
Shorts, T-shirts, hats.

days.guide: Plan outside after-dinner play in December vs. June.

questions.q: Can you play outside after a 6 p.m. dinner in December?
questions.a: Usually not — it's dark.
Yes — it stays light until about 8 p.m.

days.guide: Your child matches 8 cards to seasons.

questions.a: Summer.
Winter (in the northern half of Earth).

weeks.assessment_key: Card match: summer — long days, June/July, swimming; winter — short days, December/January, coats; spring — March/April, days getting longer; fall — September/October, days getting shorter. Proficient: 8/8 and chart filled with accurate daylight info.

weeks.prep: Daylight graph and data, paper plates, brad fastener, crayons, and NASA Space Place (spaceplace.nasa.gov) seasons activity.
misconceptions: Thinking daylight changes suddenly: it changes a little every day.
Thinking the longest day is in July: it's around June 21 (summer solstice).
Thinking spring and fall have the same weather everywhere: their daylight is similar (about 12 hours) but weather varies.

days.guide: Record this week's sunrise/sunset; add to graph; notice growth since winter.

questions.q: Is daylight longer now than in December?
questions.a: Yes — daylight grows from late December to late June.
Answers vary with date — compare with recorded numbers.

days.guide: Complete a NASA Space Place seasons activity and write a sentence.

questions.a: Example: Earth's tilt causes seasons.
Around December 21.

days.guide: Make a seasons wheel showing daylight length and pictures.

questions.q: What do you show for summer?
questions.a: Long days, sun high.
Short days.

days.guide: Your child teaches a family member how daylight changes.

questions.q: How does daylight change from winter to summer?
questions.a: Days get longer.
Days get shorter.

days.guide: Give the daylight assessment.

questions.q: Which season has the shortest days?
questions.a: Winter.

questions.q: Predict: next month (spring), longer or shorter days?
questions.a: Longer.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 5 test (suggested): read a graph showing Dec ≈ 10 h, Mar ≈ 12 h, Jun ≈ 14½ h, Sep ≈ 12 h: 1) longest = June/summer 2) shortest = December/winter 3) March and September about equal 4) predict April: longer than March (about 13 h) 5) Why? Earth's tilt. Proficient 5/5.

weeks.prep: Animal photos (Smithsonian Learning Lab or books), tweezers, a clothespin, a spoon, chopsticks, rice, gummy worms, a cup of water, marbles, and paper plates.
misconceptions: Thinking animal parts are just for looks: each external part has a job that helps the animal survive.
Thinking one beak works best for all food: different shapes suit different foods.
Thinking a turtle can leave its shell: the shell is part of its body.

days.guide: Match photos of claws, beaks, shells, fins, ears to their jobs.

questions.a: Grab, dig, or climb.
Help fish swim and steer.

days.guide: Use tools as 'beaks' to pick up foods; record which works best.

questions.q: Which tool worked best for rice?
questions.a: Tweezers (a thin, pointy beak).
The spoon — like a pelican's pouch or a scooping bill.

days.guide: Compare turtle shell, porcupine quills, armadillo plates; tell how each protects.

questions.a: They're sharp and stick into predators.

questions.q: How does an armadillo protect itself?
questions.a: Hard bony plates; some can roll into a ball.

days.guide: Compare fins, wings, flippers, legs; act out movement.

questions.a: Wings.

questions.q: What helps a sea turtle swim?
questions.a: Flippers.

days.guide: Your child draws an animal with 3 labeled parts and jobs.

questions.a: Webbed feet — swim; bill — eat; feathers/wings — fly and stay warm/dry.
Claws — climb/catch; ears — hear; whiskers — feel.

weeks.assessment_key: Rubric: 4 = animal drawn with 3 accurately labeled external parts and a correct job for each (e.g., eagle: talons grab prey, beak tears food, wings fly); 3 = 2 correct; 2 = labels without jobs; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: A celery stalk with leaves, blue food coloring, cups, a weed or flower to dissect, grass clump, rose stem or cactus photo, and tape.
misconceptions: Thinking plants eat food through roots: roots take in water and nutrients; leaves use sunlight to make food.
Thinking the stem is just a stick: it carries water up and holds the plant up.
Touching thorns or spines carelessly: look closely, but touch gently or not at all.

days.guide: Take apart a weed or flower; tape roots, stem, leaves, flower with labels.

questions.a: Holds the plant in the soil and takes in water.
Use sunlight to make food for the plant.

days.guide: Put celery in blue water; check after 4 hours and next morning.

questions.a: Blue color moved up the stem into the leaves.
The stem carries water up to the leaves.

days.guide: Pull up a weed and grass; compare roots.

questions.q: Why are weeds hard to pull up?
questions.a: Their roots grip the soil.
Grass usually has many thin, spread roots.

days.guide: Observe thorns/spines safely; discuss protection.

questions.a: To protect them from animals eating them.
Protect from animals and help shade the plant.

days.guide: Plant-parts quiz.

questions.a: The stem.
The flower.

weeks.assessment_key: Diagram labels: roots (take in water, hold plant), stem (carries water, holds up), leaves (make food from sunlight), flower (makes seeds). Matching: root–water/anchor; stem–transport/support; leaf–make food; flower–seeds; thorns–protection. Proficient: all correct.

weeks.prep: A Velcro strip, burrs or seed heads (if available), magnifier, and invention picture cards (bike helmet, swim fins, sun hat, tweezers).
misconceptions: Thinking inventions copied nature exactly: people copy an idea or shape, not the animal itself.
Thinking biomimicry is only about animals: plants inspire inventions too (burrs → Velcro).
Matching by looks instead of function: match by what the part does.

days.guide: Compare Velcro and a burr under a magnifier; draw tiny hooks.

questions.q: What do burrs have that Velcro copies?
questions.a: Tiny hooks that stick to loops (like fur or fabric).
George de Mestral, after burrs stuck to his dog's fur.

days.guide: Match inventions to nature parts.

questions.a: Duck's webbed feet.

questions.q: What does a bike helmet copy?
questions.a: A turtle's hard shell.

days.guide: Choose a human problem and draw it.

questions.q: Choose: keep head safe, stay cool, or pick up tiny things.
questions.a: Answers vary.

questions.q: What is your problem in one sentence?
questions.a: Example: I need to stay cool in the sun.

days.guide: List animal or plant parts that solve a similar problem.

questions.q: What in nature stays cool in the sun?
questions.a: Big leaves that shade; elephant's big ears; a desert animal's burrow.

questions.q: What in nature picks up tiny things?
questions.a: A bird's thin beak.

days.guide: Your child explains one biomimicry example in two sentences.

questions.a: Burrs have tiny hooks that stick to fur. Velcro copies these hooks to stick to loops.
Ducks have webbed feet to push water. Swim fins copy that shape to help people swim.

weeks.assessment_key: Rubric: 4 = names a nature part and the invention, and explains how the function is copied, plus a clear problem statement; 3 = correct pair with partial explanation; 2 = pair only; 1 = incorrect.

weeks.prep: Cardboard, tape, foil, sponges, paper plates, an egg carton, and a 4-item checklist (solves the problem? copies a nature part? labeled? sturdy?).
misconceptions: Building without connecting to the nature part: point to which part of the design copies which animal/plant part.
Choosing a design without a reason: explain why the shape will work.
Giving up when it doesn't look perfect: prototypes are first tries.

days.guide: Your child sketches two designs inspired by nature.

questions.a: A hard, curved cover over the egg like a turtle shell.
To compare and choose.

days.guide: Choose one design; list materials; explain why it'll work.

questions.q: What materials could act like a cushion?
questions.a: Sponges, cotton, bubble wrap.

questions.q: Why does a curved shape help?
questions.a: It spreads out force.

days.guide: Build the prototype.

questions.a: A first model to test an idea.

questions.q: What if a part falls off?
questions.a: Fix it with more tape or a stronger connection.

days.guide: Label parts and which nature part each copies.

questions.a: Foil dome = turtle shell; sponge = soft fat/fur cushion.
So others understand the design.

days.guide: Present to family; self-check with the checklist.

questions.a: Answers vary — must name the problem.
Answers vary.

weeks.assessment_key: Rubric: 4 = two sketches, a labeled prototype naming the nature part copied, and explanation of why it works; 3 = labels incomplete; 2 = only one sketch; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Prototypes, raw eggs or water balloons, a ruler/measuring tape, a timer, a tarp or towel for mess, and a data table. Do egg drops outside.
misconceptions: Changing height and design together: test both designs from the same heights.
Running only one trial: run 3 trials to be sure.
Thinking a broken egg means the project failed: data tells what to improve.

days.guide: Run 3 trials with design A (30, 60, 90 cm).

questions.q: Why the same heights for both designs?
questions.a: To keep the test fair.
Whether the egg broke at each height.

days.guide: Build a quick version of design B; same trials.

questions.a: Heights, egg size, landing surface.
Only the design.

days.guide: Make a T-chart of strengths and weaknesses.

questions.q: If A survived all 3 drops and B only 1, which is better?
questions.a: A.
Example: lots of padding.

days.guide: Change one thing on the better design; retest.

questions.a: So you know what made the difference.
Add padding, a parachute, a wider base.

days.guide: Your child explains what they changed, why, and if data improved.

questions.q: Did it improve? How do you know?
questions.a: Compare the new results to the old.
Answers vary.

weeks.assessment_key: Rubric: 4 = complete data table for both designs (3 trials each), T-chart, one change tested, and reflection that cites data; 3 = data and reflection with gaps; 2 = incomplete data; 1 = no data.

weeks.prep: A free Mystery Science lesson (animal or plant parts), drawing paper or a camera, and the science notebook for a field guide.
misconceptions: Labeling parts without their job: each label needs a job.
Confusing 'Guess the animal' clues with color only: give part clues (webbed feet, flat bill).
Thinking inventions can only copy animals: plants count too.

days.guide: Watch a Mystery Science lesson; answer the mystery question.

questions.a: Answers vary; must use the idea that parts help survival.
Roots, stems, leaves, thorns, etc.

days.guide: Find 4 plants/animals outside; draw each with one labeled survival part.

questions.a: Beak — eats seeds/bugs.
Roots — take in water.

days.guide: Play 'Guess the animal from its parts.'

questions.q: Webbed feet and a flat bill?
questions.a: A duck.
A giraffe.

days.guide: Present the field guide; explain one part that could inspire an invention.

questions.a: A woodpecker's beak and skull could inspire a stronger helmet.
Nature already solved similar problems.

days.guide: Give the unit assessment.

questions.a: Swim.
Velcro copies burr hooks.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 6 test (suggested): match parts to jobs — claws: grab/dig; beak: eat; shell: protect; fins: swim; roots: water/anchor; leaves: make food; thorns: protect. Biomimicry: Velcro ← burrs; helmet ← turtle shell; fins ← duck feet. Proficient: 9/10. Field guide: 4 entries with labeled parts.

weeks.prep: 'Are You My Mother?' by P.D. Eastman (library), a PBS LearningMedia emperor penguin clip, behavior picture cards (12), and chart paper.
misconceptions: Thinking all animal babies are cared for the same way: some parents feed and protect for years; some leave eggs alone.
Thinking only mothers care for babies: emperor penguin fathers keep the egg warm.
Thinking baby animals don't need care because they're born knowing everything: many learn from parents.

days.guide: Read 'Are You My Mother?' List what the baby bird needs.

questions.q: What did the baby bird do when he hatched?
questions.a: He went looking for his mother, who had gone to find food.
A kitten, hen, dog, cow, a car, a boat, a plane, and a big digger (Snort).

questions.q: What does the baby bird need from his mother?
questions.a: Food, safety, and a home/nest.

days.guide: Watch the penguin clip; list 3 ways parents keep chicks warm and fed.

questions.q: How does an emperor penguin dad keep the egg warm?
questions.a: He balances it on his feet under a warm flap of skin (brood pouch).
They bring up food from their stomachs into the chick's mouth.

days.guide: Compare how birds, mammals, and some fish care for young.

questions.a: With milk.
Bring food like worms or insects.

days.guide: Read about kangaroo pouches and crocodiles; draw one.

questions.q: Where does a baby kangaroo (joey) live?
questions.a: In its mother's pouch.

questions.q: Why does a crocodile carry babies in her mouth?
questions.a: To move them safely to the water.

days.guide: Your child sorts 12 behavior cards.

questions.a: Feed.

questions.q: Mother cat carries kitten away from danger?
questions.a: Protect.

weeks.assessment_key: Sort key (suggested 12 cards): Feed — bird brings worm, cow nurses calf, penguin feeds chick; Protect — crocodile carries babies in mouth, elephant herd circles calf, kangaroo pouch; Keep warm — penguin dad holds egg on feet, hen sits on chicks, puppies snuggle with mother; Teach — bear shows cub to fish, cat teaches kittens to hunt, duck leads ducklings to water. Proficient 11–12.

weeks.prep: Recordings of baby birds chirping and kittens mewing (PBS or library), 'Make Way for Ducklings' by Robert McCloskey, animal images (bear cubs, chimpanzees).
misconceptions: Thinking babies cry or call for no reason: calls tell parents what they need.
Thinking babies survive alone: many need parents' help and signals.
Thinking learning by copying is only for people: many animals learn by watching parents.

days.guide: Listen to baby bird chirps and kitten mews; tell what each asks for.

questions.q: What do baby birds chirping usually ask for?
questions.a: Food.

questions.q: What might a kitten's mew mean?
questions.a: It's hungry, cold, or lost and wants its mother.

days.guide: Read 'Make Way for Ducklings'; explain why the ducklings stay in line.

questions.q: Why do ducklings follow in a line?
questions.a: To stay close to their mother and be safe.

questions.q: Who helped them cross the street?
questions.a: Michael the policeman and other police.

days.guide: Read about bear cubs and young chimps learning by watching parents.

questions.q: How do bear cubs learn to find food?
questions.a: By watching their mother catch fish or dig for food.

questions.q: How do chimpanzees learn to use tools?
questions.a: By watching adults use sticks to get termites.

days.guide: Interview a parent about how your child signaled needs as a baby; record 3 answers.

questions.q: How did you signal you were hungry as a baby?
questions.a: Cried (answers vary).

questions.q: How is that like a baby bird?
questions.a: Both call out so a parent will feed them.

days.guide: Your child explains one offspring behavior and how it helps survival.

questions.a: Baby birds chirp loudly. This tells parents they're hungry, so they get fed.
Ducklings follow their mother. This keeps them safe from danger.

weeks.assessment_key: Rubric: 4 = names a behavior (calling, following, copying) and explains how it helps the baby survive in 2 clear sentences; 3 = behavior plus partial reason; 2 = behavior only; 1 = incorrect.

weeks.prep: Chart paper, library animal books (e.g., robins, bears, penguins, elephants, ducks, kangaroos), and a stapled 4-page mini-book.
misconceptions: Seeing patterns as one animal's behavior: a pattern repeats across many animals.
Writing mini-book pages with opinions: each page needs a fact.
Thinking all babies stay with parents the same time: it varies by animal.

days.guide: Make a chart: 6 animals, 'what parents do' and 'what babies do.'

questions.a: Build a nest, sit on eggs, bring worms.
Open mouths and chirp to be fed.

days.guide: Circle behaviors that repeat; state a pattern.

questions.a: Many parents feed and protect their babies; many babies call when they need help.

questions.q: Name a behavior shared by many animals.
questions.a: Feeding.

days.guide: Write a 4-page mini-book about one animal family.

questions.a: Robins lay blue eggs in a nest.
One fact and a picture.

days.guide: Read the mini-book aloud; answer questions.

questions.a: To share knowledge and check understanding.
In a complete sentence.

days.guide: Give the unit assessment with a new animal passage.

questions.q: Example passage: Mother elephants protect their calves. Calves hold mothers' tails. Parent behavior?
questions.a: Protecting.
Holding the mother's tail to stay close.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 7 test: read a short passage (e.g., 'Sea lion mothers call to find their pups on the beach. Pups bark back so mom can find them. Mothers feed pups milk.') Parent behaviors: calling, feeding milk. Offspring behaviors: barking back to be found. Proficient: names both correctly with text evidence. Mini-book: 4 accurate facts with pictures.

weeks.prep: Baby/adult animal photo pairs (10), Venn diagram paper, puppy and dog photos, a litter of kittens photo, and family photos.
misconceptions: Thinking babies look exactly like parents: they're similar but not identical.
Thinking all babies look like parents at birth: some change a lot (tadpole → frog, caterpillar → butterfly).
Discussing family looks in hurtful ways: focus on noticing, not judging.

days.guide: Match 10 baby animal photos to parents; name a trait.

questions.q: How did you match the zebra foal?
questions.a: Black-and-white stripes.

questions.q: How did you match a duckling?
questions.a: Bill and webbed feet.

days.guide: Compare a puppy and its parent in a Venn diagram.

questions.a: Same kind of ears, fur color, tail shape.
Size — the puppy is smaller.

days.guide: Look at a kitten litter; list differences.

questions.q: Are all kittens the same color?
questions.a: No — they may have different colors or patterns.
Babies get traits from both parents in different mixes.

days.guide: Compare family photos; find 2 shared traits and 2 differences.

questions.a: Example: same hair color or eye color.
Example: different height.

days.guide: Your child writes an evidence sentence.

questions.a: Young animals are like their parents because they have the same kind of body parts, but not exactly because their size or colors can differ.
The puppy has its mother's floppy ears but different spots.

weeks.assessment_key: Rubric: 4 = Venn diagram with 2+ likenesses and 2+ differences and a sentence using photo evidence; 3 = sentence with partial evidence; 2 = only likenesses or differences; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Bean or sunflower seedlings, a photo of an adult plant of the same kind, a centimeter ruler, 3 flowers of the same type (e.g., roses or dandelions).
misconceptions: Thinking all seedlings of one kind are identical: they vary a little in size and leaf length.
Measuring from the wrong end of the ruler: start at 0.
Thinking seedlings look nothing like adults: leaf shapes match even when size differs.

days.guide: Compare seedlings with an adult plant photo; list matching leaf shapes and size differences.

questions.q: How are seedling and adult alike?
questions.a: Same leaf shape.
The adult is much bigger with more leaves (and flowers/pods).

days.guide: Measure the longest leaf on 5 seedlings in cm; record.

questions.a: At 0, at the leaf's base.

questions.q: Are all leaves the same length?
questions.a: No — they vary.

days.guide: Compare 3 flowers of the same type; note differences.

questions.a: Color shade, petal size or number.

questions.q: Why are they all the same type?
questions.a: They share the same kind of petals, leaves, and shape.

days.guide: Draw and label two seedlings side by side.

questions.a: Same leaf shape.
One is taller.

days.guide: Your child writes an evidence statement.

questions.a: Young plants are like their parents because they have the same leaf shape, but not exactly because their sizes and leaf lengths are different.
My seedlings' leaves measured different lengths.

weeks.assessment_key: Rubric: 4 = statement with measured evidence (e.g., leaf lengths 3, 4, 4, 5, 6 cm) and a likeness (leaf shape); 3 = evidence partial; 2 = no measurements; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Photos of a Chihuahua and a Great Dane, 10 leaves from one tree, paper clips, grid paper, and an assessment picture (e.g., a mother horse and foal).
misconceptions: Thinking different breeds are different kinds of animals: all dogs are one kind.
Thinking leaves on one tree should be identical: variation is normal.
Measuring leaves inconsistently: measure from the base of the leaf to the tip, not including the stem.

days.guide: Compare a Chihuahua and a Great Dane.

questions.a: Same body parts — four legs, fur, tails, bark, dog-shaped bodies.
Size, ear shape, fur.

days.guide: Collect 10 leaves from one tree; measure each with paper clips.

questions.a: Paper clips end to end, starting at the leaf's base.

questions.q: Are all leaves the same length?
questions.a: No.

days.guide: Graph leaf lengths into short, medium, long.

questions.a: Example: short 1–2 clips, medium 3, long 4+.
Answers vary — read from graph.

days.guide: Discuss why leaves on one tree and puppies in one litter aren't the same.

questions.a: They get different mixes of traits from parents.
Each grows a little differently (sunlight, position, and variation).

days.guide: Give the assessment with a parent/offspring picture.

questions.a: Same body shape, mane, hooves.
Foal is smaller with longer legs compared to its body.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 8 test: compare a parent and offspring picture (e.g., horse and foal): proficient names 2 likenesses (same body parts, coat color/pattern, shape) and 2 differences (size, proportions, color). Leaf graph: title, labels, accurate bars, one sentence about variation.

weeks.prep: Cups, string, flashlight, cardboard, tape, foil, and a simple data table (trial, what happened).
misconceptions: Choosing a too-big project: pick something you can build in a day.
Testing once: test 3 times.
Changing many things after a test: change one feature.

days.guide: Your child chooses a challenge.

questions.a: Send a message across the yard with light or sound, or copy an animal part to solve a problem.
Example: I need to send a message to someone across the yard.

days.guide: Sketch two ideas, choose one, build.

questions.a: To compare.

questions.q: Which did you choose and why?
questions.a: Answers vary — needs a reason.

days.guide: Test 3 times; record.

questions.a: What happened each trial.
To make sure results are reliable.

days.guide: Change one feature based on data; test again.

questions.a: Answers vary.
Compare to earlier data.

days.guide: Get feedback: 'one thing that works, one thing to try.'

questions.a: Answers vary.
Answers vary.

weeks.assessment_key: Rubric: 4 = problem stated, 2 sketches, prototype built, 3 recorded trials, one improvement tested with results; 3 = missing one part; 2 = missing two; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Science notebook, the showcase project, poster board, markers, and a year-end review sheet (see key).
misconceptions: Presenting without data: always show test results.
Forgetting key vocabulary: review vibrate, opaque, transparent, reflect, phase, offspring.
Mixing up unit ideas: sort ideas by unit (sound, light, sky, living things).

days.guide: Page through the notebook; flag 3 favorite investigations.

questions.q: What was your favorite investigation and why?
questions.a: Answers vary.

questions.q: What did you learn from it?
questions.a: Answers vary — must be accurate.

days.guide: Make a poster: problem, design sketch, test data, improvement.

questions.a: The problem.
To show whether it worked.

days.guide: Present the project and an investigation to family.

questions.a: Clearly, using data.
In a complete sentence.

days.guide: Your child writes 3 sentences about what they learned.

questions.a: Sound is made by vibrations.
The sun rises in the east and sets in the west.

days.guide: Give the year-end science review.

questions.a: Vibrations.
An opaque object blocking light.

weeks.assessment_key: Year-end review (suggested): 1) Sound is made by vibrations 2) Thin/short/tight = higher pitch 3) We need light to see 4) Glass transparent, wax paper translucent, cardboard opaque 5) Shadow = opaque object blocks light 6) Sun rises east, sets west 7) Moon phases repeat about monthly 8) Stars are present by day but hidden by sunlight 9) Summer has more daylight than winter 10) Roots take in water; leaves make food 11) Velcro copies burrs 12) Young animals are like but not exactly like parents. Proficient 11–12. Presentation: clear problem, data, improvement.

VAPA.overview: VAPA 1 pairs a short visual-art lesson with a short music lesson most weeks (about 30 minutes a day). Show the artwork or play the recording first and ask 'What do you see/hear?', model the technique briefly, then let your child create, and finish by having them name the art or music words they used. Keep all artwork in a dated folder for the portfolio and spring art show (weeks 32-35); praise choices and effort, not 'realism.' Preview famous artworks online (museum websites) and have recordings ready before each week.

weeks.prep: Crayons, large paper, masking tape for floor lines; 'Harold and the Purple Crayon' by Crockett Johnson (library); a recording of Sousa's 'Stars and Stripes Forever'; a ticking clock and a rain-sounds clip.
misconceptions: Thinking a line has to be straight: lines can curve, zigzag, wave, spiral or be dotted.
Clapping the rhythm of the words instead of the steady beat: the beat is even like a heartbeat or clock.

days.guide: Make tape lines on the floor (straight, curvy, zigzag, wavy, dotted, spiral). Walk each one, trace it in the air, then draw each on paper while saying its name.

questions.q: What does a zigzag line look like?
questions.a: It goes back and forth with sharp points, like a lightning bolt.
A line that curls around and around a center, like a snail shell.

days.guide: Read 'Harold and the Purple Crayon'; point out that Harold creates his whole adventure with one line. Your child draws a one-line adventure using at least 4 kinds of lines.

questions.q: What does Harold use to make his adventure?
questions.a: His purple crayon; everything he draws becomes real.

questions.q: Which kinds of lines did you use?
questions.a: Names at least 4 kinds that appear in the drawing.

days.guide: Play 'Stars and Stripes Forever.' Pat knees on the steady beat, then march around the room, one step per beat.

questions.a: An even pulse in music that keeps going, like a heartbeat or clock tick.

questions.q: What kind of music is 'Stars and Stripes Forever'?
questions.a: A march (by John Philip Sousa).

days.guide: Listen to a ticking clock, the march, and rain sounds. After each, your child decides: steady beat or not?

questions.q: Does a ticking clock have a steady beat?
questions.a: Yes.

questions.q: Do rain sounds have a steady beat?
questions.a: No, the drops fall unevenly.

days.guide: Your child shows the line picture and names the lines, then leads a beat game (patting or clapping a steady beat to a song while family copies).

questions.q: Point to and name 4 lines in your picture.
questions.a: Names 4 line types correctly.

weeks.assessment_key: Line picture: labels 4 line types correctly (e.g., straight, curvy, zigzag, spiral, wavy, dotted). Beat check: pats/marches steadily with 'Stars and Stripes Forever' for 16 beats. Proficient = 4 labeled lines + steady beat; developing = 2-3 lines or beat drifts; beginning = 0-1 lines or no steady beat.

weeks.prep: Construction paper, scissors, glue, paint or crayons; image of Kandinsky's 'Squares with Concentric Circles' (search a museum site); a drum or pot and spoon; a ball.
misconceptions: Thinking all shapes are geometric: organic shapes are free-form like leaves and puddles.
Speeding up while chanting: keep patting slowly and evenly.

days.guide: Look at Kandinsky's 'Squares with Concentric Circles.' Count circles and squares and describe the colors.

questions.a: Squares, each with circles inside circles.
Circles inside each other sharing the same center, like a target.

days.guide: Fold paper into 4 squares. In each, draw or paint circles inside circles with different colors.

questions.q: Are circles and squares geometric or organic shapes?
questions.a: Geometric.

days.guide: Chant 'Hickory Dickory Dock' while tapping a steady beat on a drum or pot.

questions.a: Words spoken in rhythm, not sung.

days.guide: Sing 'Bingo' and pass a ball around the circle on each beat.

questions.a: On each beat.

days.guide: Compare your circles art with Kandinsky's and tell one way they are alike.

questions.q: How is your art like Kandinsky's?
questions.a: Example: both use circles inside squares and bright colors.

weeks.assessment_key: Artwork: 4-square grid, each square filled with circles inside circles (concentric) in varied colors. Chant: 'Hickory Dickory Dock' with a steady beat on a drum. Proficient = concentric circles in each square + steady beat throughout.

weeks.prep: Safety scissors, glue stick, pre-drawn shapes or paper to cut; a march recording or GoNoodle.
misconceptions: Carrying scissors open or pointing out: close the blades and hold them pointing down.
Using too much glue: 'dot, dot, not a lot.'

days.guide: Model walking with scissors closed, blades pointing down; cutting with thumb up; gluing with 'dot, dot, not a lot.'

questions.a: Blades closed, pointing down, walking.

questions.q: How much glue do you use?
questions.a: Dot, dot, not a lot.

days.guide: Cut circles, squares, triangles and rectangles and glue them into an animal.

questions.q: What shape did you use for the body?
questions.a: Names the shape used, e.g., 'a big circle.'

days.guide: Play a march; do pats, claps, taps and stomps, changing every 8 beats.

questions.q: How many beats before we change?
questions.a: 8 beats.

days.guide: Clap 4-beat patterns; your child echoes them exactly.

questions.a: Claps three times, then a silent beat.

days.guide: Your child presents the animal and names the shapes.

questions.q: Name a geometric shape in your animal.
questions.a: Circle, square, triangle or rectangle.

weeks.assessment_key: Shape animal: uses circles, squares, triangles and rectangles glued neatly to make an animal; child names the shapes. Tool observation: carries scissors closed and pointing down, cuts away from body, small glue dots. Proficient = all 4 shapes and safe tool use.

weeks.prep: Paper, black marker or black tape, red/blue/yellow crayons; image of Mondrian's 'Composition with Red, Blue and Yellow'; empty bottle and rice (tape the lid shut).
misconceptions: Thinking Mondrian's art is 'easy': he planned lines and color balance carefully.
Shaking the shaker continuously: shake once per beat.

days.guide: Look at Mondrian's 'Composition with Red, Blue and Yellow.' Find straight black lines and rectangles.

questions.q: What kinds of lines did Mondrian use?
questions.a: Straight, black, vertical and horizontal lines.
Red, blue and yellow plus white and black.

days.guide: Draw straight black lines with marker or tape; color some rectangles red, blue and yellow.

questions.q: What shapes are made by the lines?
questions.a: Rectangles and squares.

days.guide: Make a rice shaker; tape the lid. Play it on the beat to 'This Old Man.'

questions.a: Once on each beat.

days.guide: Sing while playing the shaker on the beat.

questions.q: Did the beat stay steady while singing?
questions.a: Yes, even shakes throughout.

days.guide: Set out unit art as a mini gallery; perform the shaker song.

questions.q: Which line or shape do you like best and why?
questions.a: Any answer naming a line or shape with a reason.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 1 portfolio: line picture, circle art, shape animal, Mondrian design (straight black lines + red/blue/yellow rectangles). Beat performance: plays shaker on the beat while singing 'This Old Man.' Proficient = all 4 pieces + steady beat; child names a favorite line or shape.

weeks.prep: Red, yellow and blue tempera, paper plates, brushes, water cup; 'Mouse Paint' by Ellen Stoll Walsh (library).
misconceptions: Thinking green is a primary color: primary colors are only red, yellow and blue.
Confusing 'long' with 'loud': long means the sound lasts longer, not louder.

days.guide: Read 'Mouse Paint' and name the three paint colors the mice find.

questions.q: What colors do the mice find?
questions.a: Red, yellow and blue.
Red, yellow and blue: colors you can't make by mixing others.

days.guide: Mix red+yellow, yellow+blue, blue+red on a plate and paint each new color.

questions.a: Orange.
Green.
Purple (violet).

days.guide: Sing a song; use long arm sweeps for long sounds (ta-a) and quick taps for short sounds (ti-ti).

questions.q: Is 'mooo' a long or short sound?
questions.a: Long.

days.guide: Listen to a song; draw long lines for long sounds and dots for short sounds.

questions.q: How do you show a short sound?
questions.a: With a dot.

days.guide: Explain the color chart and perform a long-short pattern (long, short-short, long).

questions.a: Mixed blue and red.

weeks.assessment_key: Color mixing chart: red + yellow = orange; yellow + blue = green; blue + red = purple (violet). Proficient = all three mixes correct and labeled; developing = 2; beginning = 0-1.

weeks.prep: Paint, paper plate divided into 6, images of Van Gogh's 'Sunflowers' and another sunflower painting; rhythm cards with ta (quarter note) and ti-ti (two eighth notes).
misconceptions: Thinking ti-ti is two beats: ti-ti is two quick sounds in ONE beat.
Placing colors randomly on the wheel: each secondary sits between the two primaries that make it.

days.guide: Paint red, yellow, blue in every other section; mix to paint orange between red and yellow, green between yellow and blue, purple between blue and red.

questions.q: What goes between red and yellow?
questions.a: Orange.
Orange, green and purple; made by mixing two primary colors.
